phase1.phaseName: Phase 1: Connecting (to a whole new world, primarily through one of its members) — The First 100 Hours, "Special Play in the Here-and-Now" (by Greg and Angela Thomson, 2016). Split into Phase 1A: Games for Listening and Responding Nonverbally (Meeting Plans 1–15, 30–40 hours) and Phase 1B: More Listening Games plus Constrained Two-Way Interaction Games (Meeting Plans 16–40, 50–60+ hours).
phase1.summary:
Phase 1 "Connecting" is the first 100 hours of a recommended 1,500 hours of "special growth participation." The learner (called a Growing Participator, GP) is pictured as standing outside a "wall of noise" — the host people's speech, which is meaningless sound to the outsider. A host person, the "nurturer," creates a space inside that wall by (1) talking to the GPs in ways they can understand and (2) helping GPs express themselves in ways host people can understand. The phase is built entirely around "here-and-now games": play with visible objects, pictures, and performable actions, conducted 100% in the host language by the nurturer (no translation, no other language spoken during games, no writing). The "magic moment" comes in the very first minutes: the nurturer holds up dolls saying "This is a man. This is a woman. Where is the woman?" and the GP points correctly — the first baby step inside the wall of noise.

Phase 1A (Meetings 1–15, ~300+ words) consists purely of listening games: GPs never speak during games; they respond by pointing, acting, arranging objects, or gesturing yes/no. The workhorse format is the "Rough-and-Ready Dozen" (also appearing once as "Dirty Dozens"): start with exactly two items, add one new item at a time, the nurturer asks "Where is the X?" in random order (asking the newest and weakest words most often), GPs respond by pointing or doing. The companion format LISTEN & DO is Total Physical Response: commands (stand, sit, run, "put the duck into the pitcher," "kill the fly with the hammer") that GPs physically carry out. Every game ends with a 1–2 minute audio recording of the final round plus a "Numbered Talking Picture Dictionary" recording; at home GPs "re-live" the day by replaying recordings while pointing at objects or cue cards and physically performing actions. The governing "Iceberg Principle" says: have strong, attentive first encounters with words, then keep re-encountering them in new contexts; do NOT try to master words for recall and speech — being able to point/act correctly is success. The refrain for discouraged learners is "It's in your iceberg."

Phase 1B (Meetings 16–40, adding 600+ words toward ~1,000–1,200 understood) keeps daily listening games for new vocabulary but adds constrained talking games that move the first ~300 words "up the iceberg" from comprehension into speech: the pivotal "Ladder of Success" game, information-gap games behind physical barriers (Sixteen Pictures, drawing dictation, scene duplication), role plays (marketplace, buying/selling with bargaining), structured-input games that strip out pronouns to force attention to word forms, daily 10-minute sound-discrimination work (minimal pairs, sorting cue cards into sound columns), and "form-focused" grammar games tailored to the host language. The nurturer corrects by "recasting" (naturally restating the GP's faulty utterance correctly) rather than overt correction, and talking is framed as a cooperative team effort with the nurturer's assistance, never individual performance. By the end of Meeting 40 the group celebrates and moves to Phase 2 (Emerging).
goals: Connect to the host world through a living relationship with one of its members (the nurturer) — Meeting 1's main accomplishment is launching that personal relationship, creating a shared 'little world' inside the host world
Get inside the 'wall of noise': come to understand the nurturer's speech about the visible, touchable here-and-now
Build an auditory comprehension vocabulary of 800–1,000+ words (300+ in Phase 1A, +600 in Phase 1B; ~1,000–1,200 by end), prioritizing understanding far ahead of speaking
In Phase 1B, move most of the first 300 words from understanding into actual speech through constrained two-way talking games
Learn to hear host speech sounds accurately through the ears (never through spelling), including discriminating minimal pairs
Acquire 'power tools' — survival expressions like 'What is this?', 'Please repeat', 'Speak more slowly', 'What does X mean?' — needed to fuel further learning in Phase 2

Gain initial awareness (not mastery) of the grammar essential to here-and-now communication: possessives, pronouns, plurals, locations, to/from, negation, questions, if/then, before/after/while, relative clauses
Begin reducing the 'foreign accent' in hearing, in conceptual understanding, and in expression — understanding that concepts like 'man', 'woman', 'dog' will keep becoming more host-like for years
Establish habits that sustain all later phases: recording, re-living recordings at home, the picture dictionary, cue cards, and the iceberg mindset
keyPrinciples: Comprehension before production: Phase 1A is 100% listening; GPs respond only nonverbally (point, act, arrange, nod). Talking begins only at ~300 words, and even then new words are first met in listening games and only later spoken

No translation, no other language: the nurturer speaks ONLY the host language during games; no one but the nurturer talks; even error correction happens naturally in host speech ('No, that's not the cow. That's the horse. Where's the cow?'). Sole exception: formulaic Lexicarry expressions may be identified by approximate translation
Here-and-now communication: everything talked about can be seen, touched, or acted out in the room at the moment of speaking
The Iceberg Principle: pay strong attention at first encounter, then re-encounter in new contexts; don't try to master words. 'I can't remember that word' → 'It's in your iceberg'

Start with two, add one at a time: never start with one or three items; never add two new items at once; never drill repetition — say a new word at most twice, then immediately return to random questioning

Random order, weighted to the new and the weak: the nurturer asks about the newest word and difficult words more often than others; both items and the individual responders are randomized (command first, pause, then name the responder)
Rough-and-ready, gist over detail: if you can point/do correctly you 'have it'; ignore word-form changes and function words for now — details come later
No writing during Phase 1; pronunciation and listening develop only through the ears, never from spelling (the ship/sheep experiment shows spelling doesn't improve hearing)
Play, not study: stay connected to the nurturer as a person; have fun — laughing is good; the nurturer is a playmate, not a teacher

Relationship is the point: words are experienced as interpersonal events with the nurturer (encounter → experience → strengthen → re-live → refresh → re-encounter leads to familiarity), not as items of 'a language'

Recasting over correction: in talking games the nurturer repeats the GP's faulty sentence correctly ('I hungry' → 'Yes, you ARE hungry, I am hungry too') — proven more effective and less stressful than direct correction
Talking is cooperative, not performance: GPs should attempt what is HARD, accept help from the nurturer mid-sentence, and help each other; the group is a team, not competitors
Struggler protocol: if one GP is overloaded, temporarily drop back to just two items and rebuild — applies across all games
New material in listening at least one meeting before it appears in talking games (relaxed late in 1B as an experiment)
Special-growth participation is 'supercharged': a few hours with the nurturer outproduce weeks of everyday-life exposure at this stage; lifestyle participation feeds scenarios back into sessions

activities.name: Name Game (orientation / appendix)
activities.description: At an initial social event, the nurturer gives each GP a local host-world name (chosen by sound similarity, meaning of their name, personality, or just common local names). Then a Rough-and-Ready-Dozen-style game: two named GPs step forward; nurturer tells a third GP 'This is Chanchap. This is Simap. Where is Simap?' — GP points at the person. Questions repeat in random order, adding one name at a time, with a pause after each question before indicating who must answer, until everyone readily recognizes all the new names. The nurturer uses these names for the rest of the program.
activities.materials: Just the group members; optionally a host person to help pick names. Photos for 'Photos of Us in Action' are also taken at this event.
activities.timing: Before Meeting 1, at the get-acquainted party or orientation meeting

activities.name: Rough-and-Ready Dozen (core format; once called 'Dirty Dozens')
activities.description: THE core listening-game engine used to introduce nearly all vocabulary. Mechanics: (1) Lay out exactly TWO items; say 'This is an apple. This is an orange. Where is the orange? Where is the apple?' (2) GPs respond by pointing (or doing). (3) Add ONE new item: say it once, at most twice ('This is a pear'), then immediately resume random 'Where is…?' questions mixing all items. (4) Ask the newest word and any difficult words more often. (5) First address the whole group a few times, then individuals — give the question first, pause so everyone thinks, THEN say one GP's name. (6) Use real sentences ('This is a…', 'Where is the…', 'Jump!'), never isolated word lists. (7) On errors, respond naturally in host language: 'No, that's not the cow, that's the horse. Where's the cow?' (8) If a GP is stuck, others may help if wanted; or remove items down to two and rebuild. (9) Keep adding one at a time until all GPs understand every planned item (~a dozen). (10) Then record a ~1-minute sample including all items in random order, and record the numbered Talking Picture Dictionary entries. Don'ts: no point-and-listen repetition drills, no GP talking, no writing, no trying to master words.
activities.materials: Any set of ~12 related objects/pictures: toys, real items, cue cards; recording device; Graphics Packet pages
activities.timing: Multiple times in every meeting throughout Phase 1; each set takes roughly 15–30 minutes

activities.name: The Us Game (Meeting 1, Game 1A) + Us and Our Animal Friends (1B)
activities.description: First-ever game. Nurturer lays down a man doll and woman doll: 'This is a man. This is a woman. Where is the woman?' GPs point — the 'magic moment.' One at a time adds: I (pointing to herself — 'Where am I?' GPs point at nurturer), boy, you ('Where are you?' GP points at self), girl, baby, old man, old woman, he, she, we, they, people, person, child — all mixed randomly. Then the same technique with toy animals (cat, dog, goat, bird, fish, frog, fly, spider, cow, mouse, horse), ending with the generic words 'animal' vs 'people'.
activities.materials: Dolls (old man, old woman, man, woman, boy, girl, baby), toy animals, real people in the room; recording device; start of the 'Bag of Stuff' (a bag/box where all used objects accumulate all phase)
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 1 (Day 1), first hour

activities.name: US in Action (TPR / LISTEN & DO command game)
activities.description: Total Physical Response. Nurturer says 'Stand' while standing herself (demonstrating only the first time); GPs stand. Then 'Sit.' Then random sequences: 'Stand, Sit, Sit, Stand…' with everyone responding. Then individual mode: command first ('Stand.'), pause, then a name ('Rasheed.') — only Rasheed stands. Add one action at a time (walk, run, lie down…). GPs must FULLY act: really run around the room, really lie down, not mime in place. If told to sit when already sitting, re-make the sitting motion. This LISTEN & DO format recurs constantly: with objects ('Take the goat. Give me the pencil'), locations ('Walk to the door; stand beside the blackboard; sit on the floor'), and later complex chains.
activities.materials: A large area to move in; action pictures from Graphics Packet (used as nurturer reminders only — never as substitutes for real action); cue-card envelope of actions
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 1 onward; action vocabulary needs more reinforcement than nouns, so repeated often

activities.name: Photos of US in Action (recurring, evolving)
activities.description: Photos are taken of each GP and the nurturer separately performing actions (walking, running; later eating, drinking, pouring, cutting, washing…). Game: nurturer asks 'In which photo am I walking? In which photo are you running?' — GP must decode BOTH the action word AND the person/pronoun (and its word form) to point at the right photo. Evolves across meetings: MP2 adds photos of nurturer+GP together ('In which picture are WE walking?'); MP4: for 'we' the GP points at TWO photos (nurturer jumping + self jumping); MP3 adds he/she using photos of other group members; MP9 Game 3b: photograph each GP doing 7 actions (eat, drink, pour, cut with knife, cut with scissors, point, wash), printed one page per action; MP10+: full pronoun range; MP12: 'Make it true' variant — nurturer says 'I am sleeping' and GP pairs the nurturer's photo with the line-drawing cue card for sleeping; Phase 1B: GPs themselves describe the photos ('In this photo we are running') and ask each other 'In which photo is she reading?'
activities.materials: Camera/phone; printed photo sheets (multiple draft-quality photos per page, cut apart with scissors); action cue cards
activities.timing: Introduced Meeting 1, recurs in MPs 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 21, 22, 32

activities.name: Cartoon Bubbles / Lexicarry Game (recurring every meeting)
activities.description: Teaches formulaic social expressions using pictures with empty speech bubbles (from Patrick Moran's Lexicarry book or the homemade graphics packet). Mechanics: first, puppets/dolls ACT OUT the situation (two puppets greet and part; one gives a gift, the other thanks). Then bubble pictures are shown and the nurturer asks Rough-and-Ready style: 'Who is saying Hello? Who is saying Goodbye? Who is saying Thank you? Who is saying You're welcome?' randomly repeated. ~5-6 expressions per day, understood as wholes (not analyzed into parts). Because these are formulas, approximate translations MAY be used to identify intended meaning (unique exception to no-translation). The same picture can carry different expressions on different days. Progression over the phase: greetings/farewells/thanks → sneezing, asking time, interrupting → apologies, door-answering, beggars → offering/refusing food, offering help → restaurant, comforting → gift-giving, doctor/pain, warnings → introductions, restroom, compliments → condolences, joining a table, bad taste → phone calls, prices, directions → delight, displeasure, new baby → pain, fear, refusing company, asking for change → seats, smoking, attention, birthdays → toasts, clarification → encouragement, car accidents, reassurance → affection, guessing, anger. Late-phase twists: nurturer explains WHY people say things (MP30); narrates whole strips as little stories (MP34); GPs RETELL the stories and act strips out as role plays at their own level with nurturer assistance (MP35+); indirect discourse 'Who is saying THAT he is sorry?' (MP33).
activities.materials: Lexicarry book (Pro Lingua) and/or homemade Bubble Pictures from graphics packet; puppets, dolls or stuffed animals
activities.timing: A segment of nearly every meeting, MP1 through MP40

activities.name: Two kinds of sound recordings + evening 're-living' routine
activities.description: (1) Recorded game samples: as the last item of each game is added, record ~1–2 minutes of the final round containing ALL new items in random order. (2) The Numbered Talking Picture Dictionary recording (see separate entry). At home each evening, the GP RE-LIVES the day: plays each game sample and physically responds — pointing at the actual objects (or cue cards as substitutes) and genuinely performing actions ('Run!' on the recording → actually get up and run). Repeat until familiar. If a word can't be recalled, look it up in the numbered picture dictionary to 'refresh' it — but don't memorize or mimic the dictionary. The conceptual chain taught: Encountering → Experiencing → Strengthening → Re-experiencing/Re-living → Refreshing → Re-encountering in new contexts = familiarity.
activities.materials: Recording device; the day's objects or cue cards at home; picture dictionary binder
activities.timing: Recording: end of every game. Re-living: every evening at home throughout the phase

activities.name: Numbered Talking Picture Dictionary
activities.description: A cumulative audio-visual dictionary. After each game, the new words' pictures (from the graphics packet, plus quick hand-drawn additions) are numbered sequentially continuing from the previous total, placed in a binder, and recorded in order: 'One. This is an old man. Old man. Two. This is an old woman. Old woman…'. If a game added 15 words, the next game starts numbering at 16. By the end of Phase 1 it contains 800+ numbered pictures with matching recordings. Used only as a lookup/refresh tool when a word in a game sample can't be recalled — never for memorization.
activities.materials: Two printed copies of graphics packet dictionary pages (one for binder, one to cut into cue cards); binder; recording device
activities.timing: Updated at the end of every game or at least by end of each day

activities.name: Cue Cards system
activities.description: The second copy of every picture-dictionary page is cut into individual cards ('cue cards') — one per word/concept (objects, actions, locations, feelings, pronouns, expressions). Three uses: (1) at-home substitutes for objects when re-living recordings; (2) nurturer's memory aid so games include ALL learned words instead of falling into a rut of favorites; (3) game pieces — e.g., random-draw stacks that generate sentences: nurturer draws one location card + two object cards ('behind' + 'goat' + 'paper') and must IMMEDIATELY say 'Put the goat behind the paper.' Skilled nurturers keep games moving fast; cards remove decision paralysis.
activities.materials: Printed and scissor-cut graphics packet pages; envelopes to organize by category
activities.timing: Built continuously from Meeting 1; central to games from MP3 onward

activities.name: Our Little World: From Kitchen to Office (MP2 G1)
activities.description: Rough-and-Ready Dozen with basic kitchen items then office/schoolroom objects and furniture ('This is a pen. This is a knife. Where is the knife?'). May include a generic word for 'thing' (GP points at any item). Once several names are known, commands using 'and'/'or': 'Where is the book and the spoon? Where is the glass or the cup?' Include good/bad pairs: 'Where is the good pencil? Where is the bad pencil?'
activities.materials: Book, paper, pencil, pen, knife, fork, spoon, glass, cup, bowl, teapot; toy or real furniture; a 'good' and 'bad' example of some items; Bag of Stuff
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 2

activities.name: Make It True (recurring response format)
activities.description: Inverse of pointing: the nurturer DESCRIBES a state, and GPs rearrange materials to MAKE the statement true. Variants: (a) Stick People in Action (MP2): 'The boy is running' → GP picks the right stick-figure picture; (b) cue-card-stack version (MP3 G3C): nurturer draws 'horse'+'boy'+'behind' and says 'The boy is behind the horse' → GPs physically place the boy doll behind the horse (nurturer must sometimes state the reverse); (c) house version (MP4): 'The man is sitting by the window' → arrange stick people in the toy house; (d) feelings version (MP11): 'The girl is kind' → GP places the 'kind' face cue card beside the girl doll; (e) PEOPLE version (MP6 G2C): one GP is designated 'you' (addressed) and another 'she' (talked about); nurturer tells John 'She is looking at you' → Sue must start looking at John; 'You are patting her' → John pats Sue; roles trade; (f) photo+line-drawing version (MP12).
activities.materials: Stick-figure/'triangle people' cut-outs, dolls, toy house, cue cards, photos
activities.timing: MP2 onward, recurring

activities.name: Lots of Places / Objects in Places / Strengthening Locations (location-word suite)
activities.description: Location words via Rough-and-Ready Dozen using an object with a natural front/back (large toy chair) and a dozen pencils: 'This pencil is ON the chair. This pencil is UNDER the chair. Which pencil is under the chair?' Add one location at a time (in front of, behind, in, beside, above, together with, separate from). Then 'Objects in places' recombines known objects: 'Which pencil is under the horse?' Then commands: 'Put the duck INTO the pitcher' (ignore word-form changes as long as the action is right). Cue-card stacks (two object stacks + one location stack) guarantee variety.
activities.materials: Toy chair, dozen pencils/matches, containers (glass, cup, bowl, pitcher), all Bag-of-Stuff objects, location cue cards
activities.timing: MP2 G3A–C, MP3 G3B–C, MP4 G5–6, ongoing refreshes

activities.name: Understand and Do: Putting, Taking, Giving, Pointing (MP2 G3C, MP4 G3)
activities.description: With one known object (pencil): contrast 'Take the pencil' vs 'Put down the pencil', then add 'Give me the pencil', then 'Point at the pencil' — 4 actions only. Then swap in 4–5 other objects: 'Take the goat. Give me the pencil.' MP4 'Give and Take' adds singular/plural address: 'YOU take the horse. YOU GUYS take the cow. Show me the door.'
activities.materials: Known objects from previous meetings
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 2 and 4

activities.name: Market trip: Buy One of Each
activities.description: Between meetings, GPs and nurturer go to a market; each person picks five small, genuinely common everyday objects (only items whose use the GPs understand) until there are ~15 — fodder for future Rough-and-Ready Dozens. A digital photo of the haul can serve as the picture-dictionary page. Recommended repeatedly when 'around the house' words run out ('go down the rows buying one of everything').
activities.materials: Local market, small budget, camera
activities.timing: Between MP2 and MP4; again before MP18

activities.name: Look Around Us HERE / Here-and-there in Here (room and house suite)
activities.description: Parts of the room via Rough-and-Ready Dozen (door, window, shelf, cupboard, blackboard, floor, ceiling, wall, picture). Then combine with motion/position commands: 'Point to the ceiling. Look at the floor. Walk to the door. Stand beside the blackboard. Sit on the floor.' MP4 adds a toy house (cardstock pattern in graphics packet) with bed/table/chair/sofa placed inside, adding 'house', 'stairs'. MP28 extends to rooms of a real house (living room, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, indoors/outdoors, guest room) — GPs walk/run to rooms, 'go into'/'leave'; video recording of going room to room recommended; furnishings localized (Eastern toilet, bread oven, clothesline).
activities.materials: The meeting room itself; toy house (pattern in graphics packet) + toy furniture; ideally a real local house for MP28
activities.timing: MP3 G1–2, MP4 G1, MP5 G2, MP6 G1, MP28 G4

activities.name: Body parts suite: People from Head to Toe; More Than a Pretty Face; Everybody's Body Parts; Tails and Horns
activities.description: Body parts on a doll, always possessed: 'Where is HIS foot?' (never 'Where is the foot'). Start with two, add one at a time; pairs (eyes) named however the nurturer naturally says them. Face parts next. Then 'Everybody's body parts': cross dolls with parts — 'Where is the man's nose? Where are the baby's legs?' (GPs must cope with changed word forms — pause, think hard, point; no analysis). Then animal parts (wing, feathers, tail, horn, beak): 'Where is the horse's head? Where are the goat's horns?'
activities.materials: Dolls of all family members; toy animals; body-part pages from graphics packet (nurturer may re-divide the body per host categories)
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 5, ~half hour for the first dozen parts

activities.name: All in the Family (MP5 G5)
activities.description: Doll family kinship game. One doll SITS UP in the middle; all others lie down around it — the sitter is the reference person. 'Who is HIS son? Where is HIS wife?' — add one relationship at a time. Then lay that doll down, sit up another (girl: 'Where is HER mother?'), and re-map relationships from each perspective in turn (man: wife/son/daughter/father/mother; boy: siblings/parents/grandparents; old man: grandson/granddaughter). Only nuclear three-generation family now — no in-laws/cousins. Expect host surprises: older vs younger sibling distinctions may require assigning relative ages to dolls. GPs must NOT ask for explanations or argue categories — pointing correctly IS getting it right.
activities.materials: Doll family of various ages (man, woman, 1–2 boys, 1–2 girls, old man, old woman, baby); drawings/puppets for extras
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 5; family terms recur through MP8 (giving to family members) and beyond

activities.name: Doing Things to US (MP6 G2A–D, pronoun-object suite)
activities.description: Three new actions — pat, stroke, wash — done TO people. (A) One GP stands in the middle; others are told 'Pat him. Stroke him. Look at him. Touch him. Wash him.' (B) Change the object person: 'Touch him / touch THEM / pat ME' (nurturer or her hand-puppet is 'me') — alternate randomly. (C) 'Make it true: you and he' (see Make It True). (D) 'Ourselves and one another': 'Pat EACH OTHER. Pat YOURSELF' then the full mix (me, him, yourself, us, them, each other). Cultural safeguard: use puppets/dolls or 'almost touch' for male–female contact.
activities.materials: Cloth for waterless 'washing'; puppets; dolls; cue cards for him/them/me/us and for actions; photos of nurturer (so GPs can pat the photo instead of the person)
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 6

activities.name: Possessive pronoun suite: Body Parts Yours/Mine; Stroking His Brother's Foot; Bee's Wing Pot's Lid
activities.description: 'This is MY head. This is YOUR head. Where is your head? Where is my head?' then his/her/our/their/you-guys', added one at a time (ignore singular/plural form changes if pointing is correct). Then triple-combination with the doll family: nurturer draws three cue cards (action + family relation + body part) and commands 'Wash her younger brother's ears. Touch her sister's fingers. Pat her mother's hair.' MP10 adds part-of-object possessives: 'Point to the bee's wing; pat the pot's lid; Where are my boots?' A warning anecdote: a coach who skipped possessives crippled GPs in Phase 2 — these matter.
activities.materials: Dolls, puppets, GPs' own bodies; cue cards in three stacks (actions, family, body parts)
activities.timing: MP6 G3–4, MP10 G1, talking versions in MP17, 19, 20, 21, 22

activities.name: Nurturer's Family (MP7 G1)
activities.description: The nurturer shows photos of her real family, saying who is who ('my father, my sister'). Explicitly framed as going beyond play into a real relational connection. If photos are culturally inappropriate, use dolls or stick figures to represent her family. GPs reciprocate in MP16 with their own family photos (a talking game by then).
activities.materials: Nurturer's family photos (or dolls/stick figures)
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 7; GP version Meeting Plan 16

activities.name: Grand Refreshing (MP7 G2; repeated as needed)
activities.description: Celebration checkpoint at ~150 words. ALL objects learned so far spread on a big table; the nurturer gives commands and where-questions in random order across the entire vocabulary, including combined commands ('Take the spider and run to the window'); objects may be removed as used; she finishes by checking the cue-card stack for anything missed. MP14 G7 variant: GPs choose what feels weak ('low in the iceberg') for re-strengthening. MP15 G4 'Grand Refreshing with wanting/having/seeing' empties the entire table into GPs' bags.
activities.materials: Large table; entire Bag of Stuff; full cue-card collection
activities.timing: MP7 (at ~150 words), MP14, MP15, MP36 ('New Activity Re-Run, Refreshing, Filling In Gaps')

activities.name: Color and size games: Getting Colorful; Colors in Different Sizes; Other Colored Stuff (MP7 G3–5)
activities.description: Colors via construction paper pieces: 'Where is the red paper? Where is the blue paper?' Add sizes: 'Where is the LARGE red paper? Take the SMALL white paper.' Then multi-attribute objects: 'Where is the small yellow ball? Where is the big brown horse?' and stacked-attribute commands: 'Put the green pen under the small white paper. Put the red car behind the large green paper.'
activities.materials: Construction paper cut into small/large pieces in many colors; colored object sets (Skittles, colored pencils, toy cars, paper clips, balls, buttons)
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 7

activities.name: Give/Take escalation chain (MP8 G1–5)
activities.description: Demonstration-first via puppet: nurturer tells her puppet 'Take the red candy. Give the red candy to the dog' until GPs see the pattern. Then escalating recipient complexity: (1) 'Give a large red candy to the horse' (color+size+recipient — note some GPs overload when multiple details vary); (2) possessed recipients: 'Give a small yellow candy to MY cat… to HIS cow'; (3) kin recipients: 'Give the girl's mother a candy. Give the woman's younger sister a candy' randomly interleaved with animals; (4) add me/us/yourself one at a time keeping the object constant ('Give me the button, give yourself the button, give her the button…'); (5) add 'throw' and 'show': 'Throw me a candy. Show the horse a small brown candy.'
activities.materials: Small/large colored candies (or buttons, beads, paper clips), toy animals, doll family, puppets
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 8

activities.name: Food and drink suite: Drinking and Pouring; Foods; Eat-Cut-Cook; Eating-Drinking-Giving-Taking; Eat Drink and Be Merry; Using Things to Do Things
activities.description: Local drinks via Rough-and-Ready Dozen (water, milk, juice, tea, coffee, soda), then commands 'Drink some milk', add 'pour': 'Pour me some juice. Pour the girl's brother some juice. Drink the Pepsi from the can. Pour the tea into the teacup' — mixing pour and drink. Foods: ~15 items fast, in recommended sets of ~12 (fruits; vegetables; basics like rice/bread/oil/flour/sugar/salt; dairy/protein), then verbs eat, cut, cook applied across foods. Combination game mixes drink/pour/eat/cut/cook/give/take/throw/show/touch. MP9 adds prepare, use, lift, carry, wait; then INSTRUMENTS: 'Cut the carrot WITH THE FORK. Eat the rice WITH A SPOON. Eat the carrot WITH YOUR HAND. Cut the paper with scissors.' MP12 'Remixing': feeding self/others/dolls/animals, cutting with knife/hatchet/scissors/fork/saw, drinking through a straw.
activities.materials: Real or toy foods and drinks; washed empty containers as reusable props (milk box, juice box, Pepsi can, teabag in cup); Velcro cut-apart toy foods; toy stove, cutting board, knife/fork/spoon, scissors, straw; dolls
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 8, 9, 12

activities.name: Locations True-False + recorded scene description (MP9 G5a–b)
activities.description: First yes/no and negation exposure. Teach yes/no gestures (nodding etc.). All objects spread on the table; nurturer describes locations, sometimes deliberately FALSELY. GPs say 'yes' if true; if false they say 'no' and the nurturer agrees and self-corrects: 'No, the cat is NOT in the basket; the cat is BESIDE the basket' — naturally exposing the host negative form. Then a photo of the whole arrangement is taken and the nurturer records a spoken description of the arrangement for home listening.
activities.materials: All objects so far; camera; recording device
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 9

activities.name: Clothing games (MP9 G6; MP10 G8)
activities.description: Clothing items via Rough-and-Ready Dozen in sets of 12, using real clothes or GP 'models' (which lets new body parts like beard, elbow ride along; cultural sensitivity around underwear in mixed groups). MP10 'Clothe and Unclothe': demonstrate 'put on' / 'take off', then command GPs to put on/take off shoes, hat, headscarf, glasses, jacket, ring, gloves, bracelet — or dress/undress a doll.
activities.materials: Real clothing including what people are wearing; paper dolls with clothes; easily-donned items
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 9–10, repeated later as desired

activities.name: To and From Alone (MP10 G5) — structured input
activities.description: Sneaky grammar-attention game. Objects/dolls on the table each hold a few candies/matches; each GP holds a supply. Commands: 'GIVE a candy TO the elephant. TAKE a candy FROM the cat.' Once familiar, the nurturer OMITS THE VERB: just '…from the horse'; '…to the mother.' With the verb gone, the small to/from markers suddenly become the only cue, forcing GPs to perceive them.
activities.materials: Familiar objects, dolls, candies/matches/buttons
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 10

activities.name: Alone or in Groups (singular/plural) (MP10 G6)
activities.description: A row of single objects (one dog, one cat, one chicken) faces a second row of small groups of the same kinds (several dogs, cats, chickens). Nurturer asks 'Where is the dog?' vs 'Where ARE the dogS?' — GP must hear the number marking to point at the right row.
activities.materials: Duplicate objects or pictures for plurals; digital photo taken to accompany the recording
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 10; reinforced in MP39 'General words and plurals'

activities.name: Sound-discrimination suite: Hear the Difference?; Sorting Sounds into Columns; Spot That Sound; Word Dictation
activities.description: Daily ~10 minutes from MP11 on. (1) Hear the Difference? (Listening Contrast): when two host words sound identical to GPs (like ship/sheep), the nurturer says them repeatedly in random order; GPs respond differentially (point at the cat / jump). Words must already be familiar from earlier games — never first-encountered here. (2) Sorting Sounds into Columns (MP18): go through ALL cue cards; place two cards starting with different sounds side by side; for each next card, GPs judge whether its initial sound matches column 1, column 2, or neither (start a new column) — building columns for e.g. p/b/v/f; works for middle sounds and vowels too. (3) Spot That Sound (MP22): nurturer reads through cue cards; GPs raise hands whenever they hear the designated 'sound of the day'; nurturer stops and helps when missed. (4) Word Dictation (from MP24, only if script is phonemic and GPs know the alphabet): nurturer dictates 5–10 cue-card words; GPs write from their EARS (hearing→spelling, never spelling→pronunciation). Rationale documented: spelling knowledge demonstrably does NOT improve sound discrimination; ears only.
activities.materials: Minimal-pair picture cards (e.g., a bin and a bean); full cue-card deck; paper for dictation
activities.timing: Introduced MP11; a fixed ~10-minute opener segment of every meeting MP16–40

activities.name: Feelings suite: Feeling Good Feeling Bad; Make It True; Feelings in Families; Feelings Clothes and Body Parts; Show Your Emotions (MP11, MP14)
activities.description: Emotions introduced as COMMANDS first: 'Be happy! Be angry! Be sly!' (GPs perform the feeling), with the matching face cue card displayed as each is added; ~12–20 face drawings (emotions and temperaments). The nurturer freely interprets each face in her own host terms — no translation needed, faces 'become whatever she calls them.' Then 'Who is angry? Who is sad?' pointing at face cards. Then Make-It-True placement (sad card beside girl doll), kin combos ('Where is the sad woman's daughter?'), and long-sentence gist practice ('Where is the frightened man's hat? Where is the angry boy's chin?') — nurturer breaks long sentences into natural chunks with short pauses for those who need it. MP14: 'Be sad / act sad' performed by GPs going through the whole face deck. Note: emotion words are learned more slowly than object words — plan lighter meetings.
activities.materials: ~20 face drawings from graphics packet cut into cue cards; dolls; clothing and tool props for combination games
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 11, 14, 15; faces reused constantly in 1B town/countryside games

activities.name: Power Tools / 'How do you say, How-do-you-say?' (MP11 G6, recurring)
activities.description: GPs learn the survival expressions ('language power tools') they will need to drive their own learning: 'What is this?', 'What are they doing?', 'Please repeat', 'I don't understand', 'I don't know', 'Please speak more slowly / more loudly', 'What am I doing?'. Taught via cartoon-bubble pictures (someone speaking too quietly/too fast and someone responding). MP19 makes it two-way LISTEN & DO: the nurturer asks easy questions; GP answers; then the nurturer commands 'Please repeat' / 'Speak more slowly' and the GP must comply. MP38 adds Phase-2 prep tools: 'That's a new word, please write it', 'What does ___ mean?', 'How do you say ___?', 'What is the opposite of ___?'
activities.materials: Power Tools picture cards from graphics packet (Lexicarry-like strips)
activities.timing: MP11–12 (introduced before the 300-word talking threshold), strengthened MPs 14, 15, 18, 19, 38

activities.name: Tools + Kill the Fly with the Hammer (MP11 G7–8, MP12 G1, MP13 G2)
activities.description: Tool names via Rough-and-Ready Dozen (hammer, screwdriver, saw, hatchet, pliers, wrench, nails, rope, glue, lock, key). Combined with emotions: 'Give the hammer to the SAD man.' Then insects/pests dozen plus 'hit' and 'kill': 'Kill the fly with the hammer! Hit the mouse with the hatchet! Kill the spider with the wrench!' (toy creature is flipped upside-down when 'killed'; substitute 'hit/touch' if killing is insensitive locally). Later with ordinals: 'Kill the THIRD mouse with the wrench.'
activities.materials: Real or toy tools; toy/picture pests (mouse, fly, bee, snake, spider, cockroach, ant, mosquito); optional flyswatter, water gun
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 11–13

activities.name: Numbers suite: Numbers to Ten; Money for Big Numbers; Ordinals; Show Me Seven Mice; Number Bingo (MP12–13, MP31, MP32)
activities.description: Quantities via visible sets: 'These are THREE matches. These are SEVEN matches. Where are the three matches?' one at a time to 10. Strengthen by giving: 'Give three fish to the woman. Give five matches to the baby.' Because 16 vs 60 items can't be counted at a glance, use MONEY for big numbers: 'This is 15 pesos. Where are the 13 pesos?', then 20–100 by tens, then 200, 350, 1000, a million (MP31), with 'count' and 'How many?'. Ordinals (first…tenth) on a lined-up row of ten mice, possibly added all at once if formed regularly; then 'Kill the fourth mouse with the screwdriver.' Number Bingo: each GP gets a board of 9–12 learned numbers; nurturer draws and calls numbers (GPs never see them written); GPs place beans; first complete row wins; replayed with larger numbers at MP32.
activities.materials: Matches/seeds/beans, dolls, real local money (or numbered slips), ten toy mice, bingo boards and beans
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 12, 13; big numbers and Bingo again MP31–32

activities.name: World map suite: Countries and Continents; Nationalities; Where They Live; What Language? (MP13, talking version MP27–28)
activities.description: World map Rough-and-Ready Dozens: neighboring countries + GPs' home countries (sets of 12), continents, map/world/ocean/north/south/east/west. Nationality figures: 'Who is American? Who is Indian?' Clever setup for 'What language?': a MALE figure of each nationality is placed in a country NOT his own (Chinese man in America, Indian man in Russia); the FEMALE counterparts line the bottom of the map. Five question forms added one at a time: 'Who LIVES in Russia?' (the Indian), 'Who SPEAKS Hindi?' (him), 'Who IS LEARNING Russian?' (him), 'Who IS FROM India?' (him), 'Who WANTS TO GO to Russia?' (his wife at the bottom!). MP27 converts it to a talking game — GPs answer in sentences ('The Chinese woman wants to go to Canada… Because her husband lives in Canada'); GPs can also place a face card for themselves and tell where they live and why. MP28 adds 'was born in' / 'grew up in.'
activities.materials: World map; male+female nationality figure drawings; GPs' own face cards
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 13 (listening); Meeting Plans 27–28 (talking)

activities.name: The Big Out-of-Doors + scene games (MP14–15; MP17; MP23)
activities.description: ~20 geography words fast (mountain, hill, tree, lake, grass, sun, cloud, river, desert, ocean, sky, snow, road, bridge, island, forest) on a countryside scene drawing. Then crossover games: 'People with emotions want to go places' — 'The sad boy wants to go to the lake' → GP places the sad-face figure at the lake; with actions: 'The happy girl walks to the forest.' Phase 1B talking versions: GP says 'The girl is running on the mountain' and others arrange cue cards on the scene; final arrangements are described by the nurturer, recorded, and photographed.
activities.materials: Countryside scene from graphics packet; emotion-face people cut-outs; action cue cards; camera
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 14, 15, 17, 23

activities.name: Give Me That Book (MP14 G6)
activities.description: Combines ordinals + colors + 'want': 'I want the red book on the FIFTH shelf. I want the green book on the FIRST shelf.' GP fetches it. No bookshelf? Alternative: ten lined-up mice with colored items placed around each: 'I want the red paper that is UNDER the SEVENTH mouse' — an early relative-clause-like structure.
activities.materials: Bookshelves with books, or the ten mice + colored items
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 14

activities.name: Wanting / Having / Seeing (MP15 G1–4)
activities.description: All manipulable objects on the table; each GP has a bag. (1) 'You/I/we/he/they want an X' → GP gives the object to the wanter ('The dogs want the rice; the cow wants the tree'). (2) 'Do you HAVE an X?' → GP checks bag, answers yes/no (first one-word speech!). (3) 'Do you SEE an X?' → yes/no — crucially, if it's hidden in their bag they answer NO (see ≠ have). (4) Grand mix with give/take: 'Take from me a red paper. Do you have a red paper?' 'Yes.' Game continues until the table is empty.
activities.materials: All objects; a bag/box per GP; multiples of some objects for numbers
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 15 (last 1A meeting)

activities.name: Helping One Another Up the Ladder of Success (MP16 G5 — the pivotal first talking game)
activities.description: THE bridge from comprehension to production. All objects/cards piled at one end of a table; the rest of the table is divided into four sections ('ladder rungs') with string. GPs stand around the table and take turns: choose an item and attempt to SAY its word. If 'close' (nurturer judges), it moves to rung 1. An object moves UP a rung whenever someone EXPANDS on what was previously said about it: 'Dog' → rung 1; 'Brown dog' → rung 2; 'The brown dog is running' (while moving it) → rung 3. If a GP can say numbers, they may take 3 dogs in one turn. Rounds escalate: round 1 = take 1 new item + expand 1; round 2 = 2+2; round 3 = 3+3. Pronunciation gate: fundamental mispronunciations (saying 'b' for 'p') mean the object goes back and the GP retries next turn; GPs repeat the nurturer's corrections but stop after the third attempt. Goal: move as much of the ~300-word vocabulary as possible from comprehension into speech. Must move FAST — set a time limit; encourage saying what you're confident of quickly. Continues across multiple meetings until the pile is exhausted. One GP famously produced 'The mouse is drinking milk from the cow' while staging it with toys.
activities.materials: Every object, picture, and cue card learned so far; string/yarn for 4 ladder rungs; timer
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 16–17 (Phase 1B Meetings 1–2), continuing until complete

activities.name: First talking games: GPs Name Body Parts; GPs Describe Their Families (MP16–17)
activities.description: One GP becomes a human model; others take turns naming the model's body parts ('This is his head, this is his hair…') with the nurturer assisting every attempt and GPs helping each other (not to the point of frustration). Then each GP shows their OWN family photos and tells who is who ('This is my father… this is her husband') — explicitly a relationship-deepening step. MP17 adds my/your/our/their possessive talking and 'What is your name? How old are you?' question exchanges (also strengthening numbers). Debrief time recommended at meeting's end for first-talking anxiety — early talking 'can stir very deep emotions.'
activities.materials: A volunteer model or doll; each GP's family photos; dolls with assigned ages
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 16–17

activities.name: Sixteen Pictures (MP18 G3, MP19 G5 — information gap)
activities.description: Classic info-gap. Two identical sets of 16 scenery drawings arranged 4×4 on both sides of a tabletop barrier (e.g., upright briefcase) in DIFFERENT orders. Version 1: nurturer (questioner) asks 'In your first picture, are there hills or mountains?' GPs answer in fairly complete sentences ('There are hills') with help; she eliminates candidates and keeps querying until she identifies and places picture 1, then 2, etc. Barrier removed at the end and arrangements compared. Version 2 (next meeting): two GP teams alternate asking each other ('In your second picture, is there a lake?'), each placing matched pictures turn by turn — GPs now do most of the talking; nurturer coaches from the side or joins a team, helping communication but never revealing placements.
activities.materials: Two sets of 16 scenery drawings (resource packet); a barrier; recording device for the final description
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 18 and 19

activities.name: Physical States and Needs (MP19–21, three-step progression)
activities.description: Step 1: nurturer states her own state — 'I'm hungry / thirsty / dirty / tired / sleepy / sick' — and GPs respond by telling her what to take from the table: 'Take the egg!' 'Take the washcloth!' (GPs deliberately choose their WEAKEST words, not safest). Step 2: nurturer varies the person — 'You are sleepy. We are tired.' — GPs answer appropriately ('You guys take the beet'; 'Give me the egg'); nurturer recasts errors gently ('I hungry' → 'Yes, you ARE hungry. I am hungry too'). Step 3: GPs take the nurturer's role, addressing each other and the dolls, combining objects with and/or ('Take the washcloth and the soap').
activities.materials: Household objects, foods, drinks, pillow/blanket, toy bed, pills/medicine props; feelings cue cards; dolls
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 19, 20, 21

activities.name: Here-and-Now Descriptions (structured input pronoun-drop) (MP18 G5, MP19 G8, MP20 G6)
activities.description: Grammar-attention via subtraction. Nurturer makes statements with action cue cards or photo sheets — 'HE is eating. SHE is pouring' — GPs point. Then, in pro-drop languages, she REMOVES the pronouns ('…is eating', '…is pouring'), forcing GPs to extract person/number from the VERB FORM alone. Sequence: he/she → they → we → I/you (using photos of the actual group members doing actions). Include masculine/feminine 'they' and multiple 'you' forms where they exist; skip entirely if the language doesn't inflect. GPs then attempt to produce such statements while others point.
activities.materials: Action cue cards; 'sheets of photos' (many small photos per page) of GPs/nurturer doing actions
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 18–20

activities.name: Container/appliance action games: Actions with Small Containers; Turning Off and On, Peeling (MP21–23)
activities.description: With a lidded box and jar: open, close, drop-on-purpose, drop-accidentally, push, pull, turn, turn over, roll, spin (padding on the table to break falls!). Next meeting GPs perform AND describe: nurturer models 'I am opening the jar', GP opens a jar saying 'I am opening the jar', then makes a puppet do it ('HE is opening the jar'), then describes another GP ('YOU are opening the jar') — always describing actions AS they happen (true present tense). MP22 adds appliances + 'turn on/turn off' (lamp, radio, fan, blender), 'peel' across foods, charge/call/measure/weigh/borrow/watch/answer. MP23 strengthens with multi-commands ('Drop the pencil, peel the egg and turn the radio off') and relayed commands: 'John, you tell Sue to peel the egg' → John: 'Peel the egg, Sue.'
activities.materials: Lidded box, jar, can+opener, ball, toy car, CD, teabag, cup; lamp, small radio, peeler, foods; pillow padding; action cue cards
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 21–23

activities.name: Copying Actions Through Hearing + People with Emotions Around Town/Countryside (MP23–24)
activities.description: Barrier-based action-replication chain. Two teams, each with identical sheets of face cut-outs (feelings + nationalities), barrier between. Team A cuts out faces while the nurturer narrates ('Mary is cutting out the surprised girl'); Team B, hearing but not seeing, replicates the actions purely from the descriptions. Then GPs themselves narrate ('I am cutting out the happy man'); the opposing team echoes in second person and describes themselves copying ('You are cutting out the sad man… Now WE are cutting out the sad man'). Next: faces get PLACED in identical town scenes — GP places and says 'I am putting the surprised person in the hospital'; the unseeing team replicates and says 'We are putting…'. Sentences become genuinely long ('He is putting the sad man in front of the door of the school') — reassembly, not parroting; nurturer always supplies the model sentence right before the GP needs it. Repeated on countryside scenes; final layouts photographed and described on a recording. MP24 rerun: GPs do most of the talking.
activities.materials: Duplicate face sheets, scissors, two identical town scenes (different paper colors recommended), two identical countryside scenes, barrier, camera
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 23–24

activities.name: Question Words (MP24 G4)
activities.description: Town scene populated with feeling-faces and posed people becomes the visible context for learning the question-word system. Start with two: 'WHO (is in the picture)?' → point at any person; 'WHAT?' → point at any thing. Then real questions: 'Who is by the barber shop? WHOM is the angry boy chasing? What is on the roof?' Add one question type at a time: Where? What kind of? ('What kind of girl is by the lake? A frightened girl'), How many?, Why?/Because ('Why is the sad man by the café? Because he is hungry'), plus whose, to whom, with whom, for whom. Subject vs object questions included deliberately. Repeat on the countryside scene. Iceberg rules apply — exposure, not mastery.
activities.materials: Town and countryside scenes; emotion/nationality faces; posed stick-people; recording of sample Q&A per question type
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 24, revisited MP39 with Busy Pictures

activities.name: Books suite: Kinds of Books; Places on a Book; If…Then (MP25–26)
activities.description: A pile of contrasting books makes abstract adjectives concrete: difficult/easy, thick/thin, old/new, cheap/expensive, open/closed, soft/hard, heavy/light, funny/interesting, plus genres (dictionary, novel, newspaper) — 'Where is the difficult book?' (masking-tape labels where not obvious). Then book-relative locations: far edge, near edge, right/left edge, center, inside, title, beginning, end. Then placement crosses: 'Put the rooster on the far edge of the old book. Put the baby between the funny book and the nice book', including 'the same book / a different book'. Then CONDITIONALS: 'IF the rooster is on the far edge of the old book, put it between the old book and the funny book'; personalized: 'If YOU are wearing a red shirt, put the rooster in front of the difficult book' — understanding only, not production. MP26 GPs describe the arrangements themselves ('The elephant is in the center of the thick book').
activities.materials: Many books of contrasting types; masking tape labels; small objects (incl. weak words)
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 25–26; if/then re-used with water games MP30

activities.name: Form-Focused Games (MP26 G3, MP37 note — language-specific grammar games)
activities.description: Custom games targeting a form GPs repeatedly stumble on, designed so the form must be processed/used many times with REAL meanings. Documented Kazakh example: nouns take one form for 'on the table' but a different one for 'on MY/your/his table'; game: each person has a book with distinct objects on it; nurturer asks 'Where is the sheep?' → answer requires 'on HIS book / on MY book'; roles then swap so GPs produce the forms. Second Kazakh example (MP37): possessed body-part endings differ by sentence role, so a speaker GP points and washes: 'This is my nose / your nose / his nose… I am washing my nose / your nose / his nose', rotating speakers. Designed per-language, ideally with a linguist/consultant; used whenever talking reveals a recurring struggle. Earlier possessive body-part games are retroactively identified as this category.
activities.materials: Books, familiar objects, body parts — whatever the target form requires
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 26 onward, recurring into Phase 2 as needed

activities.name: Information-gap drawing: One Draws, Others Listen and Copy + Fix That Drawing (MP27 G3B–4)
activities.description: One GP (behind a barrier with the nurturer) draws lines, shapes, and known objects on a whiteboard. The nurturer narrates each move: 'He is drawing a small crooked line at the centre bottom edge of the paper.' The other GPs, unable to see, replicate the drawing purely from the narration, free to request repetition/clarification — in host words only. Then 'Fix That Drawing': the nurturer inspects the copies and gives verbal corrections ('The flower isn't NEAR the tall man's foot — it is ON the tall man's foot') which the GPs implement before finally comparing with the original. Uses the shapes/lengths vocabulary (crooked, straight, curved, long, short, round, square, triangle, far, close) introduced just before via Rough-and-Ready Dozen.
activities.materials: Small whiteboards or paper per GP (erasable preferred), markers/colored pencils, barrier
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 27

activities.name: Quantities + town needs/wants suite (MP27–29)
activities.description: Quantity expressions on heaps of matches/beans + dolls + substances (water, flour, rice): a few, many, most, all, more, less, some, a little, any, each, every, someone, everyone, no one, nothing — mass vs count distinctions surface naturally. Then 'Wanting things in the town': nurturer says 'I want a book / a little rice / some clothes' and GPs direct her ('Go to the bookstore / grocery store / tailor'). 'Where does one go to…?' (buy carrots, play, pray, send a letter) with buy/sell/study/drive introduced by LISTEN & DO. MP29 'Things People Need': GPs tell each other 'The sad man doesn't have any toys' → 'Go to the toy store' (placing his face there), extended to full because-clauses: 'The happy man needs to go to the vegetable section of the bazaar, because he doesn't have any carrots.'
activities.materials: Matches/beans, dolls, glasses of water, plates of flour/rice, town scene, emotion faces
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 27–29

activities.name: Water suite: Water Water Everywhere; Water for the Thirsty; Getting the Doll Wet; Water Again (MP29–30, MP33)
activities.description: Real water on the table: full, empty, half full, wet, dry, cold, hot, dripping, splashing, drops, ice, melting, warm, boiling, cool, spill, flow, puddle (Rough-and-Ready). Then a talking game: GP1: 'The woman is thirsty' → GP2: 'Give her the half glass of water'; 'The woman is VERY thirsty' → 'Give her the FULL glass'; if/then versions ('If the man is very thirsty, then give him the full glass — he needs a lot of water'), with kinship roles assigned. 'Getting the Doll Wet': performers drip/splash water on a doll narrating 'Water is splashing on her' → response 'She needs a towel / Give him a towel.' MP33 warm-up: GPs do water actions and describe ('The water is dripping from the screwdriver').
activities.materials: Pitcher, glasses (full/empty/half), bowl/pot, ice on a plate, hot/warm water cups, doll, towel
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 29, 30, 33

activities.name: Actions Charades (MP29 G5)
activities.description: All action cue cards in a bowl; two teams (nurturer = a team if only one GP). A team draws a card and acts it out (or has a doll/puppet act it); the other team must SAY what is happening ('He's hammering! You all are sewing!'). The acting team corrects: 'No, I'm not swallowing, I'm eating.' Scoring: 2 points if guessed from acting alone, 1 point if a prop was needed. Doubles as a form-focused activity (progressive forms, person marking); nurturer recasts wrong forms throughout.
activities.materials: Bowl of action cue cards, props, optional dolls/puppets
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 29

activities.name: Time suite: Days/Months/Calendar; Weather+Days; Telling Time; Before/After with Time; Times of Day; Days and Dates; Seasons (MP30–33)
activities.description: Calendar-based Rough-and-Ready: days of week, yesterday/today/tomorrow, day-before-yesterday/day-after-tomorrow, week/month/year, next/last, weekend, holiday, birthday (identify 'today' first — calendars start on different days!). Weather: 'On Tuesday it will be cold' → GP points at the day AND the matching weather drawing. Telling time: clock with movable hands; the nurturer asks a PUPPET the time and the puppet answers repeatedly (recorded); then she states times and GPs point at/set clocks: hours → half hours → quarters → five-minute times. 'An hour before/after': turning the clock while narrating, then quizzing ('What is an hour after 2:30?'). Times of day on a half-white/half-black circle (sun/moon): morning, afternoon, evening, night, dawn, meal times and prayer times where relevant, then anchored to clock times ('Dawn is around 4:00 in the morning'). Dates: 'What day is October 15?' → 'Tuesday'; 'when' mixed with 'what time'. Seasons with weather pictures + months. From MP31 every meeting OPENS with the 'Day and Time' ritual — display questions ('What day is today? What time is it? What day was yesterday?'), with GPs eventually producing full recitations ('Today is Wednesday. It is April 5th. The year is 2016. It is 10:00 in the morning…'). The text defends display questions: language play IS real communication.
activities.materials: Local calendar (host language), weather drawings, movable-hand clock (or paper-plate clocks), clock-face pictures, day/night circle diagram, meal/prayer pictures
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 30–33; Day-and-Time opener daily from MP31 to MP40

activities.name: Can/Can't/Because + Maybe They Can (MP31 G3, MP34 G6)
activities.description: Reasoning game. A folded-paper 'wall' on the table with emotion-face pairs placed near/far on either side. 'Can the sad person SEE the crying person?' → 'Yes, because they are on the same side of the wall' / 'No, because there is a wall between them.' 'Can the hungry man HEAR the thirsty man?' → 'No, because they are far apart.' Weaker GPs may answer just yes/no with the nurturer supplying the reason — but talking WITH help is growth. MP34 escalates on the town scene with 'maybe' and multi-clause justifications: 'The sad person can't hear the happy person, because the sad person is standing by the bazaar, and the happy person is near the mosque. Between the mosque and the bazaar are many stores.'
activities.materials: Folded-paper wall, emotion faces (or animals/dolls if emotions are wearing thin), town scene
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 31 and 34

activities.name: Commerce suite: Buying and Selling Books; Role-play with Bargaining; The Marketplace (MP31–32, MP35)
activities.description: Step 1 (mostly listening): 'pay' introduced; nurturer directs transactions: 'Suzy, buy an easy book from John and pay 5 pesos. John, sell the book about horses to Suzy for 100 pesos.' Counting questions mixed in. Step 2 (role play): GPs buy from each other — buyer describes the desired object ('I want a new blue book'), asks 'How much is it?', seller presents and prices it, buyer comments ('It's expensive!' / 'That's cheap') and decides; bargaining added: 'I'll give you 100 riyals.' 'No, 200.' 'I only have 150.' Step 3 'The Marketplace': occupations dozen (butcher, baker, doctor, policeman, customer, storekeeper) + shop pictures; each GP runs a shop with appropriate goods and a worker puppet; the nurturer shops at each stall using the full script (greetings → 'Do you have X?' → 'I want Y' → 'How much is it?'), then GPs shop from each other; repeated later with plumber/electrician/wire/pipe added.
activities.materials: Books of all the learned types, real or play money, shop pictures or photos of local shops, occupation puppets/pictures (Lexicarry p. 80), goods per shop
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 31, 32, 35

activities.name: Paths-of-movement suite: Over Under Around Through; Driving Through a Building; Sending/Leading; Movements in Directions; Interpreting Commands (MP32, MP37–38)
activities.description: Path expressions by finger-tracing on a building drawing: through, under, over, around, past, away from, toward, out of, into ('Go through the house' → GP traces). Then a toy car through a box 'building' ('Drive the car under the building'). 'Making it personal': GPs perform AND narrate ('I am driving the car under the building') — noted in the text as an experiment in same-day comprehension→production. Take/bring/lead/send/follow with rooms as destinations; 'send' forces embedded speech: nurturer: 'John, send Julie to the bedroom' → John must SAY 'Julie, go to the bedroom!' MP37: locomotion verbs (climb, fly, swim, drive, ride, pedal, jump, crawl, travel) + 'Can you swim?' ability questions + vehicle words; whole-body versions across the room ('Fly — flap your arms — from the sofa through the door! Swim around the kitchen!'). 'Interpreting Commands: Filling in Missing Information': with toy fish/bird/car staged around box-buildings and a paper bridge, the command 'Swim under the bridge' contains no addressee — the GP must INFER it's for the fish; 'Fly through the building' → the bird. Street-map taxi directions: 'Take the green car. Start at the police station. Go straight. Turn right at the stoplight. Take the second right'; GPs then direct each other. 'How do you travel?' Q&A ('How does a fish travel to South America?' 'It swims').
activities.materials: Path drawings, toy car, cardboard-box buildings with open ends, paper bridge/roads, toy fish/bird/child/horse/airplane/stroller/bicycle, street map or town background
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 32, 33 (transportation), 37, 38

activities.name: Sequenced commands: After This Do That; Before This Do That; While Doing, Do (MP35 G3–7)
activities.description: Two cue-card piles: ongoing activities (work, dig, build, sew, sweep from MP33) vs brief events (cough, sneeze, wink, spit, smile from MP34). Nurturer composes two-action commands drawing one from each pile: 'AFTER you rest, sneeze.' Then GPs give the commands to one another. Then 'BEFORE you work, sneeze.' Then both types mixed, then 'WHILE you are doing X, do Y' added — the mix forces 'deeper processing,' which means better learning. Overwhelmed GPs are reminded the goal is just understanding enough to act.
activities.materials: Action cue cards sorted into ongoing vs brief-event piles
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 35

activities.name: Senses game: Seeing and Hearing in the Room; Tasting and Smelling (MP34 G3)
activities.description: GPs comment on live perception: 'I see a wall. I hear a car' (through window/door), extended to taste/smell/touch with strong-flavored foods: 'I taste something sweet. I smell something fragrant. I feel something smooth' (sour, salty, bitter, spicy). Historically notable: the FIRST time new words are encountered in a TALKING activity and reinforced afterward by a listening game — explicitly flagged as a foretaste of Phase 2A practice. New words get quick picture-dictionary sketches and follow-up Rough-and-Ready strengthening.
activities.materials: Foods with strong tastes/smells; Lexicarry pp. 75, 78 (tastes/smells), 79 (textures)
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 34

activities.name: Negation suite: Negation-Listening; Don't You Dare!; Negation-Talking (MP38, MP40)
activities.description: (1) Listening: the GP deliberately makes a FALSE statement while pointing ('This boy is running' about a playing boy) and the nurturer models negation: 'No, the boy is NOT running, the boy is PLAYING'; also with performed actions ('I am flying' while swimming → 'No, you are not flying, you are swimming'). (2) 'Don't You Dare!': positive and negative commands — 'Climb!' vs 'Don't climb!' (do NOTHING on don't) plus must/may/need-to/don't-need-to; has a 'Simon Says' quality when the negative marker follows the verb. (3) Talking: roles flip — the nurturer makes false statements and the GP produces the correction: 'No, you are not running, you are walking.'
activities.materials: Busy pictures of well-known activities; action cue cards from MP37
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 38 and 40

activities.name: Relative clauses: The One Who Did It; More Relative Clauses (MP39 G3, MP40 G5)
activities.description: On a busy picture: 'Show me a man WHO IS WALKING. Show me a tree THAT IS BESIDE A HOUSE' (subject relatives). MP40 adds non-subject relatives: 'Show me a woman THAT A MAN IS HELPING. Show me a table ON WHICH there is some food. Show me a boy WHO IS BEING GIVEN a parcel. Show me a shovel WITH WHICH a man is digging.' Pure listening/pointing — awareness, not mastery.
activities.materials: Busy picture(s) with many simultaneous activities
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 39–40

activities.name: Busy Picture games (MP39 G2, MP40 G2)
activities.description: A 'busy picture' (many familiar people, things, activities — e.g., a book like 'William Wanders Off') drives mixed question practice: nurturer asks 'What is he doing?', GPs answer, then GPs point and ask each other the same question types (what/who/where/how many/what kind/why). MP40: GPs attempt a full DESCRIPTION of the picture with help, deploying their power tools ('What is that?', 'That's a new word, please write it', 'What is the opposite of X?'); new words go into the picture dictionary and cue cards; the nurturer closes by describing everything discussed while GPs record it.
activities.materials: Busy pictures; recording device
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 39–40 (review/consolidation meetings — the 1,000-word goal is usually hit BEFORE MP39)

activities.name: Making Statements from cue cards (MP39 G4, MP40 G6)
activities.description: GPs draw cue cards one at a time and attempt a TRUE statement using the word ('house' → 'This house is big'), using power tools when stuck ('What does ___ mean?', 'How do you say no-big?', 'What is the opposite of big?'). If time runs short, the nurturer reads through the deck aloud, pausing on words GPs flag as weak. A whole-vocabulary production sweep before Phase 2.
activities.materials: Full cue-card deck
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 39–40

activities.name: Strengthening rituals: Yesterday's Actions; Gap-Filling; Synonyms; General Words and Plurals
activities.description: (1) Yesterday's Actions: any new action set gets re-used the following day in fresh combinations — verbs sink in the iceberg faster than nouns. (2) Quick Gap-Filling (from MP9): brief interludes to patch noticed holes (e.g., the missed Kazakh word for a brother's younger sister) at any point. (3) Synonyms (MP37): nurturer introduces commonly-used synonyms of known words via Rough-and-Ready/LISTEN & DO. (4) General words and plurals (MP39): meta-words — word/words, letter/letters, number, shape, color, sentence, example, list, phase, activity, meeting — via cut-up letter/number sheets.
activities.materials: Cue cards, letter/number sheets, calendar, colored papers
activities.timing: Woven throughout; MP9, MP37, MP39

activities.name: Plan Your Own Meeting (MP36) + planning form
activities.description: GPs and nurturer design Meeting 36 themselves using a provided form: Resources needed; Areas of new vocabulary; How many new words aimed for; Recent words to strengthen; Older words to refresh; Game instructions; Grammar aspects expected to be highlighted; How the activity combines old with new. Guidance: a good meeting re-encounters the last meeting's material, combines it creatively with new material, meets the hourly new-word goal with adequate repetition, looks forward to future re-encounters, increases speech complexity, and varies the pace. Keep the standard opener + sound games + cartoon bubbles skeleton.
activities.materials: The planning form; whatever the planned games require
activities.timing: Meeting Plan 36 (Phase 1B Meeting 21); 'feel free to plan more'

activities.name: Lifestyle-participation feed-in (1B introduction)
activities.description: Recurring real-life communication situations GPs notice out in the world (what people say when pushing to exit a subway, joining a post-office queue) are brought back into sessions three ways: as new homemade Lexicarry-like bubble pictures; as spontaneous role-plays the nurturer helps improve; or as extended LISTEN & DO scripts: 'You are riding on the subway. Hold on to the hand-rail. The subway stops. Start toward the door. Someone is in your way. Tell them: Are you getting off? Go past them.' Framed as relevance-boosting drops in the bucket — rapid rich growth matters more than narrow relevance.
activities.materials: GP observations from daily life; drawing materials for custom bubble strips
activities.timing: Any time in Phase 1B; grows in importance in later phases

activities.name: Action English Pictures (AEP) (optional)
activities.description: An optional supplementary picture-sequence resource ('Action English Pictures' — picture sequences for TPR-style narration) slotted in 'if time' at the end of several late meetings. Mechanics not detailed in this document beyond 'continue Action English Pictures.'
activities.materials: Action English Pictures book/sheets
activities.timing: Meeting Plans 37, 39, 40 (optional filler)

phase1.sessionStructure: Meetings run 2–3 hours; meeting PLANS are decoupled from meetings — if time runs out mid-plan, stop between games and resume next meeting exactly where you left off (plans deliberately keep the same numbering across all translations). A group completing ~2 plans/day, 5 days/week finishes the 40 plans in about 4 weeks. Players: 1 nurturer (host person), 2–6 GPs, optionally a coach (a GP, beginner or advanced, who silently trains the nurturer; coaches don't speak during listening games except host-language encouragements). Phase 1A meeting shape: a chain of 4–8 games — several Rough-and-Ready Dozens introducing new word sets, LISTEN & DO action games, recombination/strengthening games (Make It True, cue-card-stack games), Photos of Us in Action, and a Cartoon Bubble segment — each game ending with a ~1–2 minute recorded sample, and the day closing with Numbered Talking Picture Dictionary recording. Phase 1B adds a fixed skeleton: (1) from MP31, the 'Day and Time' opener (display questions about day/date/time); (2) ~10 minutes of sound-focus games (Hear the Difference? / Sorting Sounds into Columns / Spot That Sound / dictation); (3) a Cartoon Bubbles/Lexicarry segment; (4) a major TALKING activity re-using the PREVIOUS meeting's new words (ladder game, info gap, role play, states-and-needs); (5) new-vocabulary LISTENING games (words meet listening at least one meeting before talking); (6) form-focused or structured-input games as needed. The nurturer speaks ONLY the host language for the entire session; GPs are silent during listening games (talk freely between games); recordings + evening re-living close the loop. Homework between meetings: listen to all samples while pointing/acting, refresh via picture dictionary, prepare materials (photos, market purchases, family photos).
materials: Doll family: man, woman, boy, girl, baby, old man, old woman (plus extra siblings); puppets and stuffed animals
Toy animals (dog, cat, goat, horse, cow, mouse, bird, fish, frog, spider, camel, sheep, duck, snake…) and toy pests for the 'kill' games
The 'Bag of Stuff': cumulative bag/box of every object ever used, growing all phase

Real household objects: kitchenware, office items, containers, tools (hammer, saw, pliers, wrench), appliances (lamp, radio, fan), bathroom items, clothing, foods and drinks (incl. washed empty packaging as reusable props), water + glasses + ice

Graphics Packet (localizable drawing set): picture-dictionary pages, action drawings, stick/'triangle' people, emotion faces (~20), nationality figures, town scene, countryside scene, Power Tools strips, bubble-picture strips, toy-house cardstock pattern, paths-of-movement diagrams, day/night circle
Lexicarry book (Patrick Moran) — cartoon-bubble situation strips, occupations p.80, tastes/smells pp.75/78, textures p.79, town p.112, scenery pp.72–73
Cue cards: a second printed copy of all picture-dictionary pages cut into individual cards, organized in stacks/envelopes by category
Numbered Talking Picture Dictionary binder (800+ numbered pictures by phase end) + audio recordings
Recording device (phone) — used at the end of every game; camera for 'Photos of Us in Action' and scene snapshots; printed photo sheets cut apart
Two identical sets of 16 scenery drawings; two identical town scenes and countryside scenes (different paper colors); busy pictures (e.g., 'William Wanders Off')
Barrier for information-gap games (upright briefcase or box); small whiteboards + markers for drawing dictation
String/yarn to mark the 4-rung 'Ladder of Success' on the table
World map; local calendar; clock with movable hands (or paper-plate clocks) + clock-face pictures; real local money (or numbered slips); bingo boards + beans
Colored construction paper in two/three sizes; colored candies/buttons/beads; matches/beans/seeds for quantities
Toy house + furniture; cardboard-box 'buildings' with open ends + paper bridge/roads; toy cars/airplane/vehicles; minimal-pair picture cards (bin/bean, ship/sheep)
milestones: End of Phase 1A (Meeting 15, ~30–40 hours): understands 300+ words by ear — can point at, manipulate, or physically perform anything named, including multi-attribute commands ('Give a small green candy to the girl's younger brother'), without ever having spoken; responds yes/no; understands basic possessives, locations, plurals, numbers to 100+, family terms, emotions, body parts, colors, foods, tools; has personal host-world name and an established daily recording/re-living routine
By ~Meeting 16–17: speaks a large portion of the first 300 words via the Ladder of Success — single words, then expanded phrases, then simple sentences ('The brown dog is running')

Mid Phase 1B: holds constrained two-way exchanges — answers and asks names/ages, states needs and responds to others' states, completes information-gap tasks by asking/answering questions in sentences, gives and follows directions, role-plays buying/selling with bargaining, uses power tools ('Please speak more slowly', 'What is this?') to manage conversation
Hearing: discriminates most similar host-sound pairs that initially sounded identical; can sort words by initial/medial sounds; (where applicable) writes dictated words from hearing alone

Grammar awareness (not mastery): possessives, pronoun/verb-form mapping, to/from marking, negation, question words, if/then, before/after/while, can/can't+because, relative clauses, indirect discourse — all encountered receptively

End of Phase 1 (Meeting 40, ~100 hours): auditory recognition vocabulary of ~1,000 (goal 1,000–1,200, often reached before Meeting 39); cumulative Talking Picture Dictionary of 800+ entries with recordings; can describe busy pictures, retell simple cartoon-strip stories at own level, correct false statements, make true statements about any cue-card word, recite day/date/time; ready for Phase 2 (Emerging) — 'Congratulations! Celebrate!'
phase1.nurturerRole: The nurturer is a host-world member who PLAYS with the GPs in ways that let them understand — explicitly a nurturer/playmate, NOT a teacher 'teaching the language'. DOES: stays connected as a person and keeps it fun; talks ONLY in the host language, in real sentences; talks as to social-equal friends in informal play (adjusting register for older GPs if culturally required, letting GPs hear both registers); starts every new set with two items, adds one at a time; says each new word once (at most twice) then immediately questions; randomizes both items and responders (question first, pause, then name); weights questions toward newest/weakest words; corrects errors naturally in host speech ('No, that's not the cow, that's the horse — where's the cow?'); drops back to two items for an overloaded GP and rebuilds; breaks long sentences into natural chunks with pauses; uses cue cards to keep ALL learned words in play and to decide instantly what to say next (skilled nurturers keep games moving fast); records samples and the picture dictionary; demonstrates with puppets before asking GPs to act; in talking games, assists GPs mid-utterance like a parent helping a child say 'alligator', RECASTS errors ('I hungry' → 'Yes, you ARE hungry, I am hungry too') rather than correcting overtly, repeats mispronounced words clearly in the flow of play (max ~3 GP retry attempts, no drawn-out drills), and treats talk as cooperative teamwork. May bring her own family photos (Meeting 7), deepening the real relationship. MUST NOT: translate or speak any other language during games; repeat new words over and over ('point-and-listen' drilling — a teacherly temptation to resist); start with one or three items or add two at once; demand mastery, recall, or correct word forms; let GPs (or coach) talk during listening games; allow writing; stall deciding what to say; or expect story-perfect retellings — only the GP's best current effort. A coach (when present) silently trains the nurturer and never speaks during listening games except host-language encouragement; nurturers without coaches ideally get a week of advance training. Cautionary tale included: a coach who unilaterally deemed possessives unimportant left GPs crippled in Phase 2 — 'He should have asked us!!'
terminology: Growing Participator (GP) — the learner, reframed as someone growing in participation in a host world rather than 'studying a language'
Nurturer — the host person who creates a space inside the wall of noise, nurturing GPs into host practices; deliberately NOT called teacher/tutor
Host world / home world — the new people's lived world vs the GP's world of origin; each has a 'box of pieces of life'
Languacultural world — language and culture as one inseparable lived whole
Wall of noise — host speech as impenetrable meaningless sound to outsiders; for insiders the same speech is a window into thoughts
The magic moment — the first instant of understanding (pointing at 'the woman'), stepping inside the wall
