Special-growth participation vs lifestyle participation — structured sessions ('supercharged participation meetings') vs everyday-life interaction; the ratio inverts across phases
Here-and-now games — Phase 1 activities about only what is visible/performable right now; two types: listening games and (constrained) two-way conversation games
Rough-and-Ready Dozen — the core start-with-two/add-one/random-question listening format (~a dozen items per set; once titled 'Diry [Dirty] Dozens')
LISTEN & DO — command-response (TPR) format; LISTEN & POINT — its pointing variant
Make It True — response format where GPs rearrange the world to match the nurturer's statement
The Iceberg Principle — attend well at first encounter, re-encounter often, never force mastery; words sink and rise; refrain: 'It's in your iceberg' (local variants: volcano, well, submerged hippo)
Encountering → Experiencing → Strengthening → Re-living → Refreshing → Re-encountering — the documented life cycle of a word
Numbered Talking Picture Dictionary — cumulative numbered picture binder + audio recordings of all words
Cue cards — cut-apart picture-dictionary copies used as reminders, game pieces, and object substitutes
Bag of Stuff — the ever-growing collection of all game objects
Power tools — expressions for managing communication and learning ('What is this?', 'Please repeat', 'What does X mean?')
Lexicarry / Bubble Pictures — wordless cartoon-bubble situation pictures for formulaic expressions (from Patrick Moran's Lexicarry)
Information gap activities — barrier games where teams hold different information and must talk to solve a task
Structured input — listening games engineered to force attention to grammatical form (e.g., dropping pronouns, omitting verbs)
Form-focused games / communicative grammar activities — language-specific games making GPs process or use a troublesome form repeatedly with real meanings
Recasting — correcting by naturally restating the GP's utterance correctly; preferred over direct correction
Negotiation of meaning / communication strategies — the productive struggle when GPs attempt hard things with help
Display questions — questions asked to let GPs display ability (Day-and-Time opener); defended as legitimate 'language play'
Coach — an additional GP (novice or advanced) present to train the nurturer
Hearing/conceptual/foreign 'accents' — GPs mis-hear sounds, mis-construe concepts, and are mis-understood, all through home-world filters
Gap-filling — brief interludes patching noticed vocabulary holes
Phase 1A / Phase 1B — listening-only (MP1–15, 300+ words) vs listening + constrained talking (MP16–40, +600 words)
phase1.vocabTargets: Phase 1A: first 300+ words understood by ear across 15 meetings (30–40 hours) — roughly 150 words by Meeting 7 ('Hurrah for 150 words'), 300 by Meeting 15; the talking threshold is set at ~300 understood words. Phase 1B: add 600+ words across 25 meetings (50–60+ hours), reaching ~800–1,000+ by phase end with a stated goal of 1,000–1,200 auditory recognition vocabulary (experience shows 1,000 is usually reached before Meeting 39, so MPs 39–40 become review). Per-meeting expectations: a 'healthy number' of new words every meeting (object-dozens are easiest; some meetings deliberately lighter when strengthening dominates, e.g., MP12, MP21); pace intentionally slows in 1B (the second 300 take longer than the first 300). Comprehension is always meant to outrun production: GPs should understand far more words than they can recall and speak; Phase 1B aims to move most of the FIRST 300 into speech while comprehension keeps growing. Tracking mechanisms: the Numbered Talking Picture Dictionary provides a literal running count (sequential numbering — 800+ numbered pictures with recordings by phase end); cue-card decks double as a coverage checklist; recorded game samples archive everything encountered; GPs self-assess 'weak/low-in-the-iceberg' words and feed them back into strengthening games; a growing-participation journal is mentioned for logging sound-discrimination problems. Action words are flagged as needing more re-encounters than nouns.
appIdeas: Digital Rough-and-Ready Dozen engine (the core app mechanic): an image grid + native-speaker audio prompts ('Where is the X?') in randomized order; learner taps the image. Enforce the canonical rules in code: start with exactly 2 items, unlock 1 new item at a time only when accuracy is high, weight question frequency toward the newest/weakest items, on errors play the natural-correction audio ('No, that's the horse — where's the cow?'), and auto-drop back to 2 items for a struggling learner before rebuilding. No text labels anywhere — audio + image only, mirroring the no-writing rule

Auto-generated Numbered Talking Picture Dictionary: every word the learner encounters gets a numbered picture + audio entry appended in encounter order; browsable binder view used only as a 'refresh' lookup, with an 'It's in your iceberg' reassurance UX instead of fail states

Iceberg visualization for progress: words shown as rising/sinking in an iceberg based on re-encounter recency and accuracy (comprehension level vs production level tracked separately); celebrate milestones at 150/300/1,000 words; surface 'low in the iceberg' words back into game rotations automatically

Recorded-sample 're-living' mode: at the end of each digital game, auto-compile a 1–2 minute audio replay of all items in random order; the evening session replays it while the learner points at on-screen 'cue cards' or performs actions — recreating the home routine

LISTEN & DO / TPR mode using device sensors or self-report: audio commands ('Stand! Run to the door!'); for digital-only play, a drag-the-character variant ('Put the duck into the pitcher') where the learner manipulates a scene to obey commands

Make It True scene builder: audio statement ('The boy is behind the horse', 'The sad woman's daughter is by the lake') and the learner drags figures/face-cards onto town, countryside, house, or table scenes until the statement is true; reverse mode generates the nurturer's recorded description + snapshot at the end

Cue-card-stack sentence generator: the app digitally draws one card per stack (action + family member + body part; location + 2 objects) to generate endless randomized commands — solving the documented nurturer problem of 'ruts' and slow decision-making

Photos of Us in Action, personalized: learner (and optionally their real nurturer/friends) photograph themselves doing actions; app builds 'In which photo am I eating?' games crossing person × action, including the two-photo answer for 'we'

Cartoon Bubbles module: bubble-picture strips with recordable per-locale expressions; progression engine from 'Who is saying hello?' tapping → why-explanations → strip-as-story narration → learner story-retelling with speech recording; allow custom strips for situations the learner meets in daily life (subway, queue) — the lifestyle feed-in loop

Sound lab: (1) minimal-pair 'Hear the Difference?' drills with adaptive pair selection from the learner's confusion data; (2) drag-and-drop 'Sorting Sounds into Columns' using the learner's own known-word cards; (3) 'Spot That Sound' — tap when the target sound occurs in an audio stream; (4) optional ears-first dictation only for phonemic scripts

Structured-input games as code: pronoun-drop mode (verb-form-only listening), verb-omission to/from mode, singular/plural rows — toggled per target-language typology; a per-language 'form-focused game' template where a consultant defines the contrast and the app generates the drill

Information-gap multiplayer: two devices (or learner vs app-bot) each see a hidden 4×4 arrangement of 16 scene pictures; voice/chat-free question exchange via speech to reorder until boards match (Sixteen Pictures); drawing-dictation variant with a shared describe-and-replicate canvas plus 'Fix that drawing' correction round

Ladder of Success speech game: pile of learned-word cards; speech recognition judges 'close enough' pronunciation to move cards up 4 rungs; expansion detection (word → adjective+word → full sentence) advances cards; pronunciation gate blocks fundamentally wrong phonemes with retry-next-turn rules; timed for momentum

Role-play simulators: states-and-needs ('I'm hungry' → choose and name the right object), buying/selling with bargaining dialogue trees, the Marketplace with shop stalls, and taxi-directions on a town map ('Turn right at the stoplight'), all with recast-style feedback — the app replies with the corrected natural form rather than red X's
Time/calendar widgets: movable-hands clock, local calendar, day/night circle for times of day; the daily 'Day and Time' opener as a streak ritual the learner answers by speech every session
Number Bingo and quantity games with real local currency images for big numbers
Question-words mode over busy pictures: tap-to-answer who/what/where/what-kind/how-many/why-because; later the learner records their own questions

Negation and conditionals as game twists: app makes deliberately false statements the learner must reject (and later correct aloud); if/then conditional commands evaluated against scene state; 'Don't you dare!' Simon-Says mode

Nurturer-side companion app: session scripts per meeting plan, cue-card prompts, randomizers, recording tools, do's/don'ts coaching tips (recast don't correct, say new word only once, random order), and the Plan-Your-Own-Meeting form as a template builder

Audio-first architecture principle drawn from the text: never show target-language text in Phase 1 features; pronunciations are learned from ears, and the documented ship/sheep experiment justifies hiding spelling entirely until late 1B dictation

phase2.phaseName: Phase 2: Emerging (The Next 150 Hours — Story-Building with Pictures)
phase2.hours: 150 hours total of special-growth participation meetings, split into Phase 2A (50h, GP-led), Phase 2B (75h, nurturer-led), Phase 2C (25h, personal life stories). Recommended pace: 20-25 hours per week at the start of Phase 2.
phase2.summary:
Phase 2 (Emerging) is the bridge between Phase 1's "here-and-now" language (describing what is visibly happening right now) and Phase 3's "story speech" (displaced, past-tense narrative). The defining identity shift: "I am emerging when host people are starting to see me as a real person in their world with a particular personality," because the grower now has intermittent but real success starting verbal interactions. The grower enters with 500-1,000 familiar vocabulary items, here-and-now speech ability, and "power tools" (host-language phrases for learning more language), and exits familiar with 1,000+ additional words, able to follow long connected stories they have built with their nurturer, and beginning to understand simple explanations — though still understanding little of native-to-native speech.

The single primary activity is Story-Building with Pictures using wordless picture storybooks (e.g., Mercer Mayer's "Frog, Where Are You?"). The grower and nurturer discuss every detail of every picture page, negotiating meanings monolingually in the host language, building up an original co-created story. Everything is captured in sound recordings — page-by-page descriptions, numbered new-word recordings, and finally full past-tense narrations of the whole story — which feed a growing "listening library" the grower replays repeatedly as homework. Phase 2 splits into three sub-phases: in 2A the grower takes the lead ("getting your tongue loose" — speaking spontaneously in broken language while the nurturer smooths it out); in 2B the perspective flips and the nurturer leads, describing pictures and telling stories that the grower then "clarifies" (a recording-clarification technique central to all later phases); in 2C both parties tell real stories from their own lives using rough stick-figure drawings, deepening the personal relationship.

The pedagogy is explicitly anti-translation, anti-memorization, and anti-planning: the grower must NOT translate idea lists in advance, must NOT memorize sentences, and must struggle to compose speech on the fly — "the path to speaking well runs through the large country of speaking atrociously." A key payoff engineered into the phase is grammar salience: after dozens of hours describing pictures in here-and-now forms ("he is going"), hearing the same familiar vocabulary recast into "story event forms" ("he went") at the end-of-book narration makes past-tense grammar "hit the learner like a flying brick" — it stands out in stark relief precisely because everything around it is already familiar.
goals: Get the grower's tongue loose: move from reciting memorized material to spontaneous, self-composed (even broken) speech, with the nurturer helping smooth it out
Greatly increase ability to negotiate meanings entirely in the host language, so dependence on English/shared-language debriefing vanishes by end of phase
Become familiar with 1,000+ additional vocabulary items (7-8 new words per hour of meetings), tracked by continuous numbering from Phase 1
Transition from here-and-now speech to understanding (and beginning to produce) connected story speech 'in the past tense'
Build a listening library of co-created story recordings and re-listen extensively to strengthen comprehension
Shift from grower-controlled perspective (2A) to following the nurturer's perspective and her host-world way of seeing stories (2B)
Exchange real life stories with the nurturer using simple drawings, taking the relationship to new depths (2C)
Begin observing how host people naturally converse (eye contact, back-channel responses, turn-taking) as preparation for real conversation
Prepare for Phase 3 by getting out and about experiencing everyday host activities and pre-familiarizing with well-known host-world stories in a known language
keyPrinciples: Growing participation, not language learning: 'Don't learn the language! Rather, discover a new world as it is known and shared by the people among whom you are living.' Language growth and relationship growth are two aspects of one process
Monolingual norm: function entirely in the host language for timed blocks (30 min growing to 60-90+); when communication fails, make a written note for debriefing rather than reverting to English
No translation, no memorization, no over-planning: idea lists are for inspiration only; translating and memorizing them in advance means you have 'profoundly missed the point'
Negotiate, negotiate, negotiate: say what you can, get help, work out meanings interactively; quick translations short-circuit the learning that negotiation produces

Comprehension before production / Iceberg Principle: aim for recognition-level familiarity with new words, not recall-level memorization ('memorisation is time-consuming and for many people inefficient'); words strengthen through repeated encounters in context

Here-and-now as stepping stone: describe pictures in present/progressive forms first; only at end-of-book recast into past-tense story form, which makes new grammar forms maximally salient against familiar vocabulary
Record everything for repetition: page descriptions, word recordings, and story narrations go into the listening library — 'You really can't listen too much'

CUTE principles: Communing (growth happens inside relationships), Understanding (comprehension is the foundational skill), Talking (speech emerges from understanding), Evolving (activities must keep changing as ability grows)

The story belongs to the nurturer's world: when the nurturer 'misreads' a picture (police officer reading a law code book, not a children's book), that IS the lesson — the grower is discovering the host world's way of seeing
Group preferred: 2-4 growers per nurturer is more fun and natural than one-on-one, with care that everyone participates equally

activities.name: Phase 2A Step 1: The Monolingual Half Hour — Describe What You See (GP-led)
activities.description: A timer is set for 30 minutes during which only the host language may be used. The grower opens a wordless picture book to page 1 and tries to describe EVERYTHING: objects, positions, clothing, light, emotions, even invented dialogue for characters ('The frog is saying, I like this jar. I like you, boy.'). The grower speaks in broken language ('This is boy... Frog is in... what is this?') and the nurturer recasts each utterance correctly ('That is a boy... The frog is in a big jar'), which the grower echoes. The grower uses Phase 1 power tools (What is this? What is he doing? What kind of X is this?) and negotiates meaning for unknown words — e.g., pointing at a partial barn: 'It is a building... Cows in the building. Horses in the building.' until the nurturer supplies 'barn.' Each new word is given the next sequential number (continuing from Phase 1's count, e.g., word 948) and the nurturer writes that number on the picture next to the relevant item. Spend at least 10-15 minutes per page; spending the whole 30 minutes on page 1 is wonderful. If an idea cannot be conveyed, write a note for debriefing — do NOT switch to English. In groups, growers take equal turns. Sample idea lists exist for pages 1-5 of 'Frog, Where Are You?' (both 'things you can already say' and 'new things to learn to say'), explicitly NOT to be translated or memorized in advance.
activities.materials: Wordless picture storybook (e.g., 'Frog, Where Are You?' by Mercer Mayer), kitchen timer with bell, pencil and paper for failure notes, numbers written on picture pages
activities.timing: 30 minutes per cycle (lengthening to 60-90 min in later meetings); the core of every Phase 2A meeting; 50 hours total in 2A

activities.name: Phase 2A Step 0: Refresh Previous Pages
activities.description: From Meeting 2 onward, the monolingual block begins by going back over the pages covered in the previous one or two meetings, with the grower quickly re-describing in the host language all the things previously discussed, before moving on to new pages. Built-in spaced repetition of vocabulary and structures in their original visual context.
activities.materials: Same picture book, pages already numbered with new words
activities.timing: First minutes of each monolingual block, Meeting 2 onward

activities.name: Phase 2A Step 2: Debriefing (optional)
activities.description: Only after the 30-minute bell rings, and only if grower and nurturer share another language: up to 5 minutes in the shared language to resolve the noted failures ('Here I was trying to say the boy is dreaming about his frog. How would I have said that?'). New words from debriefing also get numbered and added to word recordings. Strict caution: debriefing is NOT for translating all new words, NOT for grammar lectures, NOT for lengthy culture explanations in English. The need for debriefing should shrink and vanish entirely by end of Phase 2 — try 'monolingual days,' then a 'monolingual week.'
activities.materials: Failure notes jotted during Step 1 by both grower and nurturer
activities.timing: About 5 minutes after each monolingual block; optional, fading to zero

activities.name: Phase 2A Step 3: Page-by-Page Recording
activities.description: The grower goes over page 1 with the nurturer, reminding her of everything discussed and all numbered new words. Then a voice recording is made of the nurturer describing that page in detail — but talking ONLY about things they actually discussed together, deliberately using all the new words and expressions that arose. Repeat for each page covered that day. This produces comprehensible-input audio where every word is anchored in negotiated, remembered experience.
activities.materials: Sound-recording device, picture book, the numbered new-word list
activities.timing: About 10 minutes per cycle

activities.name: Phase 2A Step 4: Listen and Point (and Act Out)
activities.description: Comprehension check turned game. The nurturer uses the numbers on the pages to recall the day's new words and says words/phrases/sentences containing them; the grower responds nonverbally by pointing at the right part of the picture. Example: new word 'window frame' — nurturer asks 'Where is the window frame?' and the grower points. If old word 'moon' + new word 'bright': she says 'The moon is bright' and the grower points at the bright moon. Verbs are acted out instead: for 'The dog catches a fly,' the grower plays charades — one finger is the fly, the other hand is the dog's mouth, saying 'arf arf' as the hand catches the finger. The nurturer repeats new words many times so the grower mentally processes them — familiarity for recognition, NOT memorization for recall.
activities.materials: Picture book with numbered new words
activities.timing: 5-10 minutes per cycle

activities.name: Phase 2A Step 5: Record It (brief)
activities.description: Make a short summary sound recording capturing the content of the listen-and-point activity, for evening re-listening. Homework is to listen several times to all of the day's recordings, pointing along appropriately at the pictures while listening to the listen-and-point recording, strengthening the words before the next meeting.
activities.materials: Recording device
activities.timing: A few minutes at the end of each cycle; re-listened to that evening and in following days

activities.name: Phase 2A Step 6: End-of-Book Activity — Hearing the Story Form
activities.description: When the whole book is finished (maybe meeting 7 or 10), the story is recast from here-and-now form into normal story form ('past tense'). Step 6A (careful, detailed, page by page): grower explains the plan, reviews page 1 with the nurturer recalling all agreed details, then records the nurturer telling the story up to the end of page 1 with maximal detail ('Once upon a time there was a boy and a dog. One evening the moon was shining bright...'); repeat page by page to the end, yielding a continuous full-story recording made one page at a time. Step 6B (flowing versions): (1) nurturer re-listens to the 6A recording to refresh memory; (2) she tells the whole story without pausing while still watching the pages, including as much detail as comfortable — recorded; (3) she tells the whole story from memory, not looking at the pictures at all, naturally less detailed — recorded. This is the grower's first heavy exposure to past-tense forms, with familiar vocabulary making the new grammar (e.g., Russian podkhodit -> podoshol; 'is going' -> 'went') stand out 'like a flying brick.' Both full-story versions are labeled and added to the listening library for occasional listening over years.
activities.materials: Completed picture book, recording device, listening library storage with good labels
activities.timing: Whenever a book is finished — typically after 3-10 meetings per book

activities.name: Phase 2A Step 7: Story Retelling by GPs
activities.description: Same day or later: the growers retell the story themselves as 'language play.' Crucially, the grower's version is only 'inspired by' the nurturer's — told at the GROWER's level of ability, possibly still in present tense, with the nurturer assisting conversationally. This is the point where nurturers most easily go wrong by acting like teachers expecting imitation of their version. Across Phase 2 the retellings drift naturally toward past-tense story form.
activities.materials: Picture book, optionally recording device
activities.timing: After Step 6, about 10 minutes; repeated at end of every book

activities.name: Small Talk + One New Fact (every meeting)
activities.description: Each meeting opens with 5-10 minutes of small talk in the host language only. The concrete practice: learn at least one new fact about the nurturer (and fellow growers) each day, and share one parallel fact about yourself. This keeps participation personal and slowly forms 'a new little host-world community.' Small-talk capacity visibly grows across the phase and should 'evolve naturally.'
activities.materials: None
activities.timing: First 5-10 minutes of every meeting in all sub-phases

activities.name: Phase 2B Step 1: Nurturer Describes the Pictures (nurturer-led)
activities.description: Perspective flip after ~50 hours: the grower now talks freely, so the input must shift toward how the NURTURER would say things. With a brand-new wordless book (which the nurturer may take home the night before to understand the pictures — but NOT to script her speech), the nurturer describes the situations and activities on successive pages fully and naturally, pointing at the parts of the picture as she speaks. The grower does not interrupt for clarification — just listens, and records everything. Her 'misreadings' are embraced as host-world perspective (the Kazakh nurturer who saw a police officer reading a law code book, or school-uniform shoes proving a bear-girl is six). Only plot-breaking errors (calling a mouse a dog) get corrected interactively, producing lively real disagreement.
activities.materials: New wordless picture book, recording device
activities.timing: About 10 minutes per cycle; Phase 2B is 75 hours total

activities.name: Phase 2B Step 2: Clarifying the Recording (cornerstone technique)
activities.description: Grower and nurturer listen back to the recording together. The grower stops it wherever something is not understood and they negotiate the meaning monolingually — no English. Example mechanic: for a word meaning 'in vain,' the nurturer gives example scenarios ('You swept your floor, and then people scattered trash. You swept in vain.'); the grower then invents further examples to confirm understanding. New words are numbered on the pictures and added to the word recording. This 'clarifying' process generates rich conversational interaction and is explicitly the basic technique that plays a major role in ALL remaining phases of the program.
activities.materials: The Step 1 recording, picture book, pencil for numbering
activities.timing: 30-80 minutes per cycle — the bulk of every 2B meeting

activities.name: Phase 2B Step 4: Word-Sentence-Word Vocabulary Recordings
activities.description: A special recording highlighting only the day's new words, in sandwich format: bare word, then a context sentence, then the word again — 'Churn. The woman is churning the butter. Churn.' The context sentence must be a strong reminder of meaning (counter-example given: 'Churn. I don't have a churn. Churn.' is useless because it carries no meaning cues). Growers must coach nurturers on building meaning-revealing context sentences. Enables refreshing many vocabulary items quickly by attentive listening.
activities.materials: Recording device, numbered new-word list
activities.timing: About 15 minutes per 2B cycle

activities.name: Phase 2B Steps 7-8: Whole-Story Telling and GP Retelling
activities.description: When a 2B book is finished, the nurturer tells the whole story in past tense, in the same three versions as Phase 2A Step 6 (detailed page-by-page, flowing with pictures, from memory). Then the growers retell at their own level with conversational assistance. In later 2B meetings (perhaps meeting 5, 10, or 15), when page-by-page description has become redundant ('These are trees. There is a bird in this tree.'), the format inverts: the nurturer simply tells the whole story past-tense FIRST as Step 1 (10+ min, recorded, grower following the pictures), then 30-70 minutes of clarifying that story recording, then debrief, word recording, listen-and-point, nurturer retelling, and GP retelling.
activities.materials: Picture book, recording device
activities.timing: End of each book; the inverted whole-story-first format becomes the standard meeting shape in later 2B

activities.name: Phase 2C Option 1: Draw As You Go — Telling Your Life Story
activities.description: The grower tells a true story from their own life (birth-to-present outline, or one entertaining/identity-defining episode), drawing stick figures and rough sketches of key characters and components AS each is introduced ('This is my father... This is his older sister... One day my grandfather came home. His suitcase was outside the door. The door was locked.'). Only key details are drawn — enough for the nurturer to recall the whole story. There is heavy struggling, negotiation, and vocabulary learning throughout. Step 2: once the entire story is conveyed, the nurturer retells it freely and naturally in past tense from start to finish, pointing at the relevant drawing parts — recorded (video works too). Step 3: vocabulary recording; Steps 4-5: listen-and-point and brief recording. The nurturer's clear retellings of YOUR OWN stories become prized listening-library items. Tied to pictures, the grower's telling may still be largely present tense. If this proves too hard, postpone to Phase 3 and do 25 more hours of 2B instead.
activities.materials: Pencil and paper (stick figures or 'triangle people' from Phase 1), recording device
activities.timing: 30-70 minutes telling + 10 min nurturer retelling + 15 min vocab recording + 10 min listen-and-point per cycle; Phase 2C is 25 hours

activities.name: Phase 2C Option 2: Prepare Drawings in Advance
activities.description: Same as Option 1 but the grower draws the full picture-sequence before the meeting (example: Angela Thomson's pre-drawn story of how her parents met, using triangle people). Advantage: the telling is not interrupted by drawing.
activities.materials: Pre-drawn picture story sheets
activities.timing: Alternative format within Phase 2C

activities.name: Phase 2C Option 3: All-in-One Picture
activities.description: A single rich drawing serves as a setting map for many stories — example: a nurturer drew the layout of his childhood home and grounds, then used it extensively for telling multiple events that happened in that setting.
activities.materials: One detailed setting drawing
activities.timing: Reusable across multiple 2C meetings

activities.name: Phase 2C: Stories from the Nurturer's Life
activities.description: After watching the grower draw-and-tell, the nurturer shares her own life the same way, with the grower helping her with the drawings. The act of drawing deliberately slows the story down, letting it grow bit by bit and stay understandable, while deepening the relationship in her world (explicitly NOT via socializing in English).
activities.materials: Pencil and paper, recording device
activities.timing: Interleaved with grower's stories in Phase 2C

activities.name: Phase 2C: Conversation Observation and Co-Building
activities.description: Three mechanics for moving from 'getting my point across' to natural conversation: (1) have the nurturer and ANOTHER host person interact over a wordless picture book while the grower watches a native model of interaction; (2) grower and nurturer build a story together, each contributing in balanced, natural conversational turns; (3) structured observation of two host people talking — How much eye contact? What does the listener say during the other's speech? What nonverbal reactions (nods, facial expressions)? Do people interrupt or leave long silences before turn-trading? — without over-generalizing from one pair.
activities.materials: Wordless picture book, a second host person
activities.timing: Late Phase 2C

activities.name: Supplementary: Lexicarry Story Strips
activities.description: The grower tells the nurturer what is happening in each story strip of Lexicarry (Moran's picture book of situational dialogues, used receptively in Phase 1). Moves Phase 1 comprehension-only expressions into the grower's own productive speech, embedded in understandable little stories.
activities.materials: Lexicarry: Pictures for Learning Languages (Pro Lingua Associates)
activities.timing: Occasional change-of-pace interspersed in story-building

activities.name: Supplementary: Picture Strips and Acting Out
activities.description: Use simple wordless cartoon strips (e.g., Action English Pictures) depicting everyday procedures like brushing teeth; or the grower physically acts out an everyday activity while the nurturer narrates what they are doing. A light preview of Phase 3's 'Scripts of Life' (where a 10-minute minute-detail explanation of tooth-brushing awaits; here it totals under a minute of recorded talk).
activities.materials: Action English Pictures (Takahasi & Frauman-Prickel) or similar wordless procedure strips
activities.timing: Occasional, Phase 2B/2C era

activities.name: Supplementary: Role-Plays
activities.description: Continue occasional Phase 1-style role-plays of real-life communication situations the grower actually participates in: shopping, taking a taxi, paying the phone bill, etc.
activities.materials: Props as needed
activities.timing: Occasional throughout Phase 2

activities.name: Supplementary: Grammar and Phonetic Awareness
activities.description: Repeat Phase 1 grammar-awareness activities and phonetic discrimination drills targeting sound distinctions the grower still cannot reliably hear.
activities.materials: Phase 1 activity designs
activities.timing: Occasional, as needed

activities.name: Supplementary: Busy Pictures
activities.description: Describe 'busy pictures' — scenes where many people/animals do many actions (e.g., The Big Book of Things to Spot / 1001 Things to Spot) — specifically to boost vocabulary intake when the iceberg isn't growing fast enough (below ~7-8 new words/hour) from story-building alone.
activities.materials: Busy books such as Usborne's 1001 Things to Spot
activities.timing: As needed when word-count pace lags

activities.name: Appendix Technique: Story-Building with Cuisenaire Rods or Small Objects
activities.description: For settings where wordless books are unavailable or culturally alien (pre-literate groups). Objects stand in for characters: 'This is a little red hen. This is a cat...' Build the story here-and-now style, holding up each object as its character speaks ('Who will help me plant the wheat?' / 'Not I, said the cat'), acting out events ('The hen planted the wheat'), negotiating words like 'wheat' and 'plant' as needed. First pass is full of struggle; repeat more smoothly with the same or additional host people; finally the host person tells the entire story in normal story form. Natural objects substitute freely — a rock for a sheep, a fat stick for a canoe — and stories should fit the local setting. The included ESL lesson model (Sarah Janek) adds mechanics worth borrowing: teacher builds her childhood home in rods while narrating; students retell by pointing at each block and saying what it represents; later students draw a picture of the scene from memory as a comprehension 'picture quiz,' then tell their own stories with the rods in small groups.
activities.materials: Cuisenaire rods, small toys, or natural objects (sticks, stones, leaves, seeds)
activities.timing: Alternative/supplement to wordless books, any time in Phase 2

activities.name: Homework: Listening Library Re-Listening
activities.description: After every meeting: listen several times to that day's page-description recordings, the listen-and-point summary (pointing along at the pictures while listening), and end-of-book story versions; occasionally re-listen to older recordings for years — on flights, walks, in the bathtub ('better than airline movies... You really can't listen too much'). Old picture stories can also be fully reused months later at a higher ability level.
activities.materials: All accumulated recordings, well labeled; copies of numbered picture pages
activities.timing: Daily, between every meeting

activities.name: Phase 3 Preparation (run in parallel)
activities.description: Two strands started during Phase 2: (1) Get out and about experiencing everyday host activities, since Phase 3's 'Scripts of Life' activity narrates familiar everyday routines; (2) find stories well known in the host world (Grimm tales, fables, Bible stories via listed websites), record them in a language the grower already knows, and listen repeatedly now — so that when heard in the host language in late Phase 3 they are already 'shared stories.'
activities.materials: Online story sources (grimmstories.com, languagelizard.com, etc.), recording device
activities.timing: Background activity throughout Phase 2

phase2.sessionStructure: Phase 2A meeting: (1) 5-10 min small talk in host language, including learning one new fact about the nurturer and sharing one back; (2) a repeating ~55-minute cycle: Step 0 refresh previous pages + Step 1 monolingual half hour describing picture pages (timer set; host language only; 30 min, lengthening over time to 60-90 min), Step 2 optional 5-min debrief in shared language using failure notes only, Step 3 ~10-min page-by-page recording of the nurturer describing what was discussed, Steps 4-5 ~10 min listen-and-point/act-out plus a brief summary recording; cycle repeats as time allows, with tea breaks when weary. Step 6 (three past-tense versions of the whole story) and Step 7 (GP retelling) fire only when a book is finished. Phase 2B meeting: 5-10 min small talk; then 10 min nurturer describes new pages while pointing (recorded); 30-80 min clarifying the recording monolingually; 5-10 min optional debrief; 15 min word-sentence-word vocabulary recording; 5-10 min listen-and-point plus sample recording; Steps 7-8 (nurturer whole-story + GP retelling) at end of book. Later 2B inverts: nurturer tells the entire story past-tense first (10+ min, recorded), then clarification fills the meeting. Phase 2C cycle: 5-10 min small talk; 30-70 min grower tells a life story while drawing; 10 min nurturer retells it naturally in past tense (recorded); 15 min vocabulary recording; 10 min listen-and-point plus recording. Throughout: 20-25 meeting-hours per week recommended; debriefing windows shrink toward fully 'monolingual days' and 'monolingual weeks'; homework after every meeting is repeated listening to the day's recordings.
materials: Wordless picture storybooks — primary resource (flagship: 'Frog, Where Are You?' by Mercer Mayer; first-ever book recommendation: 'The Big Fat Worm'; full annotated bibliography of ~50 titles with star ratings and cultural-fit notes included, e.g., Anno's Journey, Pancakes for Breakfast, Good Dog Carl, Tuesday, The Bear and the Fly); 5-6 books may fill 150 hours for talkative growers, up to 30 for others; cover printed words with paper/post-its
Kitchen timer with bell (enforces the monolingual half hour)
Sound-recording device (used in every single meeting; video optional in 2C)
Pencil and paper: for failure notes for debriefing, and for numbering new words directly on picture pages (extra copies of pages used that day)
Listening library: the labeled, growing archive of all recordings (page descriptions, word recordings, three story versions per book, life-story retellings)
Continuously numbered word recordings (Auditory Picture Dictionary continuing Phase 1's count, e.g., starting at word 948)
Drawing paper for stick figures / triangle people (Phase 2C)
Lexicarry (Moran), Action English Pictures (Takahasi & Frauman-Prickel), busy books (1001 Things to Spot)
Cuisenaire rods, small toys, or natural objects (sticks, stones, leaves) as picture-book substitutes
Notebook for debriefing notes (optional)
milestones: Host people start seeing the grower as a real person with a particular personality; grower can attempt conversations that 'may come to something'
Greatly increased ability to negotiate meanings monolingually; need for English/shared-language debriefing approaching zero — can work with a nurturer who knows no English
Familiar with over 1,000 additional vocabulary items beyond Phase 1's 500-1,000 (averaging 7-8 new words per meeting hour, all sequentially numbered)
Greatly increased fluency talking about the here-and-now, including everything visible in pictures
Using increasingly complex sentences in everyday speech
Understands long connected stories built with the nurturer; first solid grasp of past-tense/'story event' verb forms emerging from familiar here-and-now forms
Can retell a built story at own level, drifting from present-tense toward normal past-tense story form across the phase
Understands simple explanations from the nurturer when kept simple and meanings are negotiated; still understands relatively little of natives talking among themselves
Relationship with nurturer deepened considerably through mutual life-story sharing (in her world, not via English socializing); may be ready to live with a committed host family
Much less dependent on outside guidance in structuring own growth activities than in Phase 1; ready for Phase 3's 'stuff-we-both-know' activities
Conversations still limited to a narrow topic range — relationships cannot generally go deep yet; that pressure belongs to Phase 3
phase2.nurturerRole: In 2A the nurturer needs ZERO preparation; her job is responsive: guess what the grower is trying to say (the pictures help), recast broken utterances into well-formed ones for the grower to echo, supply words on request, write sequential numbers on pictures for each new word, record page descriptions using ONLY content actually discussed together, run listen-and-point quizzes repeating new words many times, and — at book's end — narrate the story in past tense in three versions (detailed page-by-page; flowing while watching pages; freely from memory). When she fails to get a point across she notes it for debriefing rather than switching to English. In 2B she takes the lead: may take the book home overnight to understand the pictures (but must NOT script her speech — extemporaneous only), describes pages fully and naturally while pointing, tells whole stories, sits through clarification answering with monolingual explanations and example scenarios (the 'in vain' sweeping example), and builds word-sentence-word vocabulary recordings with meaning-revealing context sentences (growers must coach her on this). In 2C she retells the grower's life stories naturally in past tense from the stick-figure drawings, and shares her own life stories the same way. What she must NOT do: translate everything into English; give grammar lectures or lengthy culture explanations in a shared language; plan/memorize her speech in advance; act like a 'teacher' during GP retellings by expecting the grower to reproduce her version — retelling is at the GROWER's level with conversational assistance only. Her 'misinterpretations' of pictures are usually host-world perspective to be welcomed, not corrected — only plot-breaking errors (mouse called a dog) warrant pushback. Phase 2A activities double as orientation for any NEW nurturer to her role; 2B activities orient nurturers to clarifying recordings.
terminology: Growing Participator (GP) — replaces 'language learner': someone becoming increasingly able and active in the host community; growth in language = growth in participation
Nurturer — replaces 'language helper/tutor/teacher': the first host community member the GP participates with, who meets them in their growth zone and supports their efforts to interact
Host language / host world — replaces 'target language': focus on joining a community, not completing a task

Special-growth participation meetings/activities — replaces 'language class/lessons': specially designed interaction times maximizing meaningful participation, vs. lifestyle growing participation (immersion in normal host life, which yields almost no growth in early phases)
Home-world hours vs host-world hours — of ~100 waking weekly hours, time lived in one's original languaculture vs. in meaningful host interaction
Here-and-now language — speech directly tied to what speakers/listeners see and do right now (Phase 1-2A register), vs. displaced communication and 'story event forms' (past-tense narrative grammar)
Negotiating meaning — interactive work to repair misunderstanding: say what you can, clarify until shared understanding; the engine of learning
Power tools — host-language expressions used to obtain more language ('What is this called?', 'What is he doing?', 'Please say that more slowly')
Clarifying (the recording) — listening back to a recording with the nurturer and monolingually working out everything not understood; the cornerstone technique of Phases 2B-6
Listening library — replaces 'comprehensible corpus': the GP's growing archive of labeled recordings for pleasurable repeated listening

Word recordings / numbers for new words — sequentially numbered new vocabulary (continuing Phase 1's count, e.g., word 948) keyed to numbers written on picture pages, captured in word-sentence-word audio
Iceberg Principle — the mass of receptively familiar words below the waterline matters more than the small tip you can actively recall; aim for recognition, not memorized recall
Growth zone — the GP's current ability level, visible only when interacting with a sympathetic native speaker
CUTE principles — Communing, Understanding, Talking, Evolving: the four principles undergirding the Six Phase Program
Debriefing — short, scheduled shared-language windows (≤5 min) strictly for failed negotiations; never for wholesale translation or grammar lectures
Communities of practice — host-community relationship networks that deepen over time
Monolingual half hour — timer-enforced block using only the host language; lengthens toward monolingual days and weeks
phase2.vocabTargets: Enter Phase 2 familiar with 500-1,000 vocabulary items (Phase 1 prerequisite). During Phase 2, become familiar with over 1,000 additional items — aiming at 7-8 new words per meeting hour (the meeting-evaluation checklist asks for 'at least eight words per hour'); if story-building alone runs slower, add busy-picture sessions. Tracking is continuous sequential numbering carried over from Phase 1 (if Phase 1's Auditory Picture Dictionary ended at word 947, Phase 2 starts at 948), so the GP always knows exactly how many words they have had strong encounters with (Iceberg Principle). Each new word gets: a number written next to the relevant picture detail on the page, inclusion in the day's word recording (word-sentence-word sandwich format with a meaning-revealing context sentence, e.g., 'Churn. The woman is churning the butter. Churn.'), reinforcement via listen-and-point, and repeated exposure through evening re-listening. Target is recognition-level familiarity, not recall-level memorization.
appIdeas: Digital wordless picture book reader with tap-to-tag hotspots: tapping any picture detail drops the next sequential word number (auto-continuing the GP's lifetime word count from Phase 1) and attaches an audio snippet — directly digitizing the 'numbers for new words' on pages

Built-in monolingual timer: a prominent 30/45/60-minute session timer with a bell; during the timer, the app hides all translation features; when it rings, a 5-minute 'debrief window' opens where the GP's queued failure-notes (typed or voice-memo'd mid-session with one tap) can be resolved

Per-page recording workflow: each book page has record slots for 'page description' (nurturer, here-and-now), and each finished book unlocks the three story-version slots (detailed page-by-page past tense, flowing with pictures, from memory) plus a 'GP retelling' slot — enforcing Steps 6-7 so they're never forgotten

Auto-organized Listening Library: every recording is labeled by book/page/date/type and assembled into replay playlists; homework mode prompts evening re-listening and resurfaces old recordings on a spaced schedule ('you really can't listen too much')

Listen-and-point as an interactive game: play back the nurturer's recorded sentences containing the day's new words; the GP taps the matching region of the picture (the hotspot tags make this auto-gradable); verbs prompt an 'act it out' camera moment or skip

Word-sentence-word vocab recorder with a guided template: prompts the nurturer to record 'word — context sentence — word' and warns/coaches that the sentence must reveal the meaning (with the churn good/bad examples as in-app guidance)
Iceberg counter dashboard: running lifetime word number, words-per-meeting-hour pace tracker against the 7-8/hour target, with a nudge to add 'busy picture' sessions when pace lags

Clarify-the-recording player (Phase 2B core): playback with one-tap 'I didn't understand this' markers that bookmark timestamps; the pair then revisits each marker, negotiates meaning monolingually, and tags the new word — turning the cornerstone GPA technique into a first-class app feature

Phase 2C drawing canvas: stick-figure/triangle-people sketching synced to audio recording, so the timeline links each drawing stroke to the story moment; supports draw-as-you-go, prepare-in-advance, and reusable 'all-in-one setting map' modes; nurturer's past-tense retelling recorded over the finished drawing

Idea-spark prompts (anti-blank-page aid): for GPs who 'can't think of much to say,' surface generic prompt categories (positions, clothing, light/time, emotions, invented dialogue, what-happens-next questions) — never translations or scripted sentences, preserving the no-memorization rule
One-new-fact relationship journal: each session opens with a small-talk card prompting 'learn one new fact about your nurturer today' and logs it, gamifying the relationship-deepening thread

Sub-phase progress tracker: hour bars for 2A (50h GP-led), 2B (75h nurturer-led), 2C (25h life stories), with the perspective-shift explained at each transition; tracks the lengthening monolingual block and celebrates first 'monolingual day' and 'monolingual week'

Virtual object/rod story-builder: draggable colored blocks or local-object sprites for book-free story-building (Little Red Hen mechanic: hold up the character object while voicing its line), for cultures where wordless books don't fit

Nurturer onboarding mode: a guided first-session script teaching a new nurturer to recast (not lecture), to note failures instead of translating, to point while describing, and to assist retellings conversationally — mirroring how Phase 2A activities orient new nurturers

Three-version story player with A/B compare: listen to the detailed, flowing, and from-memory versions side by side, and to the GP's own retelling vs. the nurturer's, making the here-and-now -> past-tense grammar shift audible and reviewable

Role-play and supplementary activity deck: occasional change-of-pace cards (shopping/taxi/bill-paying role-plays, picture procedure strips, phonetic discrimination drills, Lexicarry-style strips) interspersed by the app's session planner

activities.name: Bridge Story Activity (hearing and massaging a world story)
activities.description: The mainstay activity of Phase 3 (recommended to take at least half of all session time). A 'Bridge Story' is a story belonging to a third, neutral world — neither the grower's home world nor the nurturer's host world — e.g. world fairy tales (Cinderella, Goldilocks), Grimm/Andersen/Aesop/Arabian Nights, or Bible stories (chosen because they exist in nearly all major languages and the grower often knows them already). Because neither party owns the story's world, the nurturer doesn't assume vast host-cultural background knowledge, which radically simplifies understanding. MECHANICS: (Prep) Variant 1: find a children's storybook version in the host language that the grower already knows but has never heard in the host language. Variant 2: the nurturer takes the story home days earlier in a major language she knows, reads it 2-3 times, and comes prepared to tell it in her OWN words — adapting it culturally (e.g. Kazakh version calls the fairy an 'angel'; she opens/closes the story the way host children's stories naturally begin/end, NOT with literal translations of 'Once upon a time' / 'happily ever after') but without radically altering the plot. (Step 1) Nurturer tells or reads the story aloud slowly and carefully; the grower stays silent; the whole telling is captured on a sound recorder. (A pre-existing recording left by earlier growers can replace this step entirely — skip straight to massaging.) (Step 2 — 'massaging') Rewind to the start. Play ONE sentence. If not understood: ask for repetition (often 2-3 times), ask the nurturer to break it into smaller bits, ask what unknown words mean — all explanation strictly in the host language, never translation. If all the words are known but the sentence still isn't understood, ask the nurturer to explain it simply. The grower then actively 'dwells' on each new word: asks for examples ('Tell me an example — someone is mean'), offers his own trial examples ('A man hits his wife. He is mean?') which the nurturer confirms or gently recasts, asks related questions ('A man's wife dies — what do we call him?'), and even probes cultural side-paths ('Among your people, when a man's wife dies, maybe he will marry a widow?'). The nurturer writes each new word into the word log; the grower may pencil a rough native-language gloss beside it plus which story and where it occurred. When the basic gist of the sentence is grasped, move to the next sentence; repeat through the whole recording. The detailed worked example in the text shows this dialogue for the first sentences of Cinderella covering 'widow', 'mean', 'lazy', 'hurt your feelings', 'stepsister', 'divorced', and the causative construction 'made her do the work' (nurturer floods examples: 'A doctor made me take medicine. My mother made me get water. The policeman made me stop my car...'). DIFFICULTY CALIBRATION (explicit rubric): about 30 minutes or less of massaging per minute of recorded story, and 10 or fewer new words per minute of story (5 ideal) = right level. Two hours to massage a two-minute story with 50 new words = too hard; switch to the nurturer telling it spontaneously and simply in her own words, or fall back to Phase-2-style wordless picture stories told without looking at the pictures. The activity must feel pleasant, not tedious. (Homework) Listen to the massaged recording repeatedly before the next session, pausing and replaying the words that strike you as most useful, and keep re-listening over coming weeks until the whole story is EASY to follow — the guide warns much of Phase 3's power is lost without this.
activities.materials: Children's storybook versions of world stories (Cinderella, Goldilocks, Noah and the Great Flood, The First Man and Woman — full reference texts provided in Appendix 2); Bible storybooks; collections (Grimm, Andersen, Aesop, Arabian Nights, home-culture folk tale collections like Folk Tales from Korea); sound recorder; word log notebook; pre-existing recordings from previous growers where available
activities.timing: From Day 1 onward, throughout all of Phase 3; 2.5-4.5 hours per 5-hour session in the sample schedules; could legitimately dominate the entire 250 hours

activities.name: Script of Life Activity
activities.description: A 'Script of Life' is a 25-30-step, blow-by-blow description of an everyday host-world routine FROM THE HOST PERSON'S POINT OF VIEW (similar to the Series Method, but it only counts as a Script of Life if a host person authors it). The grower understands it because he already largely knows what to expect from living in the host world, while simultaneously refining his picture of how host people actually experience the activity. ONE-TIME TRAINING SEQUENCE (first session only): (T1) The grower physically walks to the sink and washes his hands, pausing 25-30 times, asking after each micro-step 'What did I do?' / 'What am I doing?'; the nurturer names each step and writes it down (open the door, turn on the light, walk to the sink, turn the hot tap, pick up the soap, rub soap on hands, rinse, reach for the towel, fold it, hang it, turn off the light...). This trains the nurturer in the required level of granularity. (T2) Nurturer reads her step list aloud; record it. (T3) Massage the recording (nearly everything will be understood since it was visually supported — this is the last time visual support is used; from now on familiarity with the event sequence replaces it). (T4) The grower uses an 'attempted' Script of Life he prepared in his own native language (Appendix 2 gives a 29-step Kazakh example, 'Using a Bus' — wait at the stop, guess where the door will stop, squeeze up the aisle, hold the overhead rail with one hand, hand the conductor 500 tenge, give your seat to the man with crutches, ask 'Are you getting off?' to each person between you and the door...). He does NOT show it to the nurturer even if she reads that language; instead he negotiates each step's meaning in the host language and she writes the host-language version — a second demonstration of the desired detail level. After training, the grower never authors scripts again. NORMAL FORM: (1) The nurturer makes the step list for a common activity she does (e.g. buying meat). (2) She goes through it action by action; the grower asks for explanation of anything unclear and probes for more granularity: 'After you do X and before Y, what do you do?' 'How do you do step X in smaller steps?' (3) Record the full list read straight through. (4) Massage the recording (often easier than stories because the nurturer can pantomime unknown actions); add new words to the word log. (5) Play the recording and PANTOMIME each step as you hear it. The recording joins the Listening Library. Topics must be experiences known to BOTH parties (a wedding you've never attended is not yet eligible — save unfamiliar scripts for Phase 4); a near-familiar host situation like a dentist visit is an acceptable stretch.
activities.materials: An 'attempted' Script of Life pre-written by the grower in his own language; sound recorder; word log; Appendix 3's brainstorm list of script ideas by domain (home: sweeping/mopping, lighting the stove, changing a gas bottle; food: making rice/tea, cleaning a fish; personal care: haircut, doctor visit; errands: using an ATM, recharging a cellphone, paying bills; clothing: wearing a sarong; car care: changing a tire; baby care: changing a nappy; village life: opening a coconut, feeding chickens)
activities.timing: Day 1 includes training steps; thereafter roughly 1 hour, 2-3 days per week in the sample schedule; one of the two non-postponable core activities (with Bridge Stories)

activities.name: Action Cartoon Activity
activities.description: Uses dialogue-free, action-heavy cartoons (Tom & Jerry is the stock example) as shared stories. PREP: the grower watches the cartoon PRIVATELY before the session, so the plot is already familiar to him. MECHANICS: (1) Arrange the screen so the NURTURER can see it but the grower CANNOT — this deliberately manufactures an 'information gap' so the nurturer feels she has something genuinely new to tell. She narrates the story live as she watches (she may first watch it once silently since live narration is hard); record her narration. (2) Watch the cartoon together while listening to the recording. (3) Rewind and massage the recording exactly as with Cinderella; add new words to the word log. (4) The nurturer retells the whole story WITHOUT the cartoon playing — a far more natural narrative than the play-by-play version — first reviewing the word log so she deliberately re-includes all the new vocabulary; record this second, polished version for the Listening Library. (5) Massage the new recording if needed. Listen several times before the next session. Notes on alternatives: silent films work too — Charlie Chaplin's world is so removed in time that it functions like a Bridge Story (usable early); Mr. Bean embeds so much British culture that the nurturer may misread scenes, so it is better saved for Phase 3C.
activities.materials: Tom & Jerry or similar low-dialogue action cartoons on DVD/video; player arranged for one-way viewing; sound recorder; word log; alternatives: Charlie Chaplin (earlier), Mr. Bean (Phase 3C)
activities.timing: From Day 1; about 1 hour, 2 days per week in the sample full schedule; postponable (unlike Bridge Stories and Scripts of Life)

activities.name: Shared Experience Activity
activities.description: The closing activity of a session day: grower and nurturer go out (or stay in) and DO something together — go to a coffee shop, shoot baskets, work in the vegetable garden, clean the messy kitchen, buy something, play a game, or take a walk observing everything (vary the route each time). They interact naturally in the host language throughout. The nurturer makes notes afterward about details of what was observed/done. Over time the nurturer gets into the flow of proposing experiences herself. The experience is not an end in itself: it creates fresh, genuinely shared first-person material that fuels the next day's Reminiscing Activity, and it bonds the relationship. By late Phase 3 a Shared Experience can occasionally stretch to a whole day or two (e.g. a weekend outing), yielding extensive reminiscing material.
activities.materials: None required beyond everyday settings; nurturer's notepad for post-experience notes; a running brainstormed list of Shared Experience ideas
activities.timing: Last activity of the day, about 1 hour, 2 days per week in the sample schedule; occasionally a full weekend by late Phase 3

activities.name: Reminiscing Activity
activities.description: Begins the day after a Shared Experience. (1) The grower asks the nurturer to tell about what the two of them did yesterday. (2) She narrates while a recording is made — but it must be a TRUE reminiscence, i.e. the grower interacts: he supplies back-channel listener signals appropriate to the host culture (the text gives the Canadian example: 'yeah', 'really!', 'mhm', 'I see'), recognizes turn-taking cues from pauses and content, contributes brief turns ('I was afraid'), then quickly hands the floor back so the nurturer does most of the talking. Worked example: N: 'We went to a coffee shop.' GP: 'Yeah.' N: 'We walked there together. We were talking about the traffic. You said you are afraid to cross the street.' GP: 'I was afraid.' (3) Massage the recording as with Cinderella; the recording joins the Listening Library; listen a few times before the next session. The activity doubles as deliberate training in host conversation mechanics — if the grower hasn't been observing how host listeners signal attention, he must start now.
activities.materials: Yesterday's Shared Experience notes; sound recorder; word log
activities.timing: Introduced Day 2; about 1 hour on the mornings after Shared Experience days (2 days per week in the sample schedule)

activities.name: Strengthening Vocabulary Activity (optional)
activities.description: A short warm-up review in which the GROWER does the talking: he reminds the nurturer of words learned yesterday, putting each back into its original context. Example: GP: 'I learned mean and lazy. Cinderella's sisters... uhm, not sisters. Like sisters.' N: 'Stepsisters.' GP: 'Cinderella's stepsisters were mean. They said bad things to her... They were lazy. They slept all day.' N: 'Yeah, they were mean and lazy.' Or from a Script of Life: 'I learned grind. You talked about buying meat. Maybe the butcher grinds the meat.' Words can come from ANY of yesterday's activities. Explicitly flagged as optional and dangerous to over-run: it 'can eat up too much time' so that nothing new gets done — possibly limit it to only the words that felt most important.
activities.materials: Yesterday's word log entries
activities.timing: About 20 minutes at the start of each session (after small talk), per the sample schedules

activities.name: Familiar-Place Description Activity
activities.description: The nurturer describes a place WELL KNOWN to the grower — his home, apartment building, street, the nearby market, a particular shop, the public square, or a route he commonly travels — and the description is recorded, massaged sentence-by-sentence, and re-listened to before the next session. Moves the grower toward understanding how local places are conceived of by host people, directly enriching host-world knowledge.
activities.materials: Brainstormed list of familiar places and routes; sound recorder; word log
activities.timing: Optional Phase 3A enrichment; appears as a 1-hour block in the Phase 3B 'adventuresome' sample day

activities.name: Conversations Centred Around Common Objects (Discuss-a-Prop Activity)
activities.description: A return to visual support but with free-ranging interaction: take an everyday object (sink, stove, tape recorder, bicycle, clock, car...) and discuss everything people do with and to it, while physically doing things with it. Record the whole interaction, negotiating meanings live as you go (the negotiation itself is on the recording). Real examples from the text: a family of growers spent an hour on a table lamp (bulb burning out and replacing it led to electric power, which led the nurturer to walk them to the electrical panel and meter and fold those into the discussion) and another hour on a length of rope (three growers tied each other up, dragged one another around, and did 'everything else imaginable'). Listen to the recording a few times before the next session.
activities.materials: Any common household object as a prop; sound recorder; word log
activities.timing: Optional Phase 3A enrichment activity

activities.name: Reverse Role-Play Activity
activities.description: Spontaneous (never memorized-lines) acting-out of real verbal-interaction situations from the grower's daily life — taxi rides, making a purchase, being stopped by traffic police. KEY TWIST: roles are deliberately inverted. The NURTURER plays the role the grower normally has in real life (e.g. customer) and the GROWER plays the counterpart (taxi driver, shopkeeper, police officer), acting it as best he can ('which won't be very well!'). The payoff: by hearing what the nurturer says in HIS usual role — and recording it — he gets a model of exactly how he himself could talk in those situations. Record, massage, listen before the next session. Then, on a later day after he has listened to the recording several times, swap to the Ordinary Role-Play: the grower takes his real-life role, the nurturer takes the counterpart — now modeling what he can expect to HEAR said to him. Alternatively, skip straight to the ordinary direction and let the nurturer assist him in saying what he's trying to say.
activities.materials: Brainstormed list of real-life interaction situations; sound recorder; word log
activities.timing: Optional Phase 3A onward; 15-minute block in the Phase 3B sample day (e.g. role-play of getting a haircut); reverse first, ordinary direction a few days later

activities.name: Phase 2 Carry-Over Activities (Story-Building, Free Cooperative Story-Building, Autobiographical Picture Stories)
activities.description: Phase 2 activities remain richly rewarding: Story-building with the grower in the lead (Phase 2A style — to force more talking), with the nurturer in the lead (2B — to learn new material), free cooperative story-building (neither in the lead), and Autobiographical Picture Stories (2C). FREE COOPERATIVE STORY-BUILDING mechanics: take a wordless picture storybook; both parties freely and spontaneously contribute to building the story; add words to the word log as you go; finish the whole book; then the nurturer — using the word log as a checklist of new words to re-include — tells the complete story while it is recorded; massage if needed; re-listen before the next session. Anno's Journey (Mitsumasa Anno, 1977) is specifically recommended and judged 'more suited to Phase 3 than Phase 2'. AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL PICTURE STORIES (telling stories from one's own life supported by quick sketches) would have been in the essential Phase 3 set except some people resist sketching; it is singled out — along with Shared Experiences and Reminiscing — as especially valuable for deepening the personal relationship, since Bridge Stories alone don't carry personal life content.
activities.materials: Wordless picture storybooks; Anno's Journey; pencil and paper for autobiographical sketches; sound recorder; word log
activities.timing: Optional throughout Phase 3; recommended additions especially in Phase 3B for those who used too few activities

activities.name: Structured Input Activities (grammar through forced listening)
activities.description: Repeats of Phase 1-style activities for grammar areas the grower still struggles with. An activity forces attention to a grammatical form by making it the ONLY carrier of meaning. Worked example ('to and from'): set up a doll family and a bag of candies. First the nurturer gives full commands: 'Give a candy to the mother; take a candy from the son; give a candy to me.' Then she DROPS the verbs (which redundantly imply direction) and says only 'From me; to yourself; from the father; to the baby' — now the grower must decode the to/from grammar itself to act correctly. Designable for many basic grammar elements (see the Phase 1 guide for more).
activities.materials: Props that physicalize the grammar point (doll family, bag of candies, etc.)
activities.timing: As needed in Phase 3 and later, only for persisting trouble spots

activities.name: Input Flooding
activities.description: When the grower notices he keeps TRYING to produce a certain sentence type and failing (e.g. relative clauses: 'the man who is sweeping the street'), he arranges to hear hundreds of meaningful instances of exactly that type. Mechanics with a 'busy picture' (a drawing crowded with an unnaturally large number of people each doing something — Ed King's William Wanders Off is the favorite, with 100+ people in the first picture: walking the roof peak, hanging from rafters as a ladder falls, looking through binoculars, carried into the air by helium balloons...): the grower shows the nurturer a few examples of the target form applied to the picture; then the nurturer produces it over and over — pointing ('Here is a man who is...') or, better, querying ('Where is the man who...?', which FORCES the grower to attend) — easily a hundred times per picture. Photos, photo albums, National Geographic or coffee-table books work too. Record and massage as necessary; re-listen before next session. Cardinal rule: only flood forms the grower is ALREADY trying to use in his own speech — never arbitrary grammar patterns drilled months before they're needed (the explicit anti-textbook argument).
activities.materials: Busy books: William Wanders Off / Lucy is Lost / Roving Rosie Reports (Ed King); Usborne 1001 Things to Spot series; Heather Amery's The First 1000 Words; photo sets, magazines; sound recorder
activities.timing: On demand when a production struggle is noticed; 15-minute block in the Phase 3B sample day (e.g. flooding 'This boy is trying to...')

activities.name: Output Flooding
activities.description: The production-side sequel to Input Flooding, picking up where it left off after the grower has heard the target form hundreds of times: turn to a NEW busy picture and now the GROWER attempts to produce many, many statements about people and things in it using the target construction ('Here is a man who...', over and over). Same cardinal rule: only with sentence/phrase types he is genuinely struggling to use in real interaction.
activities.materials: A fresh busy picture (different from the input-flooding one)
activities.timing: Immediately following an Input Flooding cycle on the same construction

activities.name: Scripts of Life as Input/Output Flooding material
activities.description: A highly familiar Script of Life is retold by the nurturer in a transformed grammatical frame to flood a target form: original habitual form ('I walk to the door. I reach out my hand. I take hold of the doorknob...') becomes future/intent ('In a while, I will wash my hands. First I will walk to the bathroom door...') or complex subordination ('After I walk to the door, I will reach out my hand. After I reach out my hand, I will take hold of the doorknob...'). Only done with scripts already highly familiar in their original form, and only for forms the grower is actively reaching for in his own speech. General grammar warning attached: Phase 3 exposes lots of grammar above current speaking level — don't panic; as understood-speech volume grows, rare forms become common and migrate into speech naturally; flooding is the remedy for the stubborn ones (Phase 4 adds accent/error-reduction activities).
activities.materials: Previously massaged and re-listened Script of Life recordings
activities.timing: On demand, mid-to-late Phase 3

activities.name: Host-Story-as-Shared-Story Activity (the prime Phase 3B activity)
activities.description: Converts genuinely local host stories into shared stories by pre-loading the plot via translation. Mechanics: (1) Ask the nurturer to list stories universally (or very widely) known among her people. (2) Have someone retell several of these in English (or another language the grower knows well), captured as a recording or written out. (3) HOMEWORK: the grower listens to / reads this translation EVERY DAY FOR SEVERAL DAYS until the story is highly familiar — the author's own cautionary tale: he read Russian versions of Kazakh children's texts only right before sessions instead of for days in advance, and months later those Listening Library recordings were no longer easy to follow, unlike permanently familiar world stories. (4) Only when the story feels thoroughly known, hear it in the host language in session for the first time; record and massage exactly per the Cinderella procedure; re-listen before next sessions. WHY HARDER THAN BRIDGE STORIES: with host stories there is now a vast pool of background knowledge the nurturer has and the grower lacks, so explanations get more complex; if the time-cost outweighs benefit, postpone it another 50 hours and retry. Re-listen to these recordings MORE often than Bridge Story ones (their plots fade; Bridge Story plots never do). Pioneers should leave their recordings behind so later growers can skip the prep work.
activities.materials: Nurturer's list of universally known host stories; translations (recorded or written) into the grower's strong language; sound recorder; word log
activities.timing: Phase 3B (hours 100-175); 2 hours in the 'adventuresome' sample day, 3.5 hours in the 'simple' sample day

activities.name: Make the Difficulty Keep Rising (Phase 3B calibration move)
activities.description: Explicit leveling-up mechanic at the 3A-to-3B boundary: if the grower needed greatly simplified tellings early on, have the same/new stories now told in more natural form; if spoken and written language are similar, graduate from simplified spontaneous tellings to WRITTEN stories read aloud (written language has longer sentences, more complex sentences, richer vocabulary). If the grower already started Day 1 with written stories read aloud without tedium, jump straight to host stories as shared stories. Appendix 4 (by Rebecca Huston) supplies a full 12-level difficulty ladder for Stuff-We-Both-Know resources: 1) wordless books retold without looking at pictures / other GPs' recordings; 2) world stories retold in the nurturer's own words; 3) silent videos (Tom & Jerry, Mr. Bean, Chaplin) narrated live or described afterward; 4) local pre-school stories pre-learned in translation, retold; 5) world stories READ aloud from host-language print; 6) local stories read aloud (pre-learned in translation); 7) more complex/abstract local stories with conflict or misunderstanding; 8) longer translated children's classics read aloud; 9) local children's/young-adult books, nurturer orally translating first if no translation exists, then reading as written; 10) feature-film plot retellings (GP summarizes/retells); 11) abstract school-textbook material for youth (orally translated first, then read as written); 12) abstract adult-level expository print, same method. Mixing nearby levels in one day (e.g. 2-4) is fine and gives a good balance of new-word encounters and understandable speech.
activities.materials: Appendix 4 difficulty-ladder table; progressively harder story sources; an LLA-gathered collection (recommended: 150+ children's books, silent videos, translated world stories, recordings shared by previous GPs on a CD)
activities.timing: Transition into Phase 3B and continuously thereafter

activities.name: Familiar Topic Activity (expository discourse — Phase 3C)
activities.description: Moves beyond narrative into abstract 'expository discourse' — harder than stories in general, but an abstract discussion of a topic the listener knows DEEPLY is often easier in a new language than an unfamiliar story. The nurturer tells or reads aloud about a topic highly familiar to the grower; record; massage; re-listen. Constraint: the topic must be understood SIMILARLY in home and host worlds (arithmetic fails if the host approach to discussing it differs too much). Sourcing tied to the grower's vocation/interests: health workers use public-health pamphlets (malaria prevention, prenatal health); agricultural workers use farmer-oriented materials; hobbyists find a host person who shares the interest and record them on 'how to take good care of your car'; religious growers massage sermons on familiar passages or published training materials read aloud. Builds the expository-comprehension muscle needed for Phase 4. The author's Kazakh trick: parallel Russian/Kazakh children's editions on history, geography, nature, holidays — read the Russian days in advance, then hear the Kazakh in session.
activities.materials: Pamphlets, simple textbooks, parallel-language children's nonfiction, sermons, hobby explainers; sound recorder; word log
activities.timing: Phase 3C (final 75 hours)

activities.name: Movie Plots
activities.description: The nurturer tells from memory the plot of a popular movie that the grower has seen in his own language and she has seen in hers (world hits are commonly dubbed into major languages; for minority languages she may have seen it in the regional major language, or can watch it specially). Record her telling; massage; re-listen before the next session. Pure shared-story logic applied to film.
activities.materials: A mutually known feature film; sound recorder; word log
activities.timing: Phase 3C / advanced Phase 3

activities.name: Book Summary
activities.description: Same as Movie Plots but with novels: the nurturer summarizes a novel the grower has read in his language and she has read in hers. Strategy tip: read host-world novels in English translation now for relaxation, then later hear them summarized in the host language, and later still read the originals. (Anecdote: classic Russian novels in English translation sold in the EFL section at St. Petersburg State University — 'someone there had discovered the shared-story principle.') Record, massage, re-listen.
activities.materials: Mutually known novels / translated host novels; sound recorder
activities.timing: Phase 3C / advanced Phase 3

activities.name: News Broadcasts
activities.description: Record TV/radio/Internet news in the host language and massage the recordings; or have the nurturer read a newspaper aloud for recording and massaging (for diglossic languages like Arabic: she reads the formal article, then RETELLS it in spoken Arabic, which naturally mixes formal vocabulary into speech). International/world news counts as 'familiar topics' (the grower already follows it); local news is harder unless he's locally informed — EXCEPT serially developing local stories (e.g. court trials), where following earlier installments makes new ones predictable, so advance knowledge matters less.
