Commitment warning: a few hours then quitting wastes the vocabulary flood; persisted with, news vocabulary repeats so frequently that 'what seemed like a flood of new words will be commonplace, familiar friends', creating a permanent self-serve source of comprehensible listening.
activities.materials: Recordable news broadcasts; newspapers; sound recorder
activities.timing: Phase 3C, with sustained regular time investment

activities.name: Your Old Stories Retold 'Native-to-Native' (Earlier Stories in More Advanced Versions)
activities.description: Bootstraps comprehension of fast, natural native speech (the Phase 5 target) using maximally familiar content: the nurturer takes stories she already told the grower and retells them naturally to ANOTHER HOST PERSON with the grower absent, recording herself. The result: a highly familiar core and vocabulary, but in real native-to-native register — faster, less enunciated, unsimplified. Later, grower and nurturer listen together and massage; then he re-listens alone. Recommended to try at least once near the end of Phase 3 'just to see how much more demanding it is', then continue through Phase 4. Supporting anecdote: in Pakistan the author bought 17 hours of bazaar cassettes of children's stories (mostly world stories) — native-to-native in style yet familiar, hence understandable after a few listenings even without a nurturer, about a year in.
activities.materials: Previously used story recordings; a second host person; sound recorder; commercially available native story cassettes/audio where they exist
activities.timing: End of Phase 3C, continuing into Phase 4

activities.name: Story Retelling Activity (talking-more activity)
activities.description: After hearing, recording and massaging a story, the GROWER retells it to the nurturer in his own words at his own ability level, framed as 'Let me see if I understood your story. Here is what I think you said.' He makes a deliberate effort to reuse the new vocabulary encountered in that story. Works best mid-to-late Phase 3; better with Bridge Stories than with translation-learned local stories (unless those became exceedingly familiar); some growers can start it in 3A, others find it too hard until 3B/C.
activities.materials: Any freshly massaged story plus its word-log entries
activities.timing: Mid-to-late Phase 3, whenever the grower is talking too little in sessions

activities.name: Telling Stories From Your Life (talking-more activity)
activities.description: The grower picks an interesting experience from childhood or later and tells the WHOLE story to the nurturer — explicitly forbidden to skip the hard parts; he pushes through with heavy negotiation of meaning no matter how hard it gets (the content being fixed in advance is what makes this a good stretching exercise). Once the full story has been conveyed, the NURTURER retells it and that retelling is recorded into the Listening Library. Retelling it later to other people shows measurable improvement each time.
activities.materials: Sound recorder; word log
activities.timing: Mid-to-late Phase 3 (Autobiographical Picture Stories serve the earlier part of the phase)

activities.name: Ongoing 'Epic' Stories (talking-more activity)
activities.description: The grower chooses a long, personally important story that 'goes on and on' and develops it serially — telling a new installment at each meeting with the nurturer AND re-telling each installment to other people in his developing relationships afterward. The nurturer records her retelling of each new segment. The version told now is bare-bones; in Phases 4-6 the same epic gets retold in progressively fuller, richer forms. Optional staging support: a single scene-setting picture per installment (NOT the frame-by-frame picture support of Phase 2).
activities.materials: Optional one picture per installment; sound recorder
activities.timing: Recurring serial thread through late Phase 3 and revisited in Phases 4-6

activities.name: What I Did on the Weekend (or Yesterday)
activities.description: The activity many learners gravitate to naturally: telling the tutor everything done the previous day/weekend in great detail, without avoiding hard parts, negotiating meanings as necessary; the nurturer then makes a final recording of HER retelling of the grower's account. Honest caveat in the text: it 'soon becomes highly repetitive' — return to it only when yesterday/the weekend was out of the ordinary.
activities.materials: Sound recorder
activities.timing: Occasional, event-driven

activities.name: Lexicarry Story Strips and Busy-Picture Talking
activities.description: Patrick Moran's Lexicarry contains 3-frame comic-strip communication situations (e.g. bumping into someone and needing to apologize) with EMPTY speech bubbles; the grower fills the bubbles orally from imagination. In Phase 3 the upgrade is VARIATION: tell each strip's story, then deliberately explore MANY options for what could be said in each bubble ('there is more than one way to apologise for knocking someone down'), with the nurturer suggesting alternatives; record a summary of the discussion. Profitably repeatable even if used in Phases 1-2 — discussions get richer each phase. Busy pictures and wordless books used Phase-2B-style (grower in the lead) likewise remain rich talking fodder.
activities.materials: Lexicarry (Patrick Moran); busy books; wordless picture storybooks (Anno's Journey); sound recorder
activities.timing: Talking-more option throughout Phase 3

activities.name: Matters Currently of Wide Interest in the Community
activities.description: Ask the nurturer what people in the community are talking about these days — recent events, community problems, gossip (awareness may also grow out of the news activities). Not strictly Stuff-We-Both-Know, but once introduced, a topic can be RETURNED to repeatedly for updates, and a revisited topic is much easier to discuss than a brand-new one. Record the nurturer's opinions on these matters; massage as necessary; then deliberately raise the same topics in conversations with other people the grower chats with — bridging session content into real social life.
activities.materials: Sound recorder; news sources
activities.timing: Phase 3C / late Phase 3

activities.name: Brainstorming and List-Building (special chore)
activities.description: Infrastructure work: grower and nurturer build and continually grow four idea lists — (1) Scripts of Life ideas, (2) Shared Experience ideas, (3) familiar places and routes for Familiar-Place Descriptions, (4) situations for Role-Plays. The grower carries a small pad through daily life adding activities he already participates in; he shows the list to the nurturer who builds her own complementary list; they suggest additions to each other's lists. Feeder tactic: 'get out and do things in the host world' — open a bank account, mail a letter, get a haircut, visit a tailor — both as direct experience and as list fuel (a Script of Life only qualifies if the grower knows the situation first-hand). Appendix 3 (Rebecca Huston) prescribes group brainstorming with other GPs and sharing lists; unfamiliar items (e.g. an unattended wedding) go on a separate future-Phase-4 list.
activities.materials: Pocket notepad; shared lists among multiple GPs; Appendix 3 example list for the Malay world
activities.timing: Start 'right away' in Phase 3A, ongoing

activities.name: Producing Bridge Stories (special chore / resource pipeline)
activities.description: Sourcing pipeline: free online collections (Grimm, Andersen, Aesop, Arabian Nights); Bible storybooks purchasable in most countries; home-culture collections (e.g. Folk Tales from Korea — a Korean friend flagged the 10 universally-known stories in it). Texts aren't Bridge Stories until told in the host language: a bilingual nurturer takes them home in English or another language she knows and learns them for retelling. Growers are urged to leave their recordings behind for those who follow (the LLA should gather GPs' recordings onto a CD); if no bilingual nurturer exists, a different (unspecified) approach is needed and pioneers should build Phase 3 resources for successors.
activities.materials: Internet story collections; Bible storybooks; home-culture folk tale books; Appendix 2's four ready-to-use story texts
activities.timing: Phase 3A chore, front-loaded

activities.name: Getting Serious Social Life Underway (Phase 3B requirement)
activities.description: Structural life change, not a session activity: if the paid nurturer is still the only strong host relationship, fix that now. The grower may count 3-5 hours/week of ordinary social interaction toward his 25 focused hours (no more — supercharged sessions must not shrink further). Tactics: ride taxis and talk to the driver the whole way; invite a neighbour for tea; visit shopkeepers during their identifiable slow hours; brainstorm a personal list of existing social openings. Vivid case study: in a 'closed' city where the nurturer said no one befriends unknown neighbours, the author's family prepared tea and sweets and knocked on all three nearby doors — one refusal, one no-answer, and one delighted widow whose husband had been killed a month earlier; the lesson is that starting relationships may require doing something 'uncultural'. HARD GATE: 'you do not graduate from Phase 3B to 3C until you have done this.' By late Phase 3: get the nurturer to introduce her own close friends for spin-off one-on-one relationships; consider living with a host family (NOT recommended before mid-to-late Phase 3 — earlier immersion homestays cause stress without growth), rural village stays, host roommates for singles, or taking in host student boarders.
activities.materials: Tea and sweets; a brainstormed list of social-opening settings
activities.timing: Phase 3B onward; 1 hour of stranger-conversation or neighbour-visiting appears in both Phase 3B sample days

activities.name: Starting to Read (and its two warnings)
activities.description: Phase 3 is the earliest sensible point for host-language literacy because only now is there material at the grower's level — and the massaged familiar stories themselves are ideal first reading. Research cited: L2 reading ability depends mainly on L1 reading ability and overall L2 level. Except for character-based scripts, an already-literate adult learns to read 'moderately well in a short time just by doing it a lot'. WARNING 1 (don't cheat while listening): when a nurturer reads aloud in session, glancing at the printed sentence short-circuits the listening-comprehension process — print 'just sits there motionless' while sound vanishes instantly; the strain of repeated listening IS the training. Read alone at home; never follow the text while she reads. WARNING 2 (don't pay for read-alouds by you): learners who spend tutor time reading aloud themselves while the tutor nods are wasting paid nurturer hours on something doable alone; nurturer time should go to things only a nurturer can do, like reading aloud TO you.
activities.materials: Printed versions of already-massaged familiar stories
activities.timing: Mid-to-late Phase 3, solo homework time only

activities.name: Small Talk (opening ritual + explicit warning)
activities.description: Every session OPENS with a few minutes of small talk in the host language, putting the personal relationship first ('Always take an interest in the nurturer's life and feelings, putting that ahead of your other planned activities'). Role-discipline joke: if small talk happened in the grower's language, the nurturer would become the growing participator. THE WARNING: by late Phase 3, talkative growers are tempted to fill paid sessions with chitchat. Small talk is mildly supercharged (the nurturer stays in the growth zone) but doesn't drive new vocabulary or rising difficulty — it produces the 'stuck on a plateau' effect and a private communication style with the nurturer 'that makes it unnecessary to keep growing'. Resolution: a few minutes at the start, plus natural small-talk eddies arising out of activities (massaging a story often drifts into personal lives) and occasional genuinely important personal sharing — but never hours of chat replacing activities. 'Keeping relationships at centre stage also means keeping growth in view.'
activities.materials: None
activities.timing: 10-15 minutes at the start of every session, all phases

appIdeas: Sentence-by-sentence 'massaging player': the app slices a recorded story into sentences; the learner taps Play per sentence, with one-tap Repeat (counting repetitions), 'Break it down' (sub-segment playback), and 'I understand the gist — next'. Unknown words are flagged in-line and trigger a host-language-only explanation flow (no translation shown by default; learner may privately attach a rough native-language gloss, story name, and position, mirroring the word log convention).

Auto-building word log linked to audio timestamps: every word flagged during massaging is saved with the exact second in the recording where it occurs, the activity it came from, and a learner-marked importance level ('recognize only' vs 'want to use' — the stepsister/lazy distinction). Re-listening jumps straight to flagged moments and replays them several times for extra impression.

Listening Library with 'until it's easy' tracking: each massaged recording carries a familiarity meter; the app schedules re-listens (walking, waiting, commuting reminders) and asks after each listen 'Was it easy to follow?' — recordings stay in rotation until rated easy, then resurface periodically to refresh iceberg words, directly implementing the frequency principle.

Difficulty calibration calculator: the app times massaging per minute of story audio and counts new words per story-minute, then renders the guide's explicit rubric (≤30 min massaging and ≤10 new words per story-minute = right level; 5 words/min ideal; 2 hrs + 50 words for a 2-min story = too hard) with concrete next-step advice (have it retold simply, drop to wordless-book retellings, or level up the 12-step Appendix 4 difficulty ladder).

Script of Life builder: a step-list editor where the nurturer (or a recorded host voice) enters 25-30 micro-steps; the app records each step as its own audio chip, supports the 'add a step between X and Y' and 'break step X into smaller steps' probes, and offers a pantomime playback mode (audio plays step-by-step while the learner acts each one out). Ships with the Appendix 3 idea bank (home, food, errands, clothing, car care, baby care, village life) and a separate 'save for Phase 4' bucket for not-yet-experienced situations.

Information-gap cartoon mode: plays a dialogue-free cartoon visible only on the nurturer's screen while recording her live narration; then a watch-together replay synced to her narration; then a second 'natural retelling' recording flow that shows her the session's new-word list as a checklist to weave back in — the app verifies which logged words appear in version 2.

Shared Experience + Reminiscing loop: a lightweight diary where learner and nurturer log what they did together (photos, notes, route walked); the next day the app prompts the Reminiscing recording and overlays culture-appropriate back-channel coaching ('yeah / really? / mhm' equivalents), nudging the learner to interject briefly then return the floor.

Strengthening Vocabulary warm-up with a hard timer: the app deals yesterday's flagged words as prompt cards ('Put it back in its story context'), capped at ~20 minutes because the guide explicitly warns this activity eats sessions.

Input/Output Flooding studio: load a busy picture (or photo set); pick a target construction you've been failing to produce; the app counts nurturer repetitions toward a 100+ goal in 'Where is the man who...?' quiz mode (forced attention), then flips to a NEW picture for output mode where the learner produces the construction repeatedly; gated by a self-report that the form is one you're actually reaching for in real speech — never an arbitrary drill.

Host-story prep pipeline with familiarity gating: for a host story, the app stores the English/known-language translation (audio or text) and enforces the 'listen/read daily for several days' homework with a streak; only after the familiarity threshold does it unlock the host-language first-listen and massaging session (encoding the author's own Kazakh failure story).

Reverse Role-Play scenario engine: scenario cards from the learner's own brainstormed situations (taxi, shop, police stop, haircut) with a role-swap toggle; first run records the nurturer modeling the learner's real-life role; after N re-listens the app unlocks the swapped ordinary direction.

Weekly schedule planner with canonical templates: prebuilt 25-hr full-time week (small talk 10 min, vocab 20 min, Bridge Story 2.5 hr, Scripts of Life 1 hr, Cartoon/Shared Experience 1 hr) and the simple variant (Bridge Story 3.5-4.5 hr + Scripts of Life), a part-time 2-hr morning template, plus a live dashboard tracking the 8-new-words-per-hour target and ~15 hr/week of solo listening.

Community resource commons: growers publish their massaged recordings, host-story translations, Scripts of Life, and idea lists per languaculture so newcomers 'go straight to the massaging step' — explicitly the pioneers-leave-resources vision, organized by the Appendix 4 difficulty levels 1-12.

Phase 3B social-life gate: a relationships tracker (taxi chats, neighbour teas, shopkeeper visits, nurturer's friends) where logging 3-5 hrs/week of real social interaction counts toward the weekly 25; the app withholds the Phase 3C content tier until at least one new non-nurturer relationship is logged, mirroring 'you do not graduate from 3B to 3C until you have done this'.

Anti-chitchat session guardrail: a gentle small-talk timer at session start and an end-of-session activity-mix report flagging weeks where unstructured chat displaced supercharged activities (the plateau warning).

Listening-first reading mode: printed text of a story unlocks only after its recording is rated 'easy to follow', and the reader view is disabled during live listening exercises — operationalizing 'don't cheat by looking at the printed page'.

Epic-story serial composer: the learner maintains an ongoing personal story, recording a new installment per session with one scene-setting image each; the nurturer's retelling of each segment is captured to the Listening Library, and the app tracks retellings of each segment to other real people.

Lexicarry-style empty-bubble strips: 3-frame communication-situation comics with blank speech bubbles; the learner voices multiple alternative fillings per bubble and records a variation-summary discussion with the nurturer.
goals: Understand relatively rich and complex stories (vs. the simple picture-supported narratives of Phase 2)
Understand more abstract explanations ('expository speech') WITHOUT visual-aid support — preparing for Phase 4's in-depth explanations of the host world
Grow listening vocabulary by another 2,000-3,000 words, reaching roughly 4,000-5,000 total
Attain 'basic conversational ability': discuss a wide range of topics including previously undiscussed ones, and tell simple stories
Deepen the relationship with the nurturer through shared stories, Scripts of Life, Shared Experiences and Reminiscing
Begin NEW relationships with host people beyond the paid nurturer (a hard requirement for graduating Phase 3B to 3C); consider a host-family homestay in mid-to-late Phase 3
Greatly enlarge the Listening Library and become so familiar with every recording that it is easy to follow
Grow ability to negotiate complex meanings, understand individual sentences with increasing ease, and follow richly textured stories
Increase knowledge of basic daily host-world activities (via Scripts of Life, Familiar-Place Descriptions, Shared Experiences)
Possibly begin reading, since for the first time material exists at the grower's level (the massaged familiar stories themselves)
phase3doc.hours: 250 hours total: Phase 3A = 100 hours, Phase 3B = 75 hours, Phase 3C = 75 hours (ideally ~25 hours/week of supercharged sessions plus ~15 hours/week of solo listening/reading homework; may finish early and move to Phase 4 if activities become easy)
keyPrinciples: Shared-story / 'Stuff-We-Both-Know' principle: content already largely known and predictable to the listener is understandable in the host language long before unfamiliar content, letting a whole range of listening abilities develop ahead of schedule

Understanding-led, listening-dependent (vs. traditional speech-led, writing-dependent approaches): comprehension is the foundational ability on which speaking, reading, and writing are built; listening ability is deliberately pushed FAR ahead of speaking ability
No translation in session: all explanation, negotiation, and small talk happen exclusively in the host language (the grower may privately note rough glosses in the word log)
Massaging recordings: sentence-by-sentence playback with negotiation of meaning until the whole recording can be followed with understanding
Negotiation of meaning: the engine of growth — asking, checking, recasting, exemplifying, groping for words with the nurturer's help
Iceberg Principle: no word memorization; words enter a mental iceberg through meaningful acquaintance and rise with each re-encounter; target an average of 8+ new word acquaintances per hour

Frequency principle: language processing strengthens with frequency, so massive exposure to UNDERSTOOD speech is essential — hence relentless re-listening to the Listening Library until everything is easy
Information gap: arrange activities so the nurturer genuinely has something to tell that the grower doesn't visibly know (e.g. hiding the cartoon screen from the grower)

Relationship before curriculum: the personal relationship with the nurturer stays at centre stage (small talk first, Shared Experiences, Reminiscing) — but keeping relationships central also means keeping growth in view; beware the small-talk plateau trap

Grammar only on demand: raise grammar awareness (Structured Input, Input/Output Flooding) ONLY for forms the grower is already trying and failing to produce — never arbitrary drills disconnected from current speech needs

Rising difficulty: deliberately keep increasing challenge (simplified tellings → natural tellings → written stories read aloud → host stories → expository topics → native-to-native retellings) along the 12-level resource ladder
Languaculture: language and culture are one; every activity simultaneously teaches how host people talk and how they construe their world
Growth zone (ZPD): the nurturer works to stay exactly where the grower can succeed with a bit of help
Pioneers leave resources: every recording made should be shareable so later growers can skip straight to massaging
materials: World-story / Bridge Story texts: Cinderella, Goldilocks and the Three Bears, Noah and the Great Flood, The First Man and Woman (full versions in Appendix 2); Grimm's Fairy Tales, Hans Christian Andersen, Aesop's Fables, Arabian Nights (free online); Bible storybooks (available in all major languages, often pre-recorded in hundreds of languages); home-culture folk tale collections (e.g. Folk Tales from Korea)
Sound-recording device (tape recorder, MP3 recorder, laptop, handheld) — nearly every activity produces or consumes recordings
Word log: notebook or loose-leaf paper for the running list of newly encountered words (with context notes, not for memorization)

Action cartoons with little or no dialogue: Tom & Jerry (primary); Charlie Chaplin silents (Bridge-Story-like, usable early); Mr. Bean (culture-heavy, save for Phase 3C); player arranged so only the nurturer sees the screen
An 'attempted' Script of Life pre-written by the grower (Appendix 2 model: 'Using a Bus in Kazakhstan', 29 steps)

Busy books for flooding: William Wanders Off / Lucy is Lost / Roving Rosie Reports (Ed King); Usborne '1001 Things to Spot' series; Heather Amery's The First 1000 Words; photo albums, National Geographic, coffee-table books
Wordless picture storybooks, especially Anno's Journey (Mitsumasa Anno) — 'more suited to Phase 3 than Phase 2'
Patrick Moran's Lexicarry (3-frame communication-situation strips with empty speech bubbles)
Translations (recorded or written) of host stories into the grower's strong language, for multi-day pre-familiarization
Parallel-language children's nonfiction (history, geography, nature, holidays), public-health pamphlets, farmer materials, hobby explainers, sermons — for Familiar Topic work
News broadcasts (TV/radio/Internet) and newspapers
Brainstormed idea lists: Scripts of Life, Shared Experiences, familiar places/routes, role-play situations (Appendix 3 gives a Malay-world model list)
LLA resource collection target: 150+ children's books, silent videos, commissioned translations both directions, and a shared CD of previous GPs' recordings
Doll family + bag of candies (Structured Input example); everyday props (lamp, rope, clock, bicycle) for Discuss-a-Prop
Pencil and paper; small pocket notepad carried through daily life for idea capture
milestones: Can follow rich, complex stories in the host language after moderate massaging (vs. needing picture support)
Can understand abstract explanations/expository discourse on familiar topics without visual aids
Listening vocabulary of roughly 4,000-5,000 words (gained ~2,500 in this phase, at 8+ new words per hour)
Holds 'basic conversational ability': discusses a wide range of topics including new ones, with host-partner help still needed for many conversations
Tells simple stories (own life stories, retold massaged stories, serial 'epic' installments)
Has massaged and become thoroughly familiar with many hours of Listening Library recordings (Bridge Stories, Scripts of Life, cartoons, reminiscences, host stories) — each easy to follow
Has converted genuinely local host stories into understood shared stories via the translation-prep pipeline (prime 3B milestone)
Has begun at least one real relationship with a host person beyond the paid nurturer — explicit gate for moving from 3B to 3C; by phase end, a slowly widening network
Markedly deepened relationship with the nurturer (shared stories, experiences, and reminiscences now form a common life history)
Can negotiate complex meanings in conversation and use host-appropriate back-channel/turn-taking behavior
Has sampled native-to-native-speed retellings of familiar stories and begun training for rapid natural speech (Phase 5 direction)
May read simple familiar material with developing fluency (non-character scripts)

Knows substantially more about everyday host life (scripts, places, current community topics); ready for Phase 4's deep host-world exploration — and may transition early if Phase 3 activities have become easy
Honest limitation check: speech still error-riddled and non-native-sounding; most native-to-native speech still not understandable — both expected and acceptable at this stage
phase3doc.nurturerRole: The nurturer is a paid host-person companion who 'kindly, gently, patiently' meets the grower in his growth zone; for Phase 3 she should ideally enjoy and have a knack for storytelling AND be able to simplify and gear stories to the grower's current level. WHAT SHE DOES: learns Bridge Stories at home (reading a version in a language she knows 2-3 times) and retells them spontaneously in her own words, culturally adapted (host-style openings/closings, 'angel' for 'fairy') without gutting the plot; tells/reads stories slowly and carefully for recording; explains unknown words and sentences IN THE HOST LANGUAGE ONLY, using definitions, examples, demonstrations, pantomime, posing ('acting lazy'), stern voices, and example floods ('A doctor made me take medicine. My mother made me get water...'); confirms or gently recasts the grower's trial sentences; writes every new word into the word log; authors all Scripts of Life after the one-time training (only a host person can produce a genuine host-viewpoint script) and expands them when probed; narrates cartoons live with the screen hidden from the grower, then retells naturally while deliberately re-including word-log items; leads Reminiscing about shared experiences while letting the grower back-channel; keeps growing lists of ideas for Scripts of Life and Shared Experiences; reads written stories aloud (and for diglossic languages, retells written texts in the spoken register); retells the grower's life stories for clean Listening Library recordings; records herself telling familiar stories native-to-native to another host person; suggests options for Lexicarry bubbles; introduces the grower to her own friends to seed new relationships. WHAT SHE MUST NOT DO: use the grower's language or translate (explanation is always in the host language); let sessions dissolve into hours of small talk; assume host-world background knowledge too early (that's why Bridge Stories come first); radically alter story plots; drill arbitrary grammar; sit passively listening to the grower practice reading aloud (a waste of paid nurturer time — her reading to HIM is the valuable direction); and she should not be the grower's ONLY relationship by Phase 3B.
phase3doc.phaseName: Phase 3: Knowable / Becoming Knowable — the Shared-Story ('Stuff-We-Both-Know') Phase, 250 hours (Phase 3A: 100h, Phase 3B: 75h, Phase 3C: 75h)
phase3doc.sessionStructure: Sessions run 2-5 hours with a nurturer (ideal: 25 hrs/week over 5 days, plus ~15 hrs/week solo listening/reading homework). EVERY session opens with 10-15 minutes of small talk in the host language, relationship first. CANONICAL DAY (the Day-2 model followed through 3A): small talk → Reminiscing about yesterday's Shared Experience (1 hr, on days following one) → Strengthening Vocabulary from yesterday (20 min, optional, strictly capped) → Bridge Story recording + massaging (2.5 hrs — the mainstay, ≥half of all time) → Script of Life (1 hr) → Action Cartoon (1 hr) OR Shared Experience outing (1 hr, which feeds tomorrow's reminiscing). A simpler legitimate variant: small talk + vocab + 3.5-4.5 hrs Bridge Story + Scripts of Life. Activities may each be capped at a fixed time and continued across days; 'Day 1' (Bridge Story with training-level massaging, Script of Life training steps, Action Cartoon, Shared Experience) typically actually takes several days. PHASE 3B sample day: pre-session homework (re-listen to the translation of today's host story) → 15 min small talk → 15 min vocab strengthening → 2 hrs recording/massaging a host story → 15 min Input Flooding → 15 min role-play → 1 hr Familiar-Place Description → 1 hr starting conversations with strangers in the park (or 1 hr visiting befriended neighbours in the simple variant); evening: listen to today's recordings, re-listen to next week's host-story translation, review idea lists. PART-TIME pattern: 2 hrs every morning (e.g. 7-9 am) — Bridge Stories 4 days/week, Scripts of Life 1 day/week, small talk daily — with fanatical Listening Library use filling every spare moment (walking, waiting rooms, traffic, falling asleep). Everything in session is in the host language; nearly everything is recorded; every recording is massaged and then re-listened to until easy. Universal quality bar regardless of activity mix: speech understandable with only moderate massaging, 8+ new words/hour, lots of interaction, lots of grower talking.
phase3doc.summary: Phase 3 ('Becoming Knowable' / the Shared-Story or 'Stuff-We-Both-Know' phase) occupies 250 hours, subdivided into 3A (100h), 3B (75h), 3C (75h). Its central insight: stories and descriptions whose content the grower ALREADY largely knows are understandable in the host language long before unfamiliar material is, so the phase systematically exploits shared knowledge — world fairy tales and Bible stories ('Bridge Stories' from a neutral third world requiring no host-cultural background), step-by-step descriptions of everyday routines ('Scripts of Life'), dialogue-free cartoons watched in advance, experiences grower and nurturer share and then reminisce about, and eventually genuine host stories pre-learned through translation, movie plots, book summaries, news, and abstract familiar topics. Nearly every activity follows one master loop: the nurturer tells/reads something predictable, it is sound-recorded, the recording is 'massaged' sentence by sentence (repetition, host-language-only explanation, negotiation of meaning, example trading, word-log entry), and the finished recording joins a growing Listening Library that the grower re-listens to fanatically until every item is easy to follow. The phase moves the grower from understanding simple picture-supported stories to understanding rich complex stories and his first expository (abstract) speech without visual support, grows listening vocabulary by ~2,500 words to roughly 4,000-5,000 total (target: 8+ new words per hour via the no-memorization Iceberg Principle), and produces 'basic conversational ability' — discussing a wide range of topics and telling simple stories, while speech remains decidedly non-native. Difficulty deliberately escalates through the sub-phases: 3A establishes the core activities (Bridge Story as mainstay plus Scripts of Life, Action Cartoons, Shared Experiences/Reminiscing, with optional flooding/role-play/prop activities); 3B's prime move is converting host stories into shared stories via multi-day translation pre-familiarization, alongside a non-negotiable social mandate — the grower may not graduate to 3C without starting real relationships beyond the paid nurturer; 3C pushes beyond literal narrative into expository discourse, news, movie/book retellings, native-to-native speed recordings, talking-heavy activities (story retelling, life stories, serial 'epics'), and possibly first reading. Throughout, the relationship with the nurturer stays at centre stage — sessions open with small talk and are bonded by shared experiences — but the guide pointedly warns against letting chitchat replace supercharged activities (the plateau trap). The phase prepares directly for Phase 4 (Deep Personal Relationships), and growers finding it easy may move on before the 250 hours are up.
terminology: Growing participator (GP) / grower — the foreigner becoming an ever-fuller participant in the host world; the process never completes (replaces 'language learner')
Nurturer — the paid host person who kindly, gently, patiently meets the grower in his growth zone; for Phase 3, ideally a gifted storyteller who can also simplify
Growth zone — the band of activities doable with a bit of expert help (the Zone of Proximal Development)
Supercharged participation sessions — hired, concentrated participation opportunities that solve the catch-22 that only those who can already participate get to participate
Negotiation of meaning — the back-and-forth of clarifying, checking, recasting and re-expressing until both parties understand
Massaging (stories/recordings) — replaying a recording bit by bit and negotiating the meaning of everything not understood, encountering many new words in the process
Bridge Story — a story from a neutral third world (fairy tales, Bible stories) that is neither the grower's nor the nurturer's, slashing the host-background-knowledge load
Script of Life — a 25-30-step host-viewpoint description of an everyday routine (only a host person can author one); an 'attempted' Script of Life is the grower's training mock-up
Stuff-We-Both-Know — the umbrella label for Phase 3's shared-knowledge activities
Shared story — any story made mutually known in advance (by familiarity, prior viewing, translation prep, or shared experience)
Iceberg Principle — words enter a mental iceberg by acquaintance, not memorization; frequent re-encounters float them toward the usable top
Word log — the running record of word acquaintances with context notes; explicitly NOT a memorization list
Listening Library — the cumulative archive of all session recordings, ordered by rising complexity; re-listening refreshes and 'reawakens' iceberg words
Languaculture — language and culture as a single inseparable learning object
Expository discourse — abstract explanatory speech (vs. narrative); the new frontier of Phase 3C and the staple of Phase 4
Information gap — staging (e.g. hiding the cartoon screen) so the nurturer genuinely has unknown information to convey
Input Flooding / Output Flooding — hearing, then producing, hundreds of instances of one target construction the grower is already reaching for
Reverse Role-Play — role-play with roles inverted so the nurturer models the grower's own real-life part
Reminiscing — jointly recalling a shared experience, with host-style back-channels ('yeah', 'mhm', 'really!')
Communities of practice — host groups united by purpose, shared history and common practices, the eventual target of participation
Frequency (importance of) — language processing strengthens with frequency at every level, motivating massive comprehensible exposure
Speech-led vs. understanding-led — traditional speaking-first, writing-dependent learning vs. GPA's comprehension-first, listening-dependent stance
Host world / home world — the target community's life-world vs. the grower's origin life-world
LLA (language learning advisor) — coach who helps design schedules and gathers phase resources (target: 150+ books, translations, a CD of shared GP recordings)
Small talk / chitchat — relationship-building chat; mandatory opener, dangerous as a main course (the plateau trap)
phase3doc.vocabTargets: Add roughly 2,000-3,000 listening-vocabulary words during the 250 hours (the documented Kazakh case gained ~2,500), bringing the running total to about 4,000-5,000 words. Operational pace target stated repeatedly: an average of at least 8 new-word acquaintances per hour of session time. Per-story calibration: about 5 new words per minute of recorded story is ideal, 10 is the ceiling (50 new words in a 2-minute story means the material is too hard). Tracking is via the word log — a running acquaintance record written by the nurturer during massaging (grower may add a rough private gloss plus story/location reference), explicitly NOT for memorization (Iceberg Principle: words are strengthened by re-encounter, chiefly through repeated Listening Library re-listening, which 'reawakens' faded words; words that arise outside recordings get a special host-language recording mentioning them in context). Phase 2 entry baseline: ~2,000+ words understood. Background note: research puts good English conversational ability at 5,000+ words, more recent research considerably higher.

phase3pdf.phaseName: Phase 3: Knowable / Becoming Knowable (250 hours) — official guide title: "Another 250 Hours: Getting Underway in Stuff-We-Both-Know Activities" (also called the Shared Stories Phase). Subdivided into Phase 3A (first 100 hours), Phase 3B (next 75 hours), Phase 3C (final 75 hours).
phase3pdf.summary:
Phase 3 is the "Knowable Phase" — the point where host people begin to feel the learner is someone they can come to know, at least with a little effort. The organizing concept is "stuff-we-both-know": all listening material has content that is already highly familiar and predictable to the growing participator (GP), which lets them understand rich, complex host-language speech long before they could understand unfamiliar speech. The flagship resource is the "Bridge Story" — a world story like Cinderella or a Bible story whose world belongs to neither the GP nor the nurturer, forming a cultural bridge that removes the need for deep host-world background knowledge. The GP hears the story told by the nurturer, records it, then "massages" the recording sentence-by-sentence — negotiating the meaning of everything not understood, entirely in the host language with zero translation — and adds new words to a word log and the recording to a growing Listening Library.

The phase progresses in difficulty: 3A centers on Bridge Stories, Scripts of Life (step-by-step descriptions of everyday activities from the host point of view), Action Cartoons (narrating Tom & Jerry), Shared Experiences and next-day Reminiscing. 3B moves to genuine host stories made "shared" by first becoming familiar with them in translation, and requires the GP to deliberately begin new social relationships beyond the paid nurturer. 3C pushes beyond literal stories into expository discourse on familiar topics (movie plots, book summaries, news broadcasts, native-to-native retellings of old stories), plus activities that force the GP to talk more (story retelling, life stories, epic ongoing stories, weekend recaps).

By the end, listening vocabulary roughly doubles to 4,000–5,000 words, the GP can follow complex stories and abstract explanations without visual support, tell simple stories, and has "basic conversational ability" across a wide range of topics — preparing them for Phase 4, Deep Life Sharing. Reading may also begin in this phase, since for the first time there is material at the learner's level (the familiar massaged stories themselves). Throughout, the deepening personal relationship with the nurturer stays at center stage, and the GP is repeatedly admonished to re-listen to every Listening Library recording until it is effortless to follow.
phase3pdf.hours: 250 hours total of special-growth participation sessions: Phase 3A = 100 hours, Phase 3B = 75 hours, Phase 3C = 75 hours. Recommended pace: 25 hours/week with nurturer (5 hours/day, 5 days) plus ~15 hours/week of private listening to recordings. Part-time alternative: 2 hours every morning (Bridge Stories 4 days/week, Scripts of Life 1 day/week, plus small talk daily).
goals: A deepening relationship with your nurturer (shared stories, Shared Experiences and Reminiscences bond you together)
New relationships with host people — by Phase 3B you must begin relationships beyond the paid nurturer; you do not graduate from 3B to 3C until you have done this
Familiarity with a growing quantity of speech — adding many hours of recordings to the Listening Library and re-listening until each is easy to follow
Steadily growing vocabulary — roughly 2,500 new word acquaintances, bringing listening vocabulary to 4,000–5,000 words, at an average of 8+ new words per hour
Understanding increasingly complex material — from simple picture-supported narratives (Phase 2) to rich, complex stories and abstract explanations (expository discourse) without visual aids
Understanding more of the host world — via Scripts of Life, Familiar-Place Descriptions, Shared Experiences, Reminiscing, and host stories
Basic conversational ability — able to discuss a wide range of topics, including ones never previously discussed, and to tell simple stories
keyPrinciples: Stuff-we-both-know / Shared Stories: only listen to material whose content is already highly familiar and predictable; familiarity does the work that missing language ability cannot

Comprehension before production: understanding speech is the foundational ability; listening ability is pushed deliberately far ahead of speaking ability (understanding-led, listening-dependent, vs. traditional speech-led, writing-dependent learning)
No translation: all interaction, all word explanations, all negotiation of meaning happens 100% in the host language
Negotiation of meaning: whenever the GP doesn't understand, they ask for clarification, repetition, examples, and check understanding until the meaning is grasped
Massaging recordings: working through a recording bit by bit, negotiating everything not understood — the core mechanic of nearly every activity
Iceberg Principle: don't try to master every new word; making its acquaintance puts it in the iceberg, and repeated encounters raise it higher; no word memorization
Importance of frequency: massive exposure to understood speech; re-listen to Listening Library recordings until every bit is easy to follow, and periodically thereafter

Difficulty must keep rising: calibrate story difficulty (≤30 min massaging per minute of story; ~5–10 new words per minute of story; activity should be pleasant, not tedious); move from simplified retellings to natural read-aloud written stories to host stories

Relationship at center stage: begin every session with small talk in the host language; learning goals never displace the personal relationship — but beware letting small talk eat the sessions (plateau risk)
Don't read while listening: looking at printed text short-circuits the listening-comprehension process; read alone at home, listen in sessions
Anything goes if it works: any activity is fine if it delivers understandable-but-stretching speech, 8+ new words/hour, lots of interaction, and lots of opportunity to talk
Leave resources behind: recordings made by one GP become ready-made resources for future GPs in that languaculture

activities.name: Bridge Story Activity (hearing and massaging a world story) — THE mainstay of Phase 3A
activities.description: Step 1: The nurturer tells (or reads aloud, slowly and carefully) a world story such as Cinderella — a story the GP already knows but has never heard in the host language. This is recorded. The GP stays quiet during the telling. Variant 1: nurturer reads from a children's storybook in the host language. Variant 2: a day earlier the nurturer takes home the story in a language she knows, reads it 2–3 times, and tells it in her own words, adapted to her languaculture (e.g., Kazakh 'angel' instead of 'fairy'; native story openers/closers instead of 'Once upon a time'; plot kept intact). Step 2 (massaging): rewind to the start; play one sentence. (A) If unknown words are heard, ask what they mean — explanations only in the host language. (B) If all words are known but the sentence is still opaque, ask the nurturer to explain it simply; massage until the GP can listen to it all with understanding. (C) The nurturer writes every new word in the word log (GP may pencil a rough native-language gloss beside it, plus which story and where). (D) When the basic gist of a sentence is understood, move to the next sentence. Repeat steps 1–2 sentence by sentence. The documented example dialogue (Cinderella) shows the full mechanic: GP plays a sentence, asks 'Please repeat that sentence', requests breakdowns ('Her father married…?'), asks word meanings ('I don't know the word widow'), the nurturer defines in-language ('If a man has a wife and he dies, she is a widow'), the GP tests understanding with own examples ('My grandfather died. My grandmother is a widow'), asks for examples ('Tell me an example — someone is mean'), the nurturer pantomimes (acting lazy), grammar constructions get example-flooded ('A doctor made me take medicine. My mother made me get water…'), and each new word is ordered written into the list. Difficulty check: too hard if 2 hours to massage a 2-minute story or 50 new words logged; about right if ≤30 min massaging per minute of story and ≤10 new words per minute (5 ideal). If too hard: have the nurturer learn the story in advance and tell it spontaneously in her own words, or fall back to Phase 2 wordless picture-book stories told WITHOUT looking at the pictures. Afterward: listen to the recording a few times before the next session, pausing and replaying the personally striking words.
activities.materials: World stories (Cinderella, Noah and the Great Flood, Goldilocks and the Three Bears, The First Man and Woman — full texts in Appendix 2), Bible storybooks (available in nearly all major languages, often with existing recordings), folk-tale collections from the GP's home country (e.g., Folk Tales from Korea), Grimm/Andersen/Aesop/Arabian Nights; sound recorder; word-log notebook
activities.timing: Day 1 onward; mainstay of all of Phase 3A — at least half, possibly most, of session time; sample schedules give it 2.5–4.5 hrs/day

activities.name: Script of Life Activity
activities.description: One-time training (first session only): Training step 1 — the GP demonstrates the desired granularity by actually performing 'washing hands' at the sink, pausing 25–30 times, asking 'What did I do?' / 'What am I doing?' at each micro-step; the nurturer names each step and writes it down (the guide lists all 27 steps: open the door, turn on the light, walk to the sink, reach out your hand, turn the hot tap, feel the water… hang the towel, turn off the light, close the door). Training step 2 — nurturer reads the list aloud; record it. Training step 3 — rewind and massage (almost everything will be understood since it was visually supported; this is the last visual support). Training step 4 — use the GP's pre-prepared 'attempted' Script of Life (e.g., 'Using a Bus in Kazakhstan', 27 steps including 'Guess where the door will be when it stops', 'Put five hundred tenge in his hand', 'A man with crutches gets on. Jump up and give him your seat'); without showing the written text, negotiate each step's meaning and have the nurturer write it in the host language. From then on only the nurturer creates scripts — only a host person knows what host people expect to happen. Normal ongoing form: Step 1 — nurturer lists all the things she does when doing something everyday (e.g., buying meat). Step 2 — she walks through it action by action; the GP gets her to explain anything not understood and probes for completeness ('After you do X and before you do Y, what do you do?', 'How do you do step X in smaller steps?'). Step 3 — make a voice recording of the full list. Step 4 — massage the recording (often easier than stories since actions can be pantomimed); add new words to word log. Step 5 — play the recording and physically act out (pantomime) each step as heard. Recordings join the Listening Library.
activities.materials: A pre-written 'attempted' Script of Life from the GP; brainstormed idea lists (Appendix 3 categories: Home — sweeping, washing dishes, lighting the stove, changing a gas bottle; Food — making rice, tea, cleaning a fish; Personal care — haircut, doctor visit; Errands — paying bills, using an ATM, mailing a letter; Out and About — restaurants, hotels, weddings; Clothing, Car care, Baby care, Village life. Rule: only script activities the GP has actually observed/experienced — unfamiliar ones are Phase 4 material); recorder; word log
activities.timing: Day 1 (with training) and throughout 3A–3C; ~1 hour/day in sample schedules, 2–4 days/week; one of the two non-postponable core activities (with Bridge Stories)

activities.name: Action Cartoon Activity
activities.description: Before the session the GP privately watches an action cartoon (Tom & Jerry — lots of action, few words) so the story is already familiar (keeping it stuff-we-both-know). Step 1: set up the screen so the NURTURER can see it but the GP cannot — this manufactures an information gap; the nurturer narrates the story live as she watches (she may silently pre-watch once first); record the narration. Step 2: watch the cartoon together while listening to that recording. Step 3: rewind and massage the recording as with Cinderella; add new words to the word log. Step 4: the nurturer retells the whole story WITHOUT the cartoon playing — a much more natural narrative — having first reviewed the word log so she deliberately re-includes all the new words; record this polished version for the Listening Library. Step 5: massage the new recording if needed. (Mr. Bean / Charlie Chaplin silent films also work but carry heavy British/period culture — better saved for Phase 3C.)
activities.materials: Tom & Jerry DVD/video (or Mr. Bean, Charlie Chaplin later); playback device positioned for one-way viewing; recorder; word log
activities.timing: Day 1 onward, ~1 hour, 2–3 days/week in sample schedule; optional/postponable

activities.name: Shared Experience Activity
activities.description: The closing activity of each day: GP and nurturer go do something together — go to a coffee shop, shoot baskets, work in the vegetable garden, clean the messy kitchen, buy something, play a game, or just walk a different route each time and observe everything. Interact naturally in the host language during the activity; both GP and nurturer make notes afterward about details of the experience. Its real payoff comes the next day, when it becomes the raw material for the Reminiscing Activity. Over time the nurturer starts proposing shared experiences herself, and by late Phase 3 a Shared Experience can be a whole day or two of doing something together followed by lots of reminiscing.
activities.materials: None required — real life; a notepad for after-the-fact notes; a running brainstormed list of Shared Experience ideas
activities.timing: Last activity of the day, ~1 hour, 2 days/week in sample schedule; throughout the phase

activities.name: Reminiscing Activity
activities.description: First activity of the following day. Step 1: the GP asks the nurturer to tell about what the two of them did together yesterday. Step 2: record her telling it, while the GP interacts the way a host-culture listener would — giving back-channel feedback (the host equivalents of 'yeah, really!, mhm, I see'), recognizing turn-taking cues, contributing briefly at natural pauses, then handing the floor back so the nurturer does most of the talking. (Example: N: 'We went to a coffee shop.' GP: 'Yeah.' N: 'We walked there together… You said you are afraid to cross the street.' GP: 'I was afraid.') Step 3: massage the recording exactly as with a Bridge Story. This trains real conversational listenership, mines genuinely shared autobiographical content, and deepens the relationship.
activities.materials: Notes from yesterday's Shared Experience; recorder; word log
activities.timing: Day 2 onward, first activity after small talk on days following a Shared Experience, ~1 hour

activities.name: Strengthening Vocabulary Activity (optional)
activities.description: The GP, having listened to the previous session's recordings overnight with special attention to striking new words, now tries to remind the nurturer of those words and put each back into the context it came from: GP: 'I learned mean and lazy. Cinderella's sisters. Uhm, not sisters. Like sisters.' N: 'Stepsisters.' GP: 'Cinderella's stepsisters were mean. They said bad things to her… They were lazy. They slept all day.' Words can come from any of yesterday's activities ('I learned grind. You talked about buying meat. Maybe the butcher grinds the meat.'). Optionally limit to the words that feel most personally important. Warning: it can eat up too much session time and crowd out new input.
activities.materials: Yesterday's word log; yesterday's recordings (listened to beforehand)
activities.timing: ~20 minutes near the start of most days; explicitly optional

activities.name: Familiar-Place Description Activity
activities.description: The nurturer describes a place that is well known to the GP — their home, apartment building, street, the nearby market, a particular shop, the public square, a route the GP commonly travels. Make a sound recording of the description; massage it; re-listen before the next session. Moves the GP toward understanding how local places are conceived by host people.
activities.materials: A brainstormed list of places and routes familiar to the GP; recorder; word log
activities.timing: Phase 3A optional extra; ~1 hour slots (appears in the 3B sample day too)

activities.name: Discuss-a-Prop Activity (conversations centred on common objects)
activities.description: Take an everyday object — a clock, sink, stove, tape recorder, bicycle, lamp, length of rope — and use it as the topic of free-ranging interaction while doing things with it: try to discuss everything people do with and to the object. Record the entire interaction including all negotiation of meaning; listen a few times before the next session. Documented examples: a family spent an hour with a nurturer on a table lamp (burned-out bulbs led to electric power, then to the electric panel and meter) and another hour on a rope (three GPs tied each other up and dragged each other around). It is a return to visual support, but with far more free-ranging interaction than Phases 1–2.
activities.materials: Any household object; recorder; word log
activities.timing: Phase 3A optional extra

activities.name: Reverse Role-Play and Ordinary Role-Play
activities.description: Spontaneous (never memorized lines) acting-out of everyday situations that require talking: using a taxi, making a purchase, being stopped by a traffic policeman. Reverse Role-Play: the NURTURER plays the role the GP has in real life (e.g., customer) and the GP plays the counterpart (taxi driver, shopkeeper, police officer) as best they can. The point: in hearing what the nurturer says as the 'customer', the GP gets a model of exactly how they themselves should talk in that situation. Record it, massage the recording, listen before the next session. On a later day (after several listens), trade roles — the GP plays their own real-life role while the nurturer plays the counterpart, showing the GP what to expect to hear said to them. Ordinary Role-Play variant: GP simply plays their own role from the start, with the nurturer assisting them in saying what they're trying to say.
activities.materials: A brainstormed list of real situations the GP participates in; recorder; word log
activities.timing: Phase 3A onward; 15-minute slots in the 3B sample day (e.g., role-play of getting a haircut)

activities.name: Phase 2 carry-over activities (Story-Building, Free Cooperative Story-Building, Autobiographical Picture Stories)
activities.description: Still richly rewarding in Phase 3: (a) Story-building with the GP in the lead (Phase 2A style — do more of this if you aren't talking enough); (b) story-building with the nurturer in the lead (2B — to learn more that's new); (c) Free Cooperative Story-Building: take a wordless picture storybook, discuss it freely with both parties making spontaneous contributions to building the story, add to the word log as you go, finish the whole book, then — using the word log as a reminder of new words to re-include — the nurturer tells the entire story, which is recorded, massaged if needed, and re-listened to. Anno's Journey is recommended ('more suited to Phase 3 than Phase 2'). (d) Autobiographical Picture Stories (2C): telling sketch-supported stories from one's own life; the author would have made it a core activity except some people resist drawing — it deepens the personal relationship in ways Bridge Stories cannot.
activities.materials: Wordless picture storybooks (Anno's Journey by Mitsumasa Anno), GP's own quick sketches, recorder, word log
activities.timing: Throughout Phase 3 as supplements; Autobiographical Picture Stories especially valuable in 3A–3B

activities.name: Structured Input Activity (grammar awareness)
activities.description: Repeats Phase 1-style activities for grammar points the GP still struggles with. The activity forces the GP to use a target grammatical form for UNDERSTANDING (not production drill). Worked example for 'to and from': set up a doll family and a bag of candies; the nurturer first says 'Give a candy to the mother; take a candy from the son; give a candy to me'; then she drops the verbs 'give' and 'take' (which give away the direction) and says only 'From me; to yourself; from the father; to the baby' — now the GP can only act correctly by processing the to/from markers themselves. Designable for many basic grammar elements (more examples in the Phase 1 guide).
activities.materials: Doll family, bag of candies (or analogous manipulables)
activities.timing: Phase 3 as needed, when a grammar area keeps causing trouble

activities.name: Input Flooding Activity (busy picture or Script of Life)
activities.description: Used only when the GP notices themself repeatedly failing to produce a sentence type they actually need (never for arbitrary grammar). Using a 'busy picture' — a drawing of a scene with 100+ people each doing something (William Wanders Off; 1001 Things to Spot; picture dictionaries; photo albums; National Geographic spreads): (1) choose the sentence type you keep wanting to produce (e.g., 'the man who is X-ing'); (2) show the nurturer a few example sentences of that form about the picture; (3) the nurturer then makes very many such comments about people/things in the picture ('Here is a man who is sweeping the street… the woman who is carrying a cane…'), or better, asks the GP 'Where is the man who is…?' a hundred times — which forces attention; (4) record and massage as necessary; (5) re-listen before next session. Script-of-Life variant: take a Script of Life already highly familiar from previous sessions and have the nurturer retell it in a form emphasizing the target pattern — e.g., future/intent ('In awhile, I will wash my hands. First I will walk to the bathroom door…') or complex subordination ('After I walk to the door, I will reach out my hand…').
activities.materials: Busy-picture books (William Wanders Off by Ed King; Usborne 1001 Things to Spot; The First 1000 Words), photo albums/scrapbooks, magazines; previously recorded Scripts of Life; recorder
activities.timing: Phase 3A onward, as needed; 15-minute slots in the 3B sample day

activities.name: Output Flooding Activity
activities.description: The production mirror of Input Flooding, done right after it: having now heard the target sentence type hundreds of times, the GP turns to a NEW busy picture and tries to make many, many statements about people and things in it using that same construction over and over ('Here is a man who…'). Strictly limited to sentence/phrase types the GP is already struggling to use in their own real speech — not arbitrary grammar patterns.
activities.materials: A fresh busy picture; recorder optional
activities.timing: Immediately following Input Flooding sessions

activities.name: Host-Story-as-Stuff-We-Both-Know Activity — THE prime Phase 3B activity
activities.description: Converts real host stories into 'shared' stories before listening. Procedure: (1) ask the nurturer to list stories universally (or very widely) known among her people; (2) have someone retell some of those stories in English or another language the GP knows well — as a voice recording or written out; (3) as homework, the GP listens to / reads this translation every day for several days, until the story is highly familiar; (4) only then, in a session, listen to the story in the host language for the first time — record the nurturer's telling and massage it following exactly the Cinderella steps; (5) re-listen a few times before the next session. This is notably harder than Bridge Stories because there now EXISTS a vast asymmetry of background knowledge (the nurturer's world, not the GP's), making explanations of opaque elements more complex — if it proves too time-consuming, postpone another fifty hours and come back. Re-listen to these recordings more often than Bridge Story ones (their content is less permanently memorable). Pioneers' recordings become resources for later GPs.
activities.materials: Nurturer's list of universally known host stories; translations (audio or written) made by a bilingual helper; recorder; word log
activities.timing: Phase 3B (hours 100–175); the centerpiece activity; 2–3.5 hour blocks in the 3B sample days

activities.name: Familiar Topic Activity (expository discourse) — Phase 3C
activities.description: Moves beyond narrative into expository (abstract/explanatory) speech, exploiting the fact that an abstract discussion of a HIGHLY FAMILIAR topic is much easier than an unfamiliar story. The nurturer tells, or reads aloud, about a topic the GP knows deeply — and the GP records, massages, and re-listens as usual. Topic sources keyed to the GP's life: health workers can use public-health pamphlets (malaria prevention, prenatal health); agricultural workers, farming materials; hobbyists can record someone who shares their interest explaining 'how to take good care of your car'; religious GPs can massage sermons on familiar passages or published training materials read aloud. The topic must be understood SIMILARLY in home and host worlds (arithmetic may be 'familiar', but if the host world approaches it differently it isn't a familiar topic). Caution from the author's Kazakh experience: become familiar with translated source material for SEVERAL DAYS first, to world-story-level familiarity, or months later the recordings will be hard to follow.
activities.materials: Pamphlets, school textbooks, hobby/work materials, sermons, children's nonfiction (history, geography, nature, holidays) in bilingual editions; recorder
activities.timing: Phase 3C (final 75 hours)

activities.name: Movie Plots / Book Summaries (shared-story spirit) — Phase 3C
activities.description: Movie Plots: pick a popular world movie the GP knows well from their own language and the nurturer has seen dubbed (or watches specially); the nurturer simply tells the plot from memory; record and massage, re-listen before next session. Book Summary: same mechanic with novels — the nurturer summarizes a favourite novel the GP has read in another language; works in reverse too: read host-country novels in English translation for fun now, hear them summarized in the host language later, eventually read the originals.
activities.materials: Dubbed films known to both parties; translated novels; recorder; word log
activities.timing: Phase 3C

activities.name: News Broadcasts — Phase 3C
activities.description: Record host-language TV/radio/Internet news broadcasts and massage them. World news mostly counts as 'familiar topics' if the GP follows world news; local news is harder unless the GP tracks local affairs. Alternative: the nurturer reads a newspaper aloud for recording and massaging (for diglossic languages like Arabic: she reads the formal-Arabic article, then retells its content in spoken Arabic — feeding formal vocabulary into conversation). Key counsel: commit sustained time — the initial flood of new vocabulary repeats so frequently in news language that it quickly becomes familiar, yielding a permanent self-serve source of comprehensible listening; casual dabbling lets the vocabulary fade. Ongoing local stories (court trials) get easier with each installment, so prior familiarity matters less once you're following the story.
activities.materials: TV/radio/Internet news recordings; newspapers; recorder
activities.timing: Phase 3C; requires a deliberate sustained block of effort

activities.name: Your Old Stories Retold 'Native-to-Native' — Phase 3C bridge to Phase 5
activities.description: Early in Phase 3 the nurturer adapted her speech heavily (slow, clear, simple). Now: the nurturer takes stories already used with the GP and tells them to ANOTHER host person with the GP absent, recording herself. The result: stories with a highly familiar core and familiar vocabulary, but in natural, rapid, native-to-native form. Listen together later and massage; then re-listen alone. Try at least once near the end of Phase 3 to feel how much more demanding natural speed is; continues into Phases 4–5. (Author's Urdu parallel: seventeen hours of bazaar-bought children's story cassettes — native-to-native but familiar stories — were understandable after a few listenings even without a nurturer.)
activities.materials: Previously used stories; a second host person; recorder
activities.timing: Once toward the end of Phase 3; more in Phases 4–5

activities.name: Story Retelling Activity (talking-more)
activities.description: After hearing, recording, and massaging a story, the GP tells the story back to the nurturer in their own words, at their own current level, in the spirit of 'Let me see if I understood your story. Here is what I think you said.' Deliberately works in as much of the story's new vocabulary as possible. Works best mid-to-late Phase 3, and better with Bridge Stories than translated local stories (unless those are exceedingly familiar). Some GPs use it from 3A; others find it too hard until 3B/3C.
activities.materials: Any just-massaged story; recorder optional
activities.timing: Mid-to-late Phase 3, after any story activity

activities.name: Telling Stories from Your Life (talking-more)
activities.description: By mid-to-late Phase 3 the GP can drop sketch support and just tell real stories from their own life: choose an interesting experience from childhood or later; tell the WHOLE story — don't avoid the hard parts; force through with lots of negotiation of meaning no matter how hard it gets. Once the whole story is conveyed, the NURTURER retells it, and her retelling is recorded for the Listening Library — giving the GP a native model of their own story. Telling the same story to other people afterward yields visible improvement each time.
activities.materials: Recorder; word log
activities.timing: Mid-to-late Phase 3

activities.name: Ongoing 'Epic' Story (talking-more)
activities.description: Choose an ongoing epic-scale story personally important to the GP and develop it serially — telling a new installment at each meeting with the nurturer and with other developing relationships. Don't avoid hard parts; negotiate meanings. The nurturer records her retelling of each new segment. May use a single scene-setting picture per installment (not the bit-by-bit picture support of Phase 2). The Phase 3 version will be bare-bones; the same story gets retold ever more richly through Phases 4–6.
activities.materials: Optional single stage-setting pictures; recorder
activities.timing: Mid-to-late Phase 3, recurring installments; repeats across Phases 4–6

activities.name: What I Did on the Weekend (or Yesterday) (talking-more)
activities.description: The GP tells their weekend's (or yesterday's) activities in great detail, not avoiding the hard parts, negotiating meanings as necessary; the nurturer then retells the GP's weekend and that retelling is recorded. Naturally repetitive, so return to it whenever the weekend/yesterday was out of the ordinary.
activities.materials: Recorder
activities.timing: Recurring as warranted, mid-to-late Phase 3

activities.name: Lexicarry Story Strips and Busy-Book Talk (talking-more)
activities.description: Patrick Moran's Lexicarry contains ~3-frame comic-strip communication situations (e.g., bumping into someone and needing to apologise) with EMPTY speech bubbles. The GP attempts to tell each story strip, then — the Phase 3 twist — considers MANY options for what might be said in each bubble (there's more than one way to apologise for knocking someone down), with the nurturer suggesting further variants; a recording summarising the discussion is made. Busy pictures and wordless books (Anno's Journey) likewise give endless things to attempt to talk about, with richer discussion in each successive phase.
activities.materials: Lexicarry (Patrick Moran), busy-picture books, wordless picture books; recorder
activities.timing: Any point in Phase 3; discussions deepen in later phases

activities.name: Matters Currently of Wide Interest in the Community (talking-more)
activities.description: Ask the nurturer what topics people in the community are talking a lot about these days — recent events, community problems, gossip. Record the nurturer's opinions on such matters; massage as necessary; return to the same topics from time to time for updates (much easier to discuss a topic once introduced than a totally new one); then deliberately raise these topics in conversations with other people. Not strictly stuff-we-both-know, but a powerful on-ramp to community conversation.
activities.materials: Recorder; word log
activities.timing: Mid-to-late Phase 3, recurring

activities.name: Social-Life Development (counted activity from Phase 3B)
activities.description: From 3B, three to five of the weekly 25 hours may consist of ordinary social interaction outside paid sessions: identify settings where interaction is possible (ride taxis and talk with the driver the whole way; invite a neighbour for tea; visit shopkeepers in their slow times; start conversations with strangers idling in the park); brainstorm a written list of possibilities already present in your life. Strategies: have the nurturer introduce you into her own close relationships and then develop those one-on-one; consider moving in with a host family (recommended only from mid-to-late Phase 3 — earlier immersion contributes little); the author's account of door-knocking with tea and sweets illustrates that starting relationships may require 'uncultural' moves. You do not graduate to 3C without beginning new relationships.
activities.materials: Brainstormed list of social settings; tea and sweets as needed
activities.timing: Phase 3B onward; 3–5 hours/week of the 25; 1-hour slots in sample days

activities.name: Brainstorming and List-Building (special chore)
activities.description: Ongoing meta-activity: GP carries a small pad everywhere, logging activities they already participate in; builds and maintains four lists with the nurturer (each suggesting additions to the other's lists): (1) ideas for Scripts of Life, (2) ideas for Shared Experiences, (3) familiar places/routes for Familiar-Place Descriptions, (4) situations for Role-Plays. Feed the lists by deliberately getting out and doing new things in the host world (open a bank account, mail a letter, get a haircut, visit a tailor). Also: producing Bridge Story resources (finding world-story collections online, Bible storybooks, home-culture folk-tale books; nurturer learns them at home to retell) — pioneers leave recorded resources for those who follow.
activities.materials: Small pocket notepad; story collections; Appendix 3 brainstorm sheet
activities.timing: Continuous chore of Phase 3A; lists reviewed each evening in 3B sample day

phase3pdf.sessionStructure: Full-time pattern: 25 hours/week of special-growth participation sessions with the nurturer, 5 hours/day across 5 days, plus ~15 hours/week of private listening to Listening Library recordings. Every session begins with ~10 minutes of small talk in the host language (relationship before activities — and only host language, or the roles reverse). Sample full-day (Phase 3A, rich version): small talk 10 min; Strengthening Vocabulary from previous day 20 min; recording+massaging a Bridge Story 2 hrs 30 min; recording/massaging/acting-out a Script of Life 1 hr; recording+massaging an Action Cartoon story 1 hr (alternating days: Reminiscing about yesterday's Shared Experience 1 hr; Engaging in a Shared Experience 1 hr). Simpler variant: small talk + strengthening vocab + Bridge Story 3.5–4.5 hrs + Script of Life 1 hr. Sample Phase 3B day ('adventuresome'): pre-session — re-listen to the translation of today's host story; session — 15 min small talk, 15 min vocabulary strengthening, 2 hrs recording+massaging the new host story, 15 min Input Flood ('This boy is trying to…'), 15 min role-play (getting a haircut), 1 hr Familiar-Place Description, 1 hr starting conversations with strangers in the park; evening — listen to today's recordings, listen to next week's host-story translation, review idea lists. Simple 3B variant: small talk 15, vocab 15, host story 3.5 hrs, 1 hr visiting befriended neighbours. Day 1 of the phase introduces four activities (Bridge Story, Script of Life training, Action Cartoon, Shared Experience) which may spread over several days; Day 2's lineup (small talk, Reminiscing, Strengthening Vocabulary, Bridge Story, Script of Life, Action Cartoon, Shared Experience) is the template for all of 3A. Between sessions: make notes on the Shared Experience, re-listen to all recordings (pausing on striking words), watch the next action cartoon, ensure tomorrow's Bridge Story is ready (nurturer takes one home to learn if needed). Constant target: an average of 8 new-word acquaintances per hour. Host language only at every step — never translation.
materials: World/Bridge stories: Cinderella, Noah and the Great Flood, Goldilocks, The First Man and Woman (full ~600-word retellable texts provided in Appendix 2); Grimm, Andersen, Aesop, Arabian Nights, Brer Rabbit; Bible storybooks (exist in all major languages, often pre-recorded); folk tales from the GP's home country (e.g., Folk Tales from Korea)
Sound-recording device (MP3 recorder/phone/laptop) — the single most essential tool; every activity produces recordings
Word log: notebook or loose-leaf running list of word acquaintances (with story/context noted, optional penciled native gloss) — explicitly NOT for memorization
Listening Library: the cumulative, chronologically ordered collection of all massaged recordings, re-listened to until effortless
Action cartoons: Tom & Jerry videos (Mr. Bean and Charlie Chaplin silent films for later/3C) plus playback device
Wordless picture books (Anno's Journey) and Phase 2 picture storybooks
Busy-picture books for flooding: William Wanders Off (Ed King), Usborne 1001 Things to Spot, The First 1000 Words; photo albums, scrapbooks, National Geographic
Lexicarry (Patrick Moran) — 3-frame empty-bubble communication-situation strips
Props for object conversations (lamp, rope, clock, bicycle, stove) and Structured Input manipulables (doll family, bag of candies)

Written 'attempted' Script of Life (model: 'Using a Bus in Kazakhstan', 27 steps) and Appendix 3 brainstorm sheet of script ideas by category (Home, Food, Personal care, Errands, Out and About, Clothing, Car care, Baby care, Village life)
Idea lists (4): Scripts of Life, Shared Experiences, familiar places/routes, role-play situations; pocket notepad

Phase 3B/3C: translations (audio or text) of host stories into a language the GP knows; dubbed movies; translated novels; news broadcasts/newspapers; pamphlets, school textbooks, hobby and faith materials in bilingual editions

Appendix 4 difficulty ladder (Rebecca Huston): 12 graded resource levels — 1 wordless books / other GPs' recordings; 2 world stories retold in nurturer's own words at GP level; 3 silent videos narrated; 4 local children's stories (GP pre-familiarized via translation) retold; 5 world stories READ aloud in host language; 6 local children's stories read aloud; 7 complex/abstract local stories read aloud; 8 longer translated children's classics read aloud; 9 local young-adult stories with translation; 10 movie-plot retellings by the GP; 11 youth-level abstract texts (school textbook sections) read aloud after oral-translation familiarization; 12 adult-level abstract texts likewise. Mixing nearby levels in one day is fine; LLA should assemble 150+ books/videos, arrange translations both directions, and pool GPs' recordings
milestones: Understands relatively rich and complex stories told in the host language without visual support
Understands abstract explanations (expository speech) on familiar topics without visual aids — new in this phase
Listening vocabulary has grown by ~2,000–3,000 words to a total of ~4,000–5,000
'Basic conversational ability': can discuss a wide range of topics including ones never previously discussed (with host-person help for many conversations to succeed)
Can tell simple stories, including stories from their own life, and retell stories just heard
Can negotiate complex meanings (the documented Kazakh case adds: understands individual sentences with increasing ease, richly textured stories, abstract explanations)
Has massaged and re-listened to a Listening Library of many hours, each recording easy to follow
