Has begun several new relationships with host people beyond the paid nurturer (required to pass from 3B to 3C) and can count 3–5 hours/week of real social interaction toward growth time
Markedly deepened relationship with the nurturer through Shared Experiences, Reminiscing, and hundreds of shared stories
Can handle and genuinely benefit from living with a host family (recommended from mid-to-late Phase 3)
Reading may have begun: can read the familiar massaged stories and start building reading fluency (except character-based scripts, this comes quickly at this level)
Knowledge of basic daily host-world activities greatly increased (Scripts of Life, Familiar-Place Descriptions, Shared Experiences)

By 3C may understand simple, entirely-new host children's stories — a signal that moving early to Phase 4 is allowed; limitations remain: cannot yet follow most native-to-native speech, own speech still riddled with non-native features
phase3pdf.nurturerRole: The nurturer (a kind, patient host person who meets the GP in their growth zone, paid in Phases 1–5; ideally one who loves storytelling AND can gear stories to the GP's current level) does the following in Phase 3: learns Bridge Stories at home in advance (reading a version in a language she knows 2–3 times) so she can tell them spontaneously in her own words, adapting them naturally to her languaculture (host-style openings/closings, culturally-natural substitutions like angel-for-fairy) without radically altering the plot; tells or reads stories slowly and carefully for recording; explains every unknown word and opaque sentence ONLY in the host language — definitions, examples, pantomime, acting (posing as a 'lazy person', sounding stern for 'made her do the work'), and example-flooding for grammar ('A doctor made me take medicine. My mother made me get water…'); writes every new word into the GP's word log; creates the Scripts of Life herself (only a host person knows what host people expect to happen) and answers completeness probes; narrates action cartoons live, then retells them naturally while deliberately re-including all word-log words; proposes and joins Shared Experiences, makes notes about them, and reminisces about them the next day; suggests what characters might say in Lexicarry situations; lists universally-known host stories; retells GP stories in polished form for the Listening Library, and (3C) retells stories native-to-native to another host person for recording; keeps her own running lists of Script of Life and Shared Experience ideas; opens her social network so the GP can build relationships partly independent of her. The nurturer must NOT: use the GP's language or translate (everything in the host language — otherwise the host person becomes the growing participator in YOUR languaculture: 'Let's keep the roles straight!'); assume large amounts of host-world cultural background when telling Bridge Stories; let sessions dissolve into hours of small talk or chit-chat (plateau risk — small talk opens the day and arises out of activities, never replaces them); sit and nod while the GP practices reading aloud (a waste of paid nurturer time); allow the GP to read along while listening (it short-circuits listening development); keep stories so simple there is no challenge, or so hard that massaging is tedious — she must keep the difficulty level rising as the GP grows.
terminology: Growing Participator (GP) — the learner, reframed as a foreigner becoming an ever-fuller participant in the host world; the process is never completed
Nurturer — the host person who kindly, gently, patiently assists the GP in their growth zone; paid during Phases 1–5
Growth zone (Zone of Proximal Development) — the band of activities the GP can do only with a bit of help from an experienced person; where all growth happens

Special-growth participation sessions — the paid, concentrated sessions that substitute for the rare natural experiences that let newcomers grow (resolving the catch-22 that you must participate to learn to participate)
Negotiation of meaning — the back-and-forth of clarification requests, repetitions, examples, and comprehension checks until meaning is mutually established
Massaging (a story/recording) — replaying a recording bit by bit and negotiating the meaning of everything not understood, encountering many new words in the process
Iceberg Principle — words enter a mental iceberg on first acquaintance and rise higher with each re-encounter; no memorization; thousands of words go in, frequency lifts them
Word log — a running record of word acquaintances (context noted), explicitly not a memorization list; most entries live inside Listening Library recordings, so re-listening refreshes them
Listening Library — the cumulative collection of all recordings the GP can understand, ordered by growing complexity; re-listened until effortless ('listen, listen, listen')
The importance of frequency — language processing strength tracks frequency of encounter; the programme works by making the rare frequent and constantly enlarging understood-speech volume
Languaculture — language and culture as a single inseparable way of living; learning one is learning the other
Bridge Story — a world story (Cinderella, Bible stories) whose world belongs to neither party, bridging home and host worlds and minimizing required host-cultural background knowledge
Stuff-we-both-know — the Phase 3 master principle: all material has content already known to both GP and nurturer (shared stories, shared experiences, shared scripts)

Script of Life — a host person's step-by-step list (25–30 fine-grained steps) of what is expected to happen in a common activity, from the host point of view (akin to the Series Method); an 'attempted' Script of Life is the GP's own draft, used only for training
Shared Experience / Reminiscing — doing something together so it can be talked about as genuinely shared memory the next day
Expository discourse — abstract, explanatory (non-narrative) speech; harder than stories; the gateway ability for Phase 4
Host world / host people — the people and life-world the GP is growing into
LLA (Language Learning Advisor) — coach who helps design schedules, choose activities, and gather phase resources
Phase 3A/3B/3C — the 100/75/75-hour sub-phases; 3B adds host stories + social life, 3C adds expository and native-to-native material
Communities of practice — groups united by purpose, shared history and practices, which the GP aims to join
Speech-led vs. understanding-led learning — traditional speaking-first, writing-dependent approaches vs. GPA's deliberate pushing of listening far ahead of speaking
phase3pdf.vocabTargets: Entry level: ~2,000+ understood words (from Phases 1–2). Phase 3 target: add roughly 2,000–3,000 new word acquaintances, reaching a total listening vocabulary of 4,000–5,000 by the end of the 250 hours. Operational pace target stated repeatedly: average 8 new-word acquaintances per hour of session time (the Kazakh case study logged ~2,500 words in 150 hours of story work). Per-story calibration: about 5 new words per minute of story is ideal; more than 10/minute means the material is too hard (unless still enjoyable, in which case re-listen more). Tracking method: the word log — a running, dated list written by the nurturer during massaging, with the story/context noted and optionally a rough penciled native-language gloss; explicitly NOT for memorization (Iceberg Principle — acquaintance now, strength through frequency later). Words are 'strengthened' through: overnight re-listening with pause-and-replay on striking words, the optional 20-minute Strengthening Vocabulary activity (re-contextualizing yesterday's words to the nurturer), Story Retelling using the new vocabulary, and lifetime re-encounters in the Listening Library. Words distinguished by personal salience: some only need recognition ('stepsister'), others the GP wants productively ('lazy'). If a word arises outside any recording, make a special recording mentioning the word and its context.
appIdeas: Recording + Massaging Player (core feature): record the nurturer's story in-app, auto- or tap-segment it into sentences; per-sentence loop, replay, and slow-down buttons; a 'don't understand' flag per sentence that opens a negotiation checklist (ask repeat → ask breakdown → ask word meaning → ask for examples → mark understood); words flagged during massaging flow straight into the word log with story + sentence position automatically attached

Digital Word Log with Iceberg model: running list (never flashcards) of word acquaintances, each linked to the exact audio sentence it came from; an 'iceberg level' that rises automatically each time the word is re-encountered in played recordings; tap a word to hear all its recorded contexts; optional penciled-in gloss field; per-hour acquaintance-rate tracker against the 8-words/hour target

Listening Library: chronological shelf of all massaged recordings with per-recording re-listen counts, an 'easy to follow' self-rating, and resurfacing prompts ('You haven't heard Goldilocks in 3 weeks'); background/offline playback for saturating commutes and queues, honoring the 15-hours/week listening quota

Difficulty Calibrator: after each story, auto-compute minutes-massaged per minute-of-story and new-words per minute; show green (≤30 min/story-min, ~5–10 words) / red (2 hrs per 2-min story, 50 words) guidance with the guide's prescribed remedies (have nurturer pre-learn and retell; drop to wordless-book stories without pictures)

Bridge Story Bank with the 12-level Appendix 4 difficulty ladder: ship Cinderella, Noah, Goldilocks, First Man & Woman texts; let nurturers pre-study a story in their language in-app, then record their own-words retelling; community sharing so one GP's recorded stories become Level-1 resources for the next GP in that language (a core GPA chore, perfect for software)

Script of Life Builder: step-list editor the nurturer fills in (with prompts like 'After you do X and before Y, what do you do?'), per-step audio, then an act-it-out playback mode that plays one step at a time while the GP pantomimes; seeded brainstorm categories from Appendix 3 (Home, Food, Errands, Personal care, Out and About…) and a rule-reminder that scripts must describe activities the GP has actually experienced

Information-Gap Cartoon mode: GP pre-watches a licensed/linked action cartoon; in session the app hides the video from the GP while showing it to the nurturer, records her live narration, then offers synced watch-along playback, massaging, and a 'natural retelling' second-take screen that displays her the word-log words to re-include

Shared Experience & Reminiscing journal: log what you did together (photos, quick notes); next morning the app cues the Reminiscing recording, and teaches/back-channel-trains listener-feedback phrases ('yeah, really, mhm' equivalents)

Input/Output Flooding with busy pictures: zoomable busy scenes; GP picks a sentence frame they're failing to produce; nurturer mode generates 'Where is the man who…?' hunt-and-tap rounds (forced attention through the picture); output mode flips it so the GP produces the frame about a new scene, with recording
Structured Input mini-games: digital doll-family + candy manipulables where the GP must act on hearing only the grammatical cue ('from me; to the baby') — template-able for many grammar points

Role-Play scenario deck: situation cards (taxi, shop, police stop, haircut) with Reverse Role-Play first (nurturer models the GP's role), recording, then role-swap scheduling a few days later after re-listens

Phase 3B host-story pipeline: nurturer lists universally-known host stories; app schedules the GP's daily listens/reads of the translation for several days, and only unlocks the host-language session recording once familiarity streak is met (encoding the 'become truly familiar first' rule)

Session Planner from the guide's templates: drag-and-drop weekly schedules pre-loaded with the 3A rich/simple and 3B adventuresome/simple sample days; enforces small-talk opener, tracks the 25-hr session + 15-hr listening split, and from 3B reserves 3–5 hrs/week for logged real-world social interaction

Idea Lists hub: the four running lists (Scripts of Life, Shared Experiences, familiar places, role-play situations) editable by both GP and nurturer with mutual suggestions, plus a 'get out and do something new' prompt generator (open a bank account, get a haircut, visit a tailor)

Talking-more toolkit for 3C: story-retell recorder with side-by-side compare to the nurturer's original; 'epic story' serial tracker; weekend-recap prompt; Lexicarry-style empty-bubble strips with multi-variant 'what could they say?' collection; community-topics tracker with periodic update reminders

Anti-pattern guardrails baked into UX: no translation surfaces anywhere in session mode (image/audio-only word support); no transcript visible during listening (reading short-circuits listening — transcripts unlock only in separate read-alone mode); small-talk timer; chit-chat plateau warning if sessions log no new recordings/words

Milestone & graduation checklist per sub-phase: e.g., 3B→3C gate requires logged new relationships; end-of-phase self-checks against the seven key goals; option to exit early to Phase 4 when new host children's stories become understandable un-massaged

phase4.phaseName: Phase 4: Deep Personal Relationships (with a few people — impacting all relationships) — 500 hours, the "Big Middle" third of the 1,500-hour Six-Phase Programme
phase4.summary:
Phase 4 is the giant middle one-third of the GPA programme: 500 hours of "special-growth participation activities" (Phases 1-3 total ~500h before it; Phase 5 adds another 500h). Thomson calls it the "make-or-break" or "sink-or-swim" phase — ideally lasting 4-6 months of concentrated life among host people. The core shift is from being taught by trained "nurturers" to having natural conversations with untrained "mentors": host friends willing to share their lives at a level the grower can understand. Where Phase 3 was about shared stories, Phase 4 is about Deep Life Sharing — getting to know the host world deeply by getting to know a few individual host LIVES deeply, forming genuinely deep personal relationships in the process.

The phase is built on three major activities adapted from ethnographic methods: (1) the Life Story Activity — recording a mentor's life story, clarifying the recording together, then recursively "expanding" it (a 10-minute story can explode into 10-20 hours of recorded material from one storyteller); (2) Walk-of-Life Conversations (ethnographic interviews à la James Spradley) — grand-tour and mini-tour questions about a person's daily life in a particular role (rancher, rickshaw driver, nurse, shopkeeper), plus filling in "lists of life" (cultural domains); and (3) the Detailed Observation Activity — observing a social situation, taking jottings, describing every detail to a mentor, and recording the mentor's interpretation, with triangulation across 2-3 host people. Supplementary activities (hole-finding, Record Yourself for Feedback, retelling, writing a journal) plug specific gaps in vocabulary growth, grammar, and talking time.

Phase 4 is also pivotal conceptually: it is "the great cross-over" from experiencing host life as "they stories" (interpreting everything through home-languaculture concepts — seeing a "bathrobe" where Kazakhs see a khalat) to living the host story with host people using their own story-building pieces. It is the phase when the grower must fight the gravitational pull of the expat "home-away-from-home archipelago" and start living a significant portion of real life — work, leisure, faith, social — in host contexts, moving from special-growth participation toward lifestyle participation.
goals: Develop a few genuinely DEEP personal relationships with host people, and make many other relationships meaningful (the phase name: relationships, not activities, are the real goal)
Understand host life deeply by understanding individual host lives deeply (person-centred languacultural growth, parallel to person-centred ethnography)

Complete ~500 hours of special-growth participation, e.g. a sample plan of 300h Life Story Activity with five host people + 100h Walk-of-Life Conversations across five walks of life + 100h Detailed Observation/Describe
Keep listening vocabulary growing toward the 10,000-word goal (from ~4,000 at phase start), at an average of 8+ strong new-word encounters per special-activity hour
Build a large personal Listening Library of clarified recordings (primary stories, clarification recordings, expansions, vocabulary recordings) that remain understandable and re-listenable for years
Strengthen comprehension of natural explanations and complex stories from multiple speakers with different voices and pronunciations
Greatly increase the grower's own talking: summarizing, retelling stories to many people, describing observed scenes, telling one's own life story in the host language
Cross over from experiencing host life as 'they stories' to living the host story with host people using host story-building pieces
Shift the balance of daily life from the home-away-from-home expat world toward many hours per week genuinely lived in host contexts (work, leisure, domestic, community, faith, social life)
Discover the host world from within, letting the host culture itself dictate the topics to investigate rather than imposing an outsider's checklist
keyPrinciples: Don't learn the language — discover a new world as it is known and shared by the people among whom you are living
Rule 1: No rules govern the storyteller — whatever they talk about IS the track; never steer them 'back on track'; what matters is what is important to them
Rule 2: Be genuinely interested and show it — use host-culture listening behaviors (back-channel words, eye contact, facial expressions) deliberately observed since Phase 3
Rule 3: Only ask about things the mentor has already mentioned or alluded to — never interrogate from your own curiosity list (the 'Did you have any girlfriends?' question is the canonical violation)
Rule 4: Grow in understanding of host life by understanding individual host lives — interesting topics (weddings, key events) will surface naturally if you follow up on what was mentioned
Begin with the broadest possible open questions ('Tell me the story of your life', 'Tell me about a typical day') and let all later questions grow out of the answers
Comprehension still leads production, but talking a lot now matters: retell, summarize, repeat the same story to different people 4-5 times and watch it improve
Listening is the priority in conversations — give the mentor the joy of being truly understood; your 15-second question should yield their 5-minute answer
Clarify recordings until they are largely understood, then re-listen repeatedly and archive them in the Listening Library

Confidentiality is sacred: trust comparable to a physician, lawyer, or priest; promise that only you will hear recordings, erase anything on request, keep non-personal anecdotes anonymous when retelling
Triangulate interpretations of observations with 2-3 host people before treating any explanation as culturally significant
Stay close to host experience: thick vs thin description awareness — you always see meaningfully through your own languaculture, so ask hosts what THEY see
Participation IS growth: no matter how badly a conversation goes, interacting with host people is growth happening — slog, slog, slog
Pay for mentors' time at fair local rates for extended recorded conversations (especially walk-of-life interviews)
Readiness test: if Life Story conversations go smoothly after a few days of trying, you're ready; if after 1-2 weeks they don't get easier, return to Phase 2/3 activities for a month or two

activities.name: Activity 1: The Life Story Activity (the most fruitful Phase 4 activity)
activities.description: Step 1 — Initial recording: Ask a mentor 'Please tell me the story of your life' (a grand-tour-style whole-life question) and record it. First versions may run 2-20+ minutes. The grower speaks as little as possible, shows intense genuine interest, and never steers (Rule 1: the storyteller creates the track — e.g., a Central Asian man opening with the Leningrad blockade turns out to be explaining he was born during WWII). Step 2 — Solo listen (optional): Before the next session, listen alone; mark parts not understood, note bits that could be expanded, draft questions per the expansion rules. Step 3 — Clarify the recording: Replay it WITH the storyteller, pausing whenever something isn't understood. Problems are typed: unknown word (e.g., 'wilderness' — mentor explains it), unknown concept (e.g., 'camping' — mentor gives a BRIEF explanation only; full exploration waits for the expansion step), known words in an unfamiliar idiom ('kept to myself', 'became really close to' — mentor corrects the grower's literal misreading), missing cultural background (e.g., the 12-week California school summer break), or just unclear pronunciation needing a slower repeat. All new words go into the running word log (already ~4,000 words by Phase 4) with a pointer to where in the recording they occur. The goal of clarifying: become so familiar with the recording that on any later listen you largely understand it; then add it to the Listening Library. Step 4 — Spot expansion opportunities: List possible topics ONLY from things the storyteller mentioned or alluded to (Rule 3). From George's 90-second excerpt: 'Have you been told anything about the time you were born?', 'Tell me all about those two months in 1957', 'Tell me about those ranchers' — but NOT 'What happened in 1958?', 'Did you graduate high school?', or 'Did you have any girlfriends?' (pure curiosity, never mentioned). Interests like weddings surface naturally: if George mentions his wife, ask about her; the wedding will emerge; then ask for the wedding story, then how it differed from / resembled other weddings. Step 5 — Record the expansions: Each expansion is either (a) a NEW STORY filling in the original ('the story of the events around my birth' — George's mother expecting a girl, the Hollywood cowboy roping his pregnant mom) or (b) a FULL EXPLANATION of a new concept ('Tell me what people do when they are camping'). Expansions themselves contain ~10 expandable bits each ('Did your father tell you about his army experiences?'), so the material EXPLODES: a 10-minute story → ~90 minutes of expansions → potentially 9 hours of further expansions; one storyteller easily yields 10-20 hours. The grower quickly learns to be selective. Step 6 — Re-listen: 1-2+ more times within days, attending to logged words as they 'parade by' in context. Add to Listening Library (years later these stay easy and interesting because they were calibrated to your level). Step 7 — Summarize/Retell: Tell the mentor back what you understood ('Let me see if I understood your story') — stretches talking ability and makes the mentor feel understood. Full cycle: ask whole-life question (RECORD) → clarify (RECORD) → word recordings → identify expansions → choose one → ask & record expansion → repeat 2-6 recursively → retell → archive all mentor-voice recordings.
activities.materials: Voice recorder (phone/digital recorder/computer); running word log; 'Stories to Record, Parts to Expand, Topics to Explore' tracking form with columns: topic | audio recorded ✓ | clarified ✓ | number of new words | checked for new topic ideas ✓ | listened to again ✓ | listened to later ✓; growing Listening Library of clarified recordings; optional audio editor for making vocabulary recordings
activities.timing: Throughout Phase 4; can fill 300h+ with ~5 different host people; suggested as the single most fruitful activity — could legitimately occupy the entire 500 hours

activities.name: Vocabulary Recordings (sub-technique of Life Story / all activities)
activities.description: Two formats. (a) Words-in-context: copy sentences containing each new word out of the original recording into a new audio file, sandwiching each sentence with the isolated word: 'Spent. I spent my early childhood in California. Spent.' 'Ranchers. We became really close to many of the ranchers. Ranchers.' Hearing the original context jogs memory when the meaning is forgotten. (b) Word-discussion recording (Thomson finds this more interesting to re-listen to): record yourself and the mentor going down the word-log list, briefly discussing each word's meaning IN THE HOST LANGUAGE. Track total new words per recording on the form; target 8+ new words per activity hour averaged over 4 days.
activities.materials: Word log; recorder; audio editing software for copy-paste of sentences from digital recordings
activities.timing: After each clarifying session; monitored on a rolling 4-day window — if word rate falls well below 8/hour, day 5 is reassigned to vocabulary-rich activities

activities.name: The Two-Recorder Technique (advanced alternative for Life Story & Walk-of-Life)
activities.description: Once the discrete steps are second nature, intermingle them. Step 1: record the initial life story as before (the PRIMARY recording). Step 2: play it back with the mentor while a SECOND recorder runs, capturing the whole clarify-and-expand conversation (the SECONDARY recording). The entire primary recording ends up scattered through the secondary one, interleaved with the grower's questions about unknown words ('what's a lariat?', 'what would the cowboy be doing with the lariat?'), requests for expansions, and the mentor's 5-minute answers to 15-second questions. The grower still jots written ideas for future expansions while listening. If the mentor takes off into an animated new story mid-clarification, STOP interrupting and treat it as new primary material — show interest, let them run; that stretch will itself need later clarification, captured in a TERTIARY recording (quaternary conceivable but Thomson never needed it). These layered recordings make fascinating listening material for months and years.
activities.materials: Two recorders (or one device that can play while another records); notepad for expansion ideas; word log
activities.timing: Adopt only after the step-by-step form-based procedure has become second nature

activities.name: Getting Permission to Record (onboarding sub-procedure)
activities.description: Gently convince the mentor: promise no one but you will ever hear the recordings without their permission; promise immediate permanent erasure of anything they want removed; keep the promises. Often the first life-story partner is a former nurturer already used to recording. Tactic: do a couple of days WITHOUT recording, then point out how much is being lost and ask to try recording once and clarify it; once the mentor sees the value, they typically allow recording everything. Where recording is impossible (women's voices not to be heard by strangers; government-eavesdropping cultures): write notes from memory immediately after each conversation, summarize back at the next meeting, and still record (or write) new words with illustrative sentences — that is almost always acceptable. Non-confidential topics from deep conversations can then seed informal unrecorded conversations with many other people ('Someone was telling me of the ceremony when they finished building their home... Have you ever done that?' — note the anonymity protection).
activities.materials: Recorder; notebook for the no-recording fallback
activities.timing: First days of Phase 4 with each new mentor

activities.name: Activity 2: Walk-of-Life Conversations (ethnographic conversations à la James Spradley)
activities.description: Where Life Story covers a life across years, Walk-of-Life covers daily life in a societal ROLE at the present time (Thomson's example: a Pakistani rickshaw driver, chosen because he used rickshaws constantly). Recruit people whose professions impinge on your life or interest you (nurse if you'll do medical work; shopkeeper since you shop); do several walks of life; PAY a fair local hourly rate since this involves extended recorded sessions. Step 1: Ask a TYPICAL GRAND-TOUR question ('typical' because it asks for a typical example — a typical day, a typical shift, the typical process of building a house) and record: 'Jack, tell me about your typical day on the ranch.' Emphasize two things to the teller: (1) things commonplace to them are completely unknown to you; (2) everything is genuinely interesting and you want lots of detail. Step 2: Clarify the recording exactly as in the Life Story Activity (pause at unknown words/idioms/pronunciation/cultural gaps; feed the word log). Step 3: From the account, harvest follow-up questions into the Grand Tour Form: MORE GRAND-TOUR questions (typical year; typical day in other seasons; a description of fencing; bringing hay down from the high meadow; layout of the ranch) and MINI-TOUR questions covering brief activities in fine detail (making the fire in the cookstove; putting on the coffee; breaking holes in the creek; harnessing and hitching the team; throwing hay down into the rack; descriptions of the barn and shop). A mini-tour answer can be as long as the original whole-day account — e.g., Jack's full kindling-shavings-chimney-damper monologue on lighting the cookstove, ending 'Anything I missed?' and the GP drilling further: 'What exactly do you do when you light a piece of kindling?'. Don't agonize over grand vs mini classification. Also harvest LISTS OF LIFE (see separate entry). Step 4: Ask a follow-up question and repeat. Full cycle mirrors Life Story: initial walk-of-life question (RECORD) → clarify (RECORD) → word recordings → identify grand tours/mini tours/lists of life → choose → expand (RECORD) → repeat → retell ('Let me see if I understood you') → archive to Listening Library. Question typology from Spradley to mix in: typical grand tour; SPECIFIC grand tour ('what did you do from morning to night last Wednesday' — a real day gives a different picture than 'typical'); GUIDED grand tour (mentor shows you around the barn in person while describing every place); TASK-RELATED grand tour (Jack harnesses a horse narrating each step); mini-tour; EXPERIENCE questions ('Have you had any really interesting experiences while feeding the cattle?' — reveals expectations and what happens when things go wrong); plus structural questions (filling domains) and contrast questions ('What's the difference between a day in haying season and a day in early fall?').
activities.materials: Recorder(s); Grand Tour Form with columns: grand tour questions, mini-tour questions, lists of life to explore | audio recorded | clarified | number of new words | checked for new topic ideas | checked for lists of life | listened to again | listened to later; word log; payment for the mentor at local hourly standards
activities.timing: Suggested ~100h with representatives of ~5 walks of life; multiple sessions per person

activities.name: Lists of Life / Cultural Domains (sub-technique of Walk-of-Life)
activities.description: A cultural domain is a set of same-type items existing in the language/culture (not personal preference lists). Spot implied lists in a mentor's account — from Jack's day: 'things that need workin' on', 'different places where there is hay', 'times to get up in the morning', 'different buildings on the ranch', 'Ellen's tasks', 'breaks during the day', 'times of the year (work-wise)', 'conditions of the creek', 'after-supper activities'. Fill a domain by reading the list back and asking for more: GP: 'You mentioned that after supper you read and listen to the radio. Is there anything else you might do?' Jack: 'Oh, maybe a bit of crib with Ellen. Or just kick back.' GP: 'Read, listen to the radio, play crib, kick back. Anything else?' Jack: 'Yeah read, or look at the catalogue; maybe play a bit of solitaire.' Then extend to other people (ask Ellen; read the list to OTHER ranchers to see what they add — if 'winter evening activities' turns out extensive, you've found an important domain of ranch life). Discover the host COVER TERM by reading the list and asking 'What are these examples of?'; if the mentor has no fixed term, have them coin one they're comfortable with. Spradley's nine domain relationships guide the hunt: strict inclusion (X is a kind of Y), spatial (X is a place/part in/of Y), cause-effect, rationale (X is a reason for doing Y), location-of-action (X is a place for doing Y), function (X is used for Y), means-end (X is a way to do Y), sequence (X is a step/stage in Y), attribution (X is a characteristic of Y). Thomson rates domain exploration as rewarding but no more important than descriptive (grand/mini-tour) questions.
activities.materials: Lists-of-life column on the Grand Tour Form; Spradley's relationship table as a reference card
activities.timing: Woven into every Walk-of-Life session after the first clarification

activities.name: Activity 3: Detailed Observation Activity (Observe and Describe)
activities.description: Observe a specific SOCIAL SITUATION (a place + activities + actors, per Spradley 1980 — e.g., a small food shop containing sub-places like the cash register, actors like customers and shopkeepers, activities like gathering food and checking out), then describe it exhaustively to a mentor and listen to their commentary. Step 1: Take a walk and list observable social situations; choose one. Step 2: Visit and take notes — two kinds: 'head notes' (deliberate detailed memorizing, which MUST be converted to written notes ASAP before they decay) and preferably 'jottings' (invented personal shorthand; diagram the location and code actors/positions, e.g., bus seat '3RA' = 3rd row right aisle, 'D' = driver, 'C' = conductor). Record EVERYTHING: physical details (wallpaper, a half-full 10-inch trash can right of the door, stain on the waiter's apron, aromas), facial expressions and body language, who occupies which positions, conversation patterns (who talks first, who talks how much). Crucially: do NOT limit observations to what you can already say in the host language. Modern variant (credit Tawnya Gililland): dictate the scene into a phone's voice recorder — it looks like a phone call — or even use video. Worked example given: a ~300-word minutely detailed description of a man sweeping a Central Asian petrol station at 6 a.m. (broom construction, arc of each sweep, dust clouds, the red-brick vs sloping-asphalt zones, sweepings pushed into the street). Step 3: From your jottings, describe the whole scene to your mentor — every detail, 'do not go easy on yourself' (this powerfully stretches talking ability and is a prime hole-finding exercise). Ask what the MENTOR thinks rather than offering your own speculations: Who is the man with the broom? What is behind his sweeping? Who is the sweeping important to and why? Why that time of day? Their answers reveal host values and assumptions. TRIANGULATE: discuss anything seemingly important with 2-3 other host people (e.g., several hosts infer 'labourer not supervisor' from his dress — confirmed; one suggests he sweeps early to beat the heat — others reject it, saying a business should simply be clean when it opens — unconfirmed conjecture). Step 4: The mentor then re-describes the scene as they understood your description, with their commentary on its meanings, RECORDED, deliberately working in all the new word-log words. Special case — one-time events: at rare important events (an automobile accident, a fight, a memorial meal at the fixed interval after a death), recognize the moment, take heavy head notes, convert to jottings/notes ASAP, then run Steps 3-4.
activities.materials: Notebook for jottings + personal shorthand + situation diagrams; phone voice/video recorder as covert note-taker; recorder for the mentor's summary; word log; list-of-situations brainstorm sheet (blank list provided in the guide)
activities.timing: Suggested ~100h; also doubles as a special-growth TALKING activity and a hole-finding activity whenever speech output needs a boost

activities.name: Hole-Finding (supplementary, from earlier phases — vocabulary booster)
activities.description: Try to talk about something difficult in order to expose 'holes' (unknown words, missing constructions) in your ability, which the mentor then fills. Concrete versions: watch a Tom & Jerry cartoon or silent film (Charlie Chaplin, Mr. Bean) and attempt to narrate absolutely everything that happens; open a 'busy picture' or children's busy book (e.g., The Usborne Big Book of Things to Spot) to any page and describe all you see; describing your Detailed Observation notes is itself hole-finding. Afterwards make a recap recording including all the new vocabulary. Trigger rule: if over 4 days you've averaged significantly under 8 new words per special-activity hour, dedicate day 5 to hole-finding and other vocab-rich earlier-phase activities (Phase 4's natural conversations often run vocabulary-light because mentors simplify and topics are familiar).
activities.materials: Tom & Jerry / Chaplin / Mr. Bean videos; busy pictures and busy books; wordless picture books; recorder
activities.timing: Day 5 fallback whenever the rolling 4-day new-word rate drops below ~8/hour

activities.name: Recycled Phase 2 / Phase 3 Activities (supplementary vocabulary infusions)
activities.description: Phase 2 style: take a wordless picture story never used before (Anno's Journey is recommended at this stage) and tell the story to your mentor. Phase 3 style: clarify an unused world story or host story known from translation, or build new 'scripts of life'. These reliably deliver a steady influx of new vocabulary; finish with a recap recording containing all new words. Also: Phase 3 Input Flooding and Output Flooding remain the prescribed fix when you know the words but can't combine them natively — target them at grammar patterns you notice yourself reaching for (e.g., 'the X who is Y', 'He likes to X', 'Someone helps him to X'); readiness for a grammar point is signaled by noticing it a lot and attempting it in your own speech.
activities.materials: Anno's Journey (Anno 1977) and other unused wordless picture stories; Phase 3 guide ('Getting Going in Phase 3: 250 Hours of Shared-Story Activities') for input/output flooding procedures; recorder
activities.timing: As needed for Problem 1 (slow vocab) and Problem 2 (non-native phrasing)

activities.name: Record Yourself for Feedback (supplementary — grammar/nativeness audit)
activities.description: Tell a story or discuss a topic to a mentor while recording YOURSELF. Then replay from the start, pausing after EVERY sentence. At each pause the mentor asks themselves: 'Is that something I or another host person might have said, or is it clearly different from how host people talk?' If plausible — move on. If 'no host person would say that' — log it in a three-column chart: What I said | How a host person might have said it | Optional note on the nature of the problem (examples given: 'He blew her nose' → 'She blew her nose' → ''he'' refers to males; 'My friend were there' → 'My friend was there' → was/were paradigm; third column may stay empty). The recurring grammar weaknesses harvested here become the targets for future input-flooding and output-flooding activities.
activities.materials: Recorder; three-column feedback chart (What I said / Host version / Nature of problem)
activities.timing: Periodic, as a diagnostic; feeds the flooding-activity pipeline

activities.name: Writing Activities (supplementary)
activities.description: Phase 4 is a good phase to BEGIN writing, provided the written language doesn't differ radically from the spoken language. Keep a journal addressed to a host nurturer and get their feedback on it. Like Record Yourself for Feedback, this raises awareness of non-native patterns — but Thomson stresses the bigger lever is interacting with hosts who help you formulate sentences live, and PAYING LOTS OF ATTENTION to how they help and correct you.
activities.materials: Journal/notebook; a host nurturer/mentor willing to give written feedback
activities.timing: Ongoing low-volume habit from Phase 4 onward

activities.name: Special-Growth Talking Activities: Ways to Talk a Lot (supplementary — output volume)
activities.description: Because Life Stories and Walk-of-Life are listening-heavy, deliberately engineer talking time (Problem 3). The menu: (1) Detailed Observation descriptions (stretches everyday-detail talk); (2) periodically retell in summary what a mentor has told you in Life Story / Walk-of-Life sessions; (3) retell mentors' fascinating NON-confidential stories — anonymized — to friends, co-workers, taxi drivers, your barber (rich conversation material that often prompts hearers to share similar experiences); (4) tell YOUR OWN life story to mentors, and retell key incidents to various people, steadily improving those specific stories and storytelling generally; (5) tell an EPIC story — one that goes on and on — to several people in small instalments; (6) join host groups requiring oral contribution (faith-group discussions, special-interest groups, the regular teashop circle debating current issues) — fit in unobtrusively at first, making extended contributions later in Phase 4; (7) maintain an active social life of visiting and being visited; (8) the universal multiplier: tell the same story or give the same explanation to several different people on different occasions — improvement is dramatic between the 1st and the 4th-5th telling.
activities.materials: None special — anonymized story bank from mentor sessions; one's own pre-thought life-story episodes; host group memberships
activities.timing: Woven through the phase; escalating as ability grows

activities.name: Time-Distribution Planning (meta-activity)
activities.description: At the very start of Phase 4, TRY all three major activities, then set personal hour-goals per activity. Sample allocation: 300h Life Story with 5 host people, 100h Walk-of-Life across 5 walks of life, 100h Observe-and-Describe — but spending all 500h on Life Story alone 'would not be a great calamity' since it's the most fruitful activity. Discuss the plan with a language learning advisor. Also audit life domains (work, leisure, recreation, domestic, community, faith, general social) for opportunities to let host-world life compete fairly with home-away-from-home life.
activities.materials: Personal hour-budget plan; access to a language learning advisor
activities.timing: Planning at phase start; review continuously

activities.name: Topic Discovery Discipline (cross-cutting method)
activities.description: Let the host culture tell you what to investigate (Spradley's stance) rather than arriving with a classical-anthropology checklist ('mate selection', 'bodily adornments'). Three legitimate topic sources: (1) anything the mentor already mentioned (the expansion engine); (2) 'key events' (Fetterman) you stay alert for — random major events (a house fire), life-cycle events (weddings, births, deaths), religious events, holidays, plus cyclically recurring daily/weekly/monthly/yearly events; (3) anything you personally observe or experience that puzzles you (people leaving home in all directions on Saturday morning — where are they going?; moments when people seem inexplicably upset with you; a pedestrian struck by a car and the crowd's reactions). 'Sensitizing concepts' (your interests: values, the supernatural, exchanges, alienation, reconciliation) may be pursued — but only when they arise naturally in the mentor's talk. Conversational sensitivity example: if the mentor says she's twelve years older than her youngest sister, ask what she remembers of the sister's birth (you wouldn't if the gap were three years). Pacing sensitivity: early days, don't push on the most personal items (a parent's death mentioned in the initial story — don't expand it on day one); let comfort grow; expect real laughter and real tears, and expect a strong bond to form with any extensive life-story partner.
activities.materials: Expansion-topic lists on the tracking forms; observation journal
activities.timing: Governs every session of all three major activities

phase4.sessionStructure: There is no fixed lesson template in Phase 4 — sessions are natural recorded conversations with mentors, structured by the recursive activity cycles rather than by a clock. The canonical Life Story / Walk-of-Life cycle per topic: (1) ask one broad open question and record while staying almost silent (initial tellings 2-20+ min; expansion answers ~90s-5min per 15-second question); (2) a clarification session replaying the recording together, pausing at every comprehension gap (with the Two-Recorder Technique this merges with expansion-asking and is itself recorded); (3) word-recording segment discussing each new word in the host language; (4) plan expansions on the tracking form; (5) record expansions, recycling steps 2-6 recursively; (6) solo re-listening 1-2+ times within days; (7) a retell/summary segment back to the mentor. Detailed Observation alternates fieldwork (solo observing + jotting) with a mentor session (grower describes exhaustively, mentor interprets, mentor records a summary), plus triangulation mini-conversations with 2-3 other hosts. Everything happens in the target language — mentors need no training because communication is now natural, though they instinctively simplify. Monitoring rhythm: every 4 days check the new-words-per-hour rate; if well under 8/hour, dedicate the 5th day to hole-finding / Phase 2-3 vocabulary activities. Recommended macro-allocation example: 300h Life Story (5 people) + 100h Walk-of-Life (5 roles) + 100h Observe-and-Describe, alongside ever-growing informal lifestyle participation (groups, visiting, retelling stories to many people).
materials: Voice recorder(s) — phone, digital recorder, or computer; two devices for the Two-Recorder Technique; phone voice-memo/video as covert observation note-taker
Running word log (carried over from earlier phases, ~4,000 words at entry) with per-recording location references
'Stories to Record, Parts to Expand, Topics to Explore' form (Life Story tracking: audio recorded / clarified / # new words / checked for new topics / listened again / listened later)
'Grand Tour Form' (Walk-of-Life tracking: adds a 'checked for lists of life' column)
Listening Library — the cumulative archive of all clarified recordings (primary stories, secondary/tertiary clarification recordings, expansions, vocabulary recordings, mentor scene-summaries)
Vocabulary recordings (word-in-context sandwich files, or recorded word-discussions in the host language)
Notebook for observation jottings, personal shorthand, and location diagrams (e.g., bus-seat coding '3RA', 'D'=driver)
Record-Yourself-for-Feedback three-column chart (What I said / How a host would say it / Nature of problem)
Hole-finding media: Tom & Jerry cartoons, silent films (Chaplin, Mr. Bean), busy pictures, The Usborne Big Book of Things to Spot
Wordless picture books not yet used — notably Anno's Journey (Anno 1977)
Phase 3 guide for Input Flooding / Output Flooding procedures
Journal addressed to a host nurturer (writing activity)
Payment budget for mentors at fair local hourly rates (especially walk-of-life interviewees)
Spradley's cultural-domain relationship table (kind-of, part-of, cause-effect, rationale, location-of-action, function, means-end, sequence, attribution) as a reference
milestones: Can elicit, clarify, and largely understand a mentor's recorded life story, reaching the point where re-listening yields near-full comprehension (the explicit readiness/success test for the phase)
Has built 10-20+ hours of recorded, clarified story-and-explanation material per main storyteller, archived in a personal Listening Library
Listening vocabulary has grown substantially beyond the entry ~4,000 words toward the 10,000-word programme goal, sustained at ~8+ new words per activity hour
Comfortably understands extended natural explanations (expository language) and complex stories from multiple speakers with differing voices and pronunciations

Can summarize and retell a mentor's moderately complex stories, give the same story/explanation to several different people with marked improvement by the 4th-5th telling, and tell their own life story in the host language
Can describe a minutely observed social scene in exhaustive detail and discuss its cultural meanings, triangulating interpretations across 2-3 host people
Has formed a few genuinely deep host relationships (shared joys and hurts, laughter and tears) plus many meaningful ones — deep relationships are mandatory in Phase 4, not optional
Participates orally in host group life (faith groups, teashop discussions, interest groups), making extended contributions that flow with the group by late Phase 4
Daily life has measurably shifted toward host contexts across work/leisure/domestic/faith/social domains — the 'great cross-over' from they-stories toward living the host story
Has begun writing (journal with mentor feedback) where written and spoken language are close

Is positioned for Phase 5: ready for native-to-native Discourses, 'doing things with words' (requests, apologies, commitments), and style/register issues already kept in view by asking about universally-known themes, people, places, and events
phase4.nurturerRole: In Phase 4 the special host helpers are called MENTORS, not nurturers — they need NO training because the communication is natural; they just need to interact at a level the grower can understand and participate in (they instinctively simplify, which is why recordings stay re-listenable). Mentors should be paid a reasonable local hourly rate for extended recorded sessions, especially walk-of-life interviews. What the mentor DOES: tells their life story and daily-life accounts at whatever length and in whatever direction they choose; pauses on demand to clarify unknown words, idioms, pronunciations, and cultural background (spending money vs spending time; what camping is; the 12-week school break); gives brief explanations during clarification and full explanations during expansions; answers grand-tour, mini-tour, experience, structural, and contrast questions; helps fill and name lists of life; re-describes and interprets observed scenes (Who is the sweeping man? Why 6 a.m.?); judges every sentence in Record-Yourself-for-Feedback ('would a host person say that?') and supplies the native version; discusses each word-log entry in the host language for vocabulary recordings; helps the grower formulate sentences live and corrects gently — the grower must pay close attention to these corrections. What the mentor (and grower) must NOT do: the grower must never steer the storyteller 'back on track' (there is no track but theirs), must not ask about anything not yet mentioned or alluded to, must not push personal/painful topics in the first days, must not substitute their own speculations for the mentor's interpretations of observed scenes, and must guard confidentiality absolutely — physician/lawyer/priest-level trust: never replay recordings to others without permission, erase anything on request, retell only non-personal anecdotes and only anonymized; a grief such as a miscarriage is never to be repeated in any identifying way. Expect (and welcome) the by-product: a strong personal bond reliably forms with anyone who shares their life story at this depth — that bond is the actual point of the phase. A separate 'language learning advisor' figure helps the grower plan time allocation and life-domain restructuring.
appIdeas: Life Story Workbench: a recording-centric workspace where the user records (or imports) a mentor's life story, then replays it with tap-to-mark 'I don't understand this part' pins; each pin becomes a clarification card typed by problem kind (unknown word / unknown concept / idiom / cultural background / pronunciation), mirroring the George-story worked examples

Expansion Tree ('the story explodes'): visualize each story as a node; the app prompts the user to extract mention-based expansion candidates and enforces Rule 3 with a gentle check — 'Was this actually mentioned in the story?' — flagging pure-curiosity questions (the 'girlfriends' anti-example) before they're saved; expansions nest recursively, showing the 10-min → 90-min → 9-hour explosion as a growing tree

Digital 'Stories to Record' and 'Grand Tour' forms: per-topic checklist rows (recorded ✓ / clarified ✓ / # new words / checked for topics ✓ / checked for lists of life ✓ / listened again ✓ / listened later ✓) auto-linked to the actual audio segments

Listening Library with smart re-listen scheduling: every clarified recording is archived and resurfaced for the prescribed 1-2 re-listens within days, then spaced repetition over months/years; recordings tagged primary/secondary/tertiary for Two-Recorder workflows

One-tap Vocabulary Recording builder: select sentences in a recording's timeline containing a logged word and auto-generate the 'Word. Sentence. Word.' sandwich audio file; alternative mode records a live word-discussion session straight down the word-log list

Word log with velocity gauge: rolling 4-day new-words-per-hour meter against the 8/hour target; when it dips, the app automatically schedules a 'Day 5 vocabulary infusion' and suggests hole-finding content (silent-film narration, busy-picture description, an unused wordless story like Anno's Journey)

Hole-finding mode: plays a Tom & Jerry-style silent clip or shows a busy picture; user records themselves narrating everything; gaps they couldn't express become a 'holes' list to bring to the next mentor session — all image/video based, zero translation

Lists-of-Life (cultural domain) collector: spot a list implied in a transcript, name it provisionally, then run the fill-in script ('Read the list back, ask: anything else?'), track contributions per informant (Jack, Ellen, other ranchers), prompt for the host cover term ('What are these examples of?'), and classify by Spradley's nine relationship types

Walk-of-Life question generator: from a clarified typical-day recording, scaffolded buckets for new grand-tour, specific-day, guided-tour, task-related, mini-tour, experience, structural, and contrast questions, with examples (Jack/the cookstove) as inline coaching

Detailed Observation field tool: covert voice-memo dictation mode ('looks like a phone call'), shorthand jotting pad with a scene-diagram canvas (drag-and-drop actor codes like 3RA/D/C), a head-notes decay timer nudging immediate write-up, and a describe-to-mentor session mode that records the mentor's interpretive summary

Triangulation tracker: any interpretation of an observed detail gets a confidence state (1 host / 2 hosts / 3+ hosts confirm; contested) — visualizing Fetterman-style triangulation before a 'cultural insight' is marked trusted

Record Yourself for Feedback player: sentence-by-sentence playback with a per-sentence mentor verdict button ('a host could say this' / 'no host would say this'), auto-building the three-column chart and feeding flagged grammar patterns into suggested input/output-flooding drills

Retell prompter: after each clarified story, schedules a 'Let me see if I understood you' summary session; separately tracks the tell-the-same-story-to-5-people loop with per-telling self-ratings to surface the 1st-to-5th-telling improvement curve

Confidentiality-by-design: recordings local/encrypted by default, per-recording mentor-consent flags, one-tap permanent erase honoring the 'erase on request' promise, and an anonymization checklist before any story is marked 'retellable to others'
Relationship dashboard: per-mentor view of hours together, recordings, stories shared, depth markers — reframing progress as relationships (the phase's true metric) rather than lessons completed

Phase-4 readiness self-check and tough-times coach: guided check ('Do Life Story conversations get easier after a few days?'), with the prescribed fallback path (return to Phase 2/3 activities + informal interaction for 1-2 months) and 'slog on' encouragement content

Life-domain audit ('escape the archipelago'): checklist across work/leisure/domestic/community/faith/social life rating home-world vs host-world hours per week, prompting concrete commitments to add host contexts (a group to join, a standing visit), revisited monthly

They-story journal: a reflective feature where the user logs moments they caught themselves interpreting host life through home concepts (bathrobe vs khalat) and records the host story-building piece they learned instead
Time-budget planner: set and track the 500-hour allocation (e.g., 300/100/100 across the three major activities and 5 mentors / 5 walks of life), with advisor-shareable progress reports
phase4.hours: 500 hours (the middle third of the 1,500-hour programme; ideally compressed into 4-6 months of concentrated living)
phase4.vocabTargets: Entry level: acquaintance with roughly 4,000 words in the running word log by the start of Phase 4. Programme goal: 10,000 words of listening vocabulary (words understood when heard), so the pace must not slacken. Operational target: an average of eight or more strong encounters with new vocabulary items per hour of special-growth activity. Because Phase 4's natural conversations tend to run vocabulary-light (mentors simplify; topics are everyday), the rule is: if over any four-day window the rate falls significantly below 8 new words/hour, dedicate the fifth day to vocabulary-rich activities (hole-finding, unused wordless picture stories like Anno's Journey, Phase 3 shared-story activities). Tracking mechanics: every new word/idiom enters the running word log with a reference to the recording and position where it occurred; the tracking forms log the number of new words per recording; vocabulary recordings (word-sentence-word sandwich files, or recorded host-language word discussions) recycle the log for re-listening, and re-listens deliberately attend to logged words 'parading by' in their original contexts.
terminology: Growing Participator (GP) — the learner, reframed as someone growing in participation in a host world rather than 'learning a language'
Growing Participation Approach / Six-Phase Programme — Thomson's 1,500-hour framework (Phases 1-3 ≈ 500h; Phase 4 = 500h; Phase 5 = 500h; Phase 6 ongoing)
Special-growth participation (activities/times/sessions) — concentrated paid sessions with special host people, needed because everyday life offers only scattered growth opportunities
Nurturer — the trained, paid host helper of Phases 1-3
Mentor — the Phase 4-5 counterpart: an untrained host friend who shares life naturally at an accessible level (the first mentor is often a former nurturer)
Host world / host people / host languaculture — the new world the GP is being nurtured into; 'home world' is the GP's native languaculture, which competes for every waking hour
Languaculture (Agar) — language and culture as one inseparable flow of lived and spoken stories; thought and experience operate through culturally given symbols (Vygotsky)
Symbol = form + concept — e.g., the word-form 'tomato' plus the tomato concept; languages are massive toolkits of such symbols

Story-building pieces — the words, objects, actions, and scripts a languaculture builds its lived and told stories from (bathrobe vs khalat: the identical object is a different piece of life in each world)

They stories — stories built about host people using home-languaculture pieces ('a customer in her bathrobe drinking tea from a bowl'), radically different from the story the host person is living; Phase 4 is 'the great cross-over' away from them
The host Story — the shared life host people are living, which the GP gradually joins
Clarifying (a recording) — replaying audio with a host person, pausing at every comprehension gap until the recording is largely understood on re-listen
Word log — the running vocabulary register (~4,000 entries entering Phase 4)
Listening Library — the cumulative archive of clarified, re-listenable recordings

Primary / secondary / tertiary recording — Two-Recorder Technique layers: the original story; the recorded clarification/expansion conversation about it; the recorded clarification of new stories that erupted during the secondary
Expansion — a follow-up either as a new story growing out of the first, or a full explanation of a new concept; expansions recursively 'explode'
Grand tour question (Spradley) — broad descriptive question about a long stretch (typical day/shift/year/process or a large place); subtypes: typical, specific, guided, task-related
Mini-tour question — same idea for a brief activity in fine detail (lighting the cookstove)
Experience question — 'Have you had any really interesting experiences while X?'
Structural / contrast questions — filling a cultural domain vs probing differences within it

Lists of life / cultural domains (Spradley) — culturally shared sets of same-type items ('after-supper activities'), with cover terms and nine relationship types (kind-of, part-of, cause-effect, rationale, location, function, means-end, sequence, attribution)
Social situation vs cultural scene (Spradley) — place+actors+activities described thinly vs with cultural meaning attached; thin vs thick description (Geertz's wink vs eyelid contraction)
Head notes vs jottings (Emerson, Fretz & Shaw) — memorized observations (decay fast; write up ASAP) vs shorthand field notes with diagrams and codes
Triangulation (Fetterman) — confirming an interpretation with two or three host people before trusting it
Key events (Fetterman) — revealing major events (house fires, weddings, births, deaths, holidays, cyclic events) to stay alert for
Sensitizing concepts — the GP's own interest areas (values, the supernatural, exchanges, reconciliation), pursued only when they arise naturally
Hole-finding — talking about something hard to expose gaps (unknown words/constructions) for the mentor to fill
Input flooding / output flooding — Phase 3 grammar-awareness techniques recycled for stubborn patterns
Record Yourself for Feedback — sentence-by-sentence native-plausibility audit of one's own recorded speech
Discourse vs discourses — the society-wide ongoing 'big conversation' on a topic (hockey, the stock market) vs individual conversations within it; full entry is Phase 5 work, previewed in Phase 4
Home-away-from-home world / the archipelago — the transplanted expat world of home-life islands that competes with host life and must be 'broken down a bit' in this sink-or-swim phase
Person-centred ethnography (Wolcott) — knowing a people deeply by knowing several persons deeply; the GP analogue is person-centred languacultural growth
Lifestyle participation — the Phase 6 destination: life itself provides rich growth, beyond special sessions

phase5.phaseName: Phase 5: Widening Understanding (such that we can fit in naturally in groups of host people) — Phase 5 of the Six-Phase Programme, subtitled "Another 500 Hours: Getting Underway with Conversations about Native-to-Native Discourses" (Greg Thomson, 2016 version)
phase5.summary:
Phase 5 attacks the single biggest plateau experienced by advanced learners: "I can do pretty well communicating with one host person who knows me, but when host people are talking to one another and ignoring me, I understand very little." Through Phases 1-4 (~1,000 hours) the growing participator (GP) learned from speech that hosts deliberately simplified and adapted for a foreigner. That accommodated speech puts a cap on growth. In Phase 5 the GP works massively and systematically on NATIVE-TO-NATIVE DISCOURSES — recordings of host people talking to host people with no concessions to a foreign listener — because by now such speech has finally entered the GP's "growth zone" (understandable with help, not without). The GP is "shedding training wheels to ride with the gang."

The core activity is the "supercharged participation meeting" with a paid MENTOR (the Phase 5 successor to the nurturer — no training needed, since communication is now natural). The GP obtains recordings of native-to-native speech (hired life-story interviews recorded while the GP is absent, hot-topic discussions among friends, radio, TV dramas, films, audiobooks, mentor read-alouds of books), attempts to understand them alone, then sits with the mentor and CLARIFIES them: pausing every phrase or two, asking for slow repetitions of garbled stretches, getting unknown words elaborated conversationally into a parallel "word recording," expanding cultural references with Phase 4 interview techniques (grand-tour/mini-tour questions, domains of life, "tell me more"), and retelling the content back in the GP's own words. A worked fictitious transcript (a GP clarifying a Fox TV interview of Michelle Obama by Mike Huckabee) shows the mechanics line by line.

The purpose of Phase 5 is to deliver the GP into Phase 6 (Ever Participating / self-sustaining growth), where ordinary life alone feeds growth because the GP understands most of what is heard — requiring a comprehension vocabulary of probably over 10,000 instantly-recognized words and high-speed sentence processing built from "experience, experience, experience." The recommended dose: 500 hours of supercharged meetings (one-third of the 1,500-hour programme), within which roughly 330 hours go to clarifying 100-125 hours of collected native-to-native recordings (rule of thumb: ~3 hours of work per 1 hour of recording), with the remainder for talking activities, and no more than 100-200 hours of ordinary social visiting counted toward the total. By the end, the GP participates in host "communities of practice" as a valued belonger who understands everything going on even when nobody is addressing them.
goals: Understand speech NOT addressed to you: normal native-to-native talk among host people, with no simplification or accommodation for foreigners
Reach Phase 6 self-sustaining growth, where all of host life feeds growth because you understand most of what you hear without special help
Build a comprehension vocabulary of many thousands of words (probably over 10,000) recognized and understood instantly
Develop high-speed processing: understand each sentence fully and quickly enough to let it go and tackle the next incoming sentence
Clarify 100-125 hours of native-to-native discourse recordings, converting them into a personal listening library of highly intelligible material
Widen understanding of host life itself — keep encountering new realms of life and associated vocabulary so your knowledge approaches host people's knowledge
Move from outside guest to valued 'belonger' in host communities of practice (work groups, clubs, classes, mosque/church, teashop regulars)
Keep improving talking ability through hole-finding and stretching activities, so words and patterns familiar from listening emerge in your own speech
Begin heavy-duty reading (in literate languacultures) as a growth engine — 86% of adults who reached near-native ability were voracious readers
keyPrinciples: Native-to-native discourse principle: learn from the model you want to become — hosts talking to hosts. Accommodated foreigner-directed speech is an unnatural model, like learning only from people shouting in noise or talking to the hard-of-hearing

Growth zone / temporal dimension: 'authentic' materials are NOT used from day one (a criticism of other approaches); native-to-native discourses only become relevant when they are within reach with help — basically Phase 5

Communication ability is joint, not individual: it resides in the PAIR or group (two young mothers vs. a mother and a trucker have different joint abilities). You must apprentice into pairs/groups of hosts communicating naturally
Comprehension before production: massive clarified listening drives growth; words, combinations and constructions encountered with high frequency 'increasingly emerge in your own speech'

The Iceberg Principle: don't memorize vocabulary to mastery; give each new word one strong first encounter (elaboration), then let massed re-encounters in comprehensible input make words rise naturally toward the tip (instant recall)
Elaboration aids vocabulary: each new word is discussed conversationally in context (uses, examples, contrasts), not defined or translated in one line
It's not a language to be learned but a life to be lived: clarifying must stay a real CONVERSATION and relationship, never a mechanical 'what does that word mean, next bit' routine
GP must be absent when native-to-native recordings are made, so speech is never adapted for a newcomer
Easier-to-harder discourse progression: start with strangers talking (they state details explicitly), move toward intimates talking (much left implicit — extra hard)
Don't read along while listening: following a transcript with your eyes can short-circuit the listening process if you decode print faster than speech
Supercharged activities remain essential: ordinary social visiting alone stalls growth (especially vocabulary) before self-sustaining growth is reached — cap how much of it you count

Grammar patience: everyone still makes many grammar errors at this hour count regardless of method (per ILR/US government data); near-native ability averages 17 years (Leaver) — host-likeness in sociolinguistics, pragmatics, turn-taking etc. mostly comes in Phase 6 through participation
phase5.hours: 500 hours of supercharged participation meetings (hours ~1,000-1,500 of the programme; one-third of the 1,500-hour total). Inside that: ~330 hours clarifying 100-125 hours of recordings (~3 hours work per 1 hour of recording; 1 hour of meeting clarifies ~20 minutes of recording), ~170 hours for talking and other activities; at most 100-200 hours of ordinary social visiting may be counted. Pacing scenarios: Li Fang at 25 hrs/wk finishes Phase 5 in 4.5 months; Amelia at 10 hrs/wk in 1 year; Sam at 3 hrs/wk in 3 years.
terminology: Growing Participator (GP) — the learner, framed as someone growing into participation in host life rather than 'studying a language'

Mentor — the Phase 4/5 successor to the 'nurturer' of Phases 1-3; a host person (often paid) who needs no special training because communication is now natural, but who interacts at a level the GP can understand
Native-to-native discourse — speech by host people to host people in normal host life, recorded without the GP present, with no accommodation to foreigners
Clarifying — taking a text/recording a bit beyond comprehension and discussing it with a host person (pausing, repeating slowly, explaining words and life background) until it is understood
Supercharged participation activities/meetings — the structured growth sessions; 'supercharged' = far more growth-dense than ordinary interaction
Word recording — a separate running audio file containing little conversational discussions ('elaborations') of each new word encountered during clarifying
Listening library — the GP's accumulated collection of clarified recordings and word recordings, re-listened to periodically
Iceberg Principle — vocabulary model: strong first encounters put words into the iceberg; repeated natural encounters make them rise toward the tip (permanent, easy, rapid recall)
Growth zone — material understandable with help but not without; where learning happens
Expanding — asking the mentor to 'tell me more details' about something said or seen
Hole-finding activity — talking tasks designed to expose what you cannot yet say, so the holes can be filled
Grand-tour / mini-tour questions — Phase 4 descriptive interview questions reused on discourse content
Domains of life — Phase 4 technique: spotting a category in discourse (e.g., 'things you can share', 'levels of government leaders') and asking for all its members
Retelling by the GP / by the mentor — GP retells to stretch speaking; mentor retells to simplify (native-to-non-native paraphrase) or to render the GP's story in host-like form
Host / host-like — GPA prefers 'host people' and 'host-like' over 'native-like' (less individualistic/cognitivist)
Languaculture — language and culture as one inseparable whole
Community of practice — a group that spends time together for a purpose (work crew, aerobics club, teashop regulars); the GP moves from outside guest to 'belonger'
Self-sustaining growth — Phase 6 condition: all of life feeds growth because most of what is heard is understood
discourse vs Discourse (Paul Gee) — small-d: what is said; big-D: the whole situated practice (setting, roles, actions, objects) around what is said

activities.name: Acquiring native-to-native recordings (Option A: hired life-story interview)
activities.description: The GP hires one of the host people they did Phase 4 life-history interviews with (so the person already knows the format) to record SOMEONE THE GP DOESN'T KNOW telling their life story. Best if interviewer and storyteller also don't know each other well — strangers state more details explicitly, making the discourse easier to understand. Target length: about an hour, twenty minutes minimum. Crucially, the GP must NOT be present when the recording is made, so nothing is adapted for a newcomer.
activities.materials: A host person who can record; recording equipment for them to use
activities.timing: Before each meeting; ongoing throughout Phase 5 — can begin collecting in Phase 4 or even Phase 3

activities.name: Acquiring native-to-native recordings (Option B: hot-topic discussion)
activities.description: GP asks friends what topics 'a lot of people are talking about currently,' then arranges for two or three talkative acquaintances to discuss one or more of these hot topics on tape (or has a friend arrange it with people the GP doesn't know). GP is absent during recording. Aim for an hour, twenty minutes minimum. Providing refreshments helps the meeting happen. Over time, deliberately progress from easier discourse (between strangers, explicit detail) to harder discourse (between intimates, much left unsaid).
activities.materials: Two or three talkative host people, recorder, refreshments
activities.timing: Ongoing; need roughly 20 minutes of fresh recording per meeting hour (e.g., ~5 hours of recording per week at full intensity)

activities.name: Solo pre-clarifying (listening on your own)
activities.description: Before the meeting, the GP listens to the recording alone, in units of a phrase or two at a time, pausing to process each chunk before going on. If content is within reach, repeated listening alone can achieve high comprehension. Everything understood without help builds confidence and 'improves your understanding machine.' With ready-made media (a TV drama), the GP can also pause a lot, rewind, and use a dictionary for unknown words.
activities.materials: The recording, a player with easy pause/rewind, optionally a dictionary
activities.timing: Between obtaining the recording and the meeting

activities.name: The 10-step conversation with a mentor about a native-to-native discourse (master template)
activities.description: Step 1: Acquire a recording of a native-to-native discourse. Step 2: Listen once through and see how much you (think you) understand. Step 3: Summarize to your mentor what you (thought you) understood. Step 4: Record your mentor's response to your summary. Step 5: Clarification step — go through the original with the mentor bit by bit. Step 6: Make the new-word recording as you go along. Step 7: Watch for and note details you don't understand because you don't know something about life in the host world. Step 8: Expand on the points noted in Step 7. Step 9 (optional): Ask Grand/Mini-Tour questions, List-of-Life questions, experience questions, etc. from Phase 4. Step 10: GP retells the discourse at his/her current ability level with the mentor's help.
activities.materials: Native-to-native recording, second recorder for the word recording and mentor responses
activities.timing: The skeleton of every clarifying meeting throughout the 500 hours

activities.name: Clarifying the recording with a mentor (core mechanics)
activities.description: GP and mentor listen to a new 5-10 minute segment together, then go back to the beginning and work through it bit by bit. The GP: (a) asks the mentor to repeat slowly and clearly any phrases that were too rapid, 'sloppy' or 'garbled' for a non-native at their level; (b) discusses unknown words and immediately records a little conversation about each one in the word recording; (c) asks for explanations of longer stretches that puzzle them for any reason (often the GP won't initially know WHY they don't understand); (d) uses EXPANDING — has the mentor talk in greater detail about something said or seen, via grand-tour/mini-tour descriptive questions, exploring 'domains of life,' or simply 'Tell me more about this!'; (e) asks the mentor to describe whole areas of host life when incomprehension stems from unfamiliar life background; (f) may have the mentor give a summary paraphrase in simpler, clearer native-to-non-native language (retelling by the mentor). Then repeat with additional segments. The worked Huckabee–Obama transcript shows the texture: GP pauses after 'thank you for joining me here today,' repeats the sentence to check hearing, asks 'President Obama's wife join? I don't think I understand'; the mentor explains 'join,' flags register ('It sounds fancy — they're on national television'); for 'initiative' the mentor elaborates (a program, something official, started to really do something) and the GP records a mini word-discussion; the mentor corrects an overgeneralization ('Let's Move' as name vs. ordinary meaning of 'let's move'); for an unparseable long question the GP says 'Please repeat slowly,' rewinds and replays repeatedly while the mentor reconstructs it in pieces; GP mishears ('hocus?' for 'focused', 'Payental?' for 'parental', 'An eye shed?' for 'I shared') and the mentor disambiguates with use-examples (parental responsibility/rights/love); a 'domain of life' question emerges naturally ('What else do people share?' → jokes, dreams, secrets, problems); the GP asks the mentor's own opinion ('How have things changed for families?') triggering a long digression; the GP asks the mentor to write down listed items. Note: gifted mentors elaborate richly on their own; often you must coax elaborations out of the mentor.
activities.materials: Recording + player with pause/rewind, word-recording device, notebook for the mentor to write lists
activities.timing: 80-90 minutes of every 2-hour meeting; ~1 hour of clarifying per 20 minutes of recording

activities.name: Making and maintaining the word recording
activities.description: A running separate sound file containing little CONVERSATIONS about each new word (elaboration), made in the moment during clarifying. Model entry ('whetstone'): 'Whetstone. In the story, Jack sharpened his knife on a whetstone. Whetstones are usually rectangular, though sometimes round, made of black, coarse, stone-like material. Small enough to carry in your pocket... or too large to carry. You put oil on the whetstone and rub the knife blade on it to sharpen it.'
