In the Obama example the GP and mentor riff conversationally on 'initiative' (government program vs. 'show initiative' = effort; 'a pretty fancy word, we don't use it that much') and 'focus' (camera/binoculars/glasses, blurry vs. in focus, 'focus on children' = especially look at/think about/help children), with the GP trying the word in his own sentences and being corrected. Volume math: even at 1% new words, ~10-15 new words per 30 meeting minutes ≈ 1,500 new words per 20 hours of recording clarified. If the mentor is literate (or the GP can transcribe), also keep a WRITTEN list of new words in the order they occur, ideally with each word's location in the sound file. Review technique: make a copy of the word recording and gradually DELETE discussions of words that have become highly familiar — the file shrinks and shrinks until nothing is left, concentrating review on the pesky words that resist learning. These recordings 'make fascinating listening months and years later.'
activities.materials: Separate recorder/track from the main clarifying recording; optional written index with timestamps
activities.timing: Continuous during clarifying (Step 6); re-listened to the same evening and periodically thereafter

activities.name: Post-meeting listening-library review
activities.description: Soon after the meeting — e.g., the same evening — the GP listens again to the entire portion of the recording clarified that day plus the day's word recordings. Also re-listens to PREVIOUSLY clarified recordings and older word recordings. As clarified native-to-native recordings and word recordings accumulate into a growing listening library, the GP cycles through all of them periodically, driving the iceberg mechanism (repeated encounters raise words toward instant recall).
activities.materials: The listening library (all clarified recordings + word recordings)
activities.timing: Same evening after every meeting, plus ongoing periodic rotation

activities.name: Next-day retelling by the GP (warm-up summary)
activities.description: Near the start of each meeting, the GP summarizes in their own words the portion of the recording clarified the previous day — the retelling technique used since Phase 2. This is a stretching activity for speaking; the mentor helps. At the end of working through a discourse the GP also retells the whole discourse at their current ability level (Step 10). Retellings can themselves be recorded and used with record-for-feedback.
activities.materials: None beyond yesterday's clarified content
activities.timing: A few minutes at the start of each meeting, after small talk

activities.name: Meeting using ready-made media: clarifying a movie or TV drama
activities.description: Before the meeting, record a TV broadcast (e.g., a drama). In the meeting, watch and listen to a segment together for the overall idea, then go back through it bit by bit with all the standard clarifying moves (slow repetition, word recording, explanations, expanding, mentor retelling). A movie adds a built-in supercharged TALKING activity: much of it is non-verbal, so the GP gives the mentor a highly detailed description of what they see, describing simply and interpreting as little as possible, while the mentor — like a Phase 4 interviewee — supplies the insider's interpretation of the scene. Warnings: 'what you hear is a wall of noise, and what you see is an illusion' — learners wrongly assume they understand the visuals; even with dubbed foreign films (not first choice) the mentor often 'is not seeing what you are seeing.' In a movie less is expressed verbally than in a radio play, since visuals carry meaning.
activities.materials: Recorded TV broadcast/film/DVD, playback with pause/rewind, word-recording device
activities.timing: Alternative format for the 80-90 minute clarifying block

activities.name: Supercharged talking activities (in-meeting block)
activities.description: Examples given for the 20-30 minute block: (1) Take illustrated magazines such as National Geographic and discuss the pictures for 15-20 minutes, deliberately hunting for HOLES in speaking ability — activities, objects or situations in the picture the GP cannot describe or explain; (2) Explain aspects of a topic in which the GP has special training and the mentor does not; (3) Discuss a topic on which the GP holds a firm opinion, defending it against opposing views (argumentative discourse is important to continued growth).
activities.materials: Illustrated magazines or other picture sources
activities.timing: 20-30 minutes at the end of every 2-hour meeting

activities.name: Appendix talking activities: hole-finding
activities.description: Talking with a view to finding what you cannot yet say: contrast some aspect of life at home with life in the host world; look at complex pictures (such as those in 'busy books') and attempt to describe EVERY detail; watch a cartoon or silent movie (or any movie with lots of meaningful action) and discuss everything that happens and how you understand it. The mentor helps the GP say what they were trying to say and fills the discovered holes.
activities.materials: Busy-book style complex pictures, cartoons, silent movies
activities.timing: Talking activities may take up to one-quarter to one-half of supercharged participation time; include one or more daily

activities.name: Appendix talking activities: ongoing topic discussions
activities.description: Sustained multi-day discussions of particular topics: hobbies and recreational activities, the GP's professional area, topics from their academic training, or areas of passion (the environment, poverty, moral issues, comparison of spiritual experiences, politics in the home country). Choose two or three topics and continue each for 10-15 minutes per day. Passion/commitment guarantees argumentative discourse.
activities.materials: None special
activities.timing: 10-15 minutes per topic per day, two or three topics running

activities.name: Appendix talking activities: epic storytelling
activities.description: Carried over from Phase 4: tell an ongoing story continued for perhaps hours total, adding a bit each day. In the Phase 4 version each day's increment improves as it is retold to several separate people, each of whom interacts and helps; the same can be done in Phase 5.
activities.materials: None
activities.timing: A bit each day, ongoing

activities.name: Appendix talking activities: talks and teaching lectures
activities.description: Like topic discussions but in LECTURE style rather than conversational style. Prepare a talk on any topic — everyday ('driving safety') or specialized ('Overview of molecular biology') — with the constraint that it must take the audience's background into account (the audience is probably a single mentor). Especially suited to the Record-for-Feedback technique: record yourself speaking for several minutes, then get the mentor's feedback on ways your speech was not like host people's (system detailed in the Phase 4 guide).
activities.materials: Recorder for self-recording
activities.timing: Periodic; part of the talking-activities allocation

activities.name: Keeping it interesting, fun and personal: discussion-question sets
activities.description: Antidote to clarifying becoming impersonal and mechanical ('What does that word mean? OK, I get it. Next bit.'). For each segment of a STORY, GP and mentor genuinely discuss: What happened in this stretch? What do we know / want to know about the characters? What did they say, why did they say it like that, could they or someone else have said it differently? Did problems arise, and what might other people do when such a problem arises? What things were used (tools, objects, food) and what was their role? Was what the person said/did good or bad — why? What can we learn that will make us wiser? What does this make me think about in my own life? For a CONVERSATION recording: Who are they (roles) and what is their relationship, and how did that affect the conversation? What did they talk about? Did they agree/disagree, and how did they support their views? Do you agree with one or the other — why? Will anything change because of the conversation? How do you think they felt afterward? For a POLITICAL SPEECH: Who is the speaker and where do they fit in the political situation? What points did he try to make and why? Did he make them? Will people agree, and why? How important are these issues to me? Broader lens: consider what people in the text are SAYING, DOING, BEING (roles), VALUING and BELIEVING. These discussions can themselves be recorded and added to the listening library. Always: pay special attention to anything that doesn't make sense and discuss it until it does; expand parts ('tell me more about that'); ask descriptive questions; ask list questions ('What are all the problems this man faces?'); and retell later.
activities.materials: Question prompt lists per discourse type
activities.timing: Woven into every clarifying session

activities.name: Clarifying culture-loaded items (joke example)
activities.description: Model anecdote: the author clarified a local joke (husband reads 'the chair verse' before sleep so his wife stays out of his dreams). Google/Wikipedia could give facts but not the mentors' body-language reaction to the punch line or how LOCAL friends understand the reference; the mentors explained it is a Koranic verse read before sleep to ward off evil beings. Lesson: use mentors, not just reference tools, to clarify humor, allusion, and shared cultural knowledge — and the GP found the joke genuinely funny once clarified.
activities.materials: Jokes, proverbs, allusions encountered in discourses
activities.timing: As they arise

activities.name: Reading programme (literate languacultures)
activities.description: Phase 5 is when heavy-duty reading becomes possible. Practical rules: do lots of SOLITARY reading at home (with a bilingual or monolingual dictionary; note some languages require grammar knowledge to find dictionary forms), but do NOT spend meeting time on the GP reading aloud — instead have the MENTOR read texts aloud as naturally as possible, record it, and clarify the recording, because that grows listening comprehension in a way the GP can't do alone (and the mentor reads more easily than she can understand the GP reading aloud). Never follow the written text with your eyes while listening, or listening may be short-circuited by faster decoding. Rationale: decoding maps written words onto the auditory mental lexicon, so listening ability sets the ceiling for reading ability; reading then improves simply by doing it lots and lots. Caveat: match the host culture's actual literacy practices (don't import your home culture's role for reading; e.g., everyday spoken Arabic isn't written, Chinese literacy is a massive valued domain of its own). Leaver's research: 86% of 51 adults who reached near-native levels were voracious readers in the host language.
activities.materials: Newspapers, magazines, textbooks (elementary through university), children's books and comics, technical books, popular-interest prose, fiction, joke collections and plays (everyday vernacular in written form), internet sites/blogs/Wikipedia, poetry and proverbs, religious books; dictionaries
activities.timing: Lots, solo, outside meetings; mentor read-alouds inside meetings

activities.name: Participation in communities of practice
activities.description: Alongside meetings, the GP joins groups of host people who spend time together for a purpose — workers on a job, a leisure club (e.g., aerobics group), a class of host people, a church or mosque, regulars in a teashop — or organizes a small group themselves, provided it is dominated by host people doing things their way. The GP starts as an outside guest and steadily moves toward being a clear belonger whose role is valued. By the end of Phase 5, communities of practice become 'supercharged' because the GP understands all that is going on even when people talk to one another and not to the GP — finally learning from a model of normal adult interaction.
activities.materials: Real host-world groups
activities.timing: Ongoing through Phase 5 into Phase 6

activities.name: Ordinary social visiting (counted with a cap)
activities.description: Normal social interaction with patient, committed partners who meet the GP in their growth zone does count for a lot — but depending too much on it before self-sustaining growth 'may spell the end of our growth': vocabulary in particular stalls without special effort below ~10,000 words. Rule: count at most 100-200 of the 500 hours as ordinary social visiting (use the higher allowance deliberately if you're retreating into reclusiveness or expat-dominated life), while ideally enjoying many hundreds of UNcounted social hours.
activities.materials: None
activities.timing: Max 100-200 of the 500 counted hours

phase5.sessionStructure: Typical supercharged participation meeting = 2 hours: (1) Small talk, 5-10 minutes — GPs grow through specific relationships; find out what matters to the mentor today (e.g., ask 'What are you thinking about?' and wait five seconds), learn something new about her life, share something about yourself. (2) GP retells in own words the portion clarified the previous day. (3) Clarifying the recording, 80-90 minutes — listen to a new 5-10 minute segment together, then loop back through it bit by bit: slow repetitions of garbled phrases, word-recording mini-conversations for each new word, explanations of puzzling stretches, expanding via grand-tour/mini-tour questions, domains of life, 'tell me more,' host-life background explanations, optional simpler retelling by the mentor; repeat with further segments. (4) Supercharged talking activities, 20-30 minutes (picture discussion, opinion defense, teaching a topic, appendix activities). After the meeting (same evening): re-listen to the clarified portion plus the word recording, and rotate through older listening-library items. The session is conducted in the target language throughout (mentor uses natural host speech, simplifying into native-to-non-native paraphrase only as a clarifying technique — no translation language involved). Roughly two-thirds of weekly supercharged time goes to clarifying; talking activities may take one-quarter to one-half. Each meeting hour consumes ~20 minutes of recording, so a 25-hr/wk learner needs ~5 hours of fresh recordings weekly.
materials: Recordings of native-to-native discourse made for the GP: hired life-story interviews, hot-topic group discussions, hangout conversations, family mealtime conversations, public speeches/sermons/health talks/announcements, campfire stories and legends, memorable-incident stories, autobiographical narratives, host-conducted walk-of-life interviews, assigned-topic conversations, unplanned small talk ('just converse about whatever you want')
Recording equipment for host people to use (GP absent during recording)
A second recording channel for the running word recording, plus optional written word lists with timestamps

Broadcast/electronic media (major languages): shortwave radio (hundreds of languages, archived online), local AM/FM (news, interviews, talk shows, phone-ins, religious programs, radio plays, children's stories, streaming), television (news, dramas, sitcoms, soap operas, stage shows, documentaries, nature/cooking/reality/how-to shows, speeches, sermons, stand-up, cartoons, children's shows, sports; satellite/streaming), commercial CDs (children's stories, humour, audiobooks), commercial DVDs (TV-series box sets, feature films, documentaries, instructional video — the author's Russian haul included clay modelling, aerobics, guitar, fishing, auto care, sewing, childbirth, baby care, origami, drawing, gardening, speech-therapy-for-children programs)
Capture tech for broadcasts (internet streaming capture, USB TV device/TV card, DVD recorder — whatever current technology allows)

Printed media: newspapers, magazines, school and university textbooks, children's books, comic books, technical books, popular-interest prose, fiction, joke collections, plays, internet sites, poetry/proverbs, religious books — used by having the mentor read them aloud naturally and clarifying the recording
Illustrated magazines (e.g., National Geographic) and busy-book complex pictures for hole-finding description
Cartoons, silent movies, host feature films for detailed observation-and-description
Dictionaries (bilingual or monolingual) for solitary reading
The growing listening library: all clarified recordings, word recordings, and recorded discussions/retellings
Caveat: in some languacultures broadcast/print language is a formal variety unlike everyday speech — don't clarify hundreds of hours of it in Phase 5
milestones: Can understand recorded native-to-native speech after clarifying, and increasing amounts without help — the recordings' content has become 'highly intelligible'
Has collected and clarified 100-125 hours of native-to-native discourse recordings, now part of a large personal listening library

Comprehension vocabulary approaching the many-thousands level needed for Phase 6 (target trajectory: 10,000+ instantly-recognized words; ~1,500 new words enter the iceberg per 20 hours of recordings clarified)

Understands what host people say to each other in groups even when not addressed — 'communities of practice become supercharged'; can begin to fit in naturally as a belonger rather than an outside guest
Processes sentences fully and quickly enough to release each one and track the next; familiarity with how hosts talk in specific situations and for specific goals
Words, word-combinations and constructions met frequently in listening now emerge in the GP's own speech; can retell discourses, defend opinions, give prepared talks adapted to an audience
Reading (where culturally relevant): able to do heavy-duty solitary reading with a dictionary

Realistic grammar expectations met, not perfection: still makes many non-native-sounding errors (normal for ~1,300 hours under ANY method per ILR data); sociolinguistic/pragmatic/turn-taking/stylistic/kinesic host-likeness is Phase 6+ business
Crossed into self-sustaining growth (Phase 6): whenever hosts talk to one another and the GP listens, it feeds growth; all of life has become supercharged
phase5.nurturerRole: In Phase 5 the helper is called a MENTOR, not a nurturer — the term changed in Phase 4 because communication is now natural and the helper needs no special training; mentors are typically paid for clarifying meetings. What the mentor DOES: makes small talk as a real relationship; listens to segments with the GP; repeats rapid/garbled phrases slowly and clearly; elaborates each new word conversationally with contexts, examples, register notes ('it sounds fancy — they're on national television') and corrections of the GP's trial sentences; explains puzzling stretches and whole areas of host life the GP lacks; answers expanding/descriptive/domain-of-life questions and shares personal opinions and digressions; gives summary paraphrases of the discourse in simpler native-to-non-native language; retells the GP's own stories in a more host-like way; gives feedback on the GP's recorded speech; writes down word lists if literate; reads printed texts aloud naturally for recording; supplies the 'insider's view' on movie scenes the GP describes. Separate host people (not necessarily the mentor) make the native-to-native recordings — always WITHOUT the GP present. What the mentor/GP must NOT do: the mentor must not be present-as-audience in source recordings (that would de-nativize them); don't reduce word help to bare definitions — elaboration must be coaxed if the mentor doesn't offer it naturally; don't let clarifying become impersonal and mechanical ('What does that word mean? OK, next bit'); don't have the GP read aloud to the mentor (wasted paid time — GP can practice that alone; mentor reads aloud instead); don't let the GP follow a transcript visually while listening; don't expect or demand polished grammar at this stage; and there is no translation-based instruction — meaning is built through host-language conversation, paraphrase, and shared life knowledge.
phase5.vocabTargets: Phase 6 readiness requires a comprehension vocabulary of many thousands of words — probably over 10,000 — recognized and understood 'instantly.' Mechanism: even if only 1% of running words are new, clarifying yields ~10-15 new words per 30 meeting minutes, i.e., roughly 1,500 new words per 20 hours of recording clarified; at the suggested 100+ hours of recordings that is several thousand strong first encounters. Tracking is AUDIO-first via the word recording (one conversational elaboration per word, in order of occurrence), optionally indexed by a written list with sound-file locations. Review uses the shrinking-copy method: duplicate the word recording and progressively delete entries for well-known words until the file empties, concentrating repetition on stubborn words. Phase 5 increasingly surfaces lower-frequency words ('initiative,' 'parental') that life won't re-supply often, making deliberate word-recording review essential; below ~10,000 words, vocabulary barely grows from ordinary social interaction without this special effort. Per the iceberg principle, mastery is not demanded at first encounter — strong impressions plus massed re-encounters in the listening library raise words toward permanent, easy, rapid recall.
appIdeas: Segment-based clarifying player: load any audio/video (uploaded recording, podcast, radio stream capture); auto-chunk into 5-10 minute segments and phrase-level micro-segments with one-tap pause, rewind-2-seconds, loop, and slow-replay — mirroring the GP's constant pause/rewind/replay moves in the Huckabee-Obama transcript

Two-track session recorder: while a clarifying session plays, a single tap opens a 'word recording' overlay that captures a mini audio conversation about the new word, auto-timestamped and linked to the exact spot in the source recording — digitizing Step 6 and the written word-index in one gesture

Iceberg word library: every captured word clip lives in an ordered audio playlist per discourse; a 'shrinking copy' review mode plays all clips and lets the learner swipe away words that are now instant, so each review pass gets shorter until empty — a direct digital port of Thomson's copy-and-delete technique, with no flashcard translation pairs ever shown

Ten-step session wizard: guides each meeting through the canonical flow (listen once → record your summary → record mentor's response → clarify bit by bit → word recording → flag culture gaps → expand → optional Phase 4 questions → final retell), with a timer template for the 2-hour structure (small talk 5-10 / retell / clarify 80-90 / talking 20-30)

Mentor-side prompt cards (in target language, icon-supported): 'repeat that slowly,' 'use it in three different situations,' 'tell me more about this,' 'what are all the kinds of X?,' 'retell it more simply,' 'how would a host person say what I just said?' — coaching untrained mentors to elaborate instead of define, since 'often you will find that you have to coax the elaborations out of the mentor'

Comprehension self-check before clarifying: app plays the raw recording once, learner records a spoken summary and rates per-segment understanding on a simple visual scale; after clarifying, the same segments are re-rated to visualize the comprehension delta — making Steps 2-4 measurable

Culture-gap flagging: during playback the learner drops a '?' marker typed as 'word I don't know' vs. 'life I don't know' (Step 7); life-flags generate an expansion queue of grand-tour/mini-tour/domain-of-life question prompts for the next mentor session

Discussion-question generator keyed to discourse type: tag a recording as story / conversation / speech and the app surfaces Thomson's exact reflective question sets ('What things were used and what was their role?', 'Who are they and what is their relationship?', 'Will people agree with him, and why?') as conversation cards, keeping sessions personal rather than mechanical

Listening-library scheduler: every clarified segment, word recording, and recorded discussion enters a rotation queue; a same-evening push notification ('listen to today's clarified portion now') plus spaced periodic resurfacing of older items implements the repetition engine of the iceberg principle

Retell studio: record the GP's next-day summary and end-of-discourse retell against the original; keep dated versions side by side so growth is audible; optional mentor-feedback layer where the mentor records 'how a host person would say it' (retelling by the mentor) aligned to the GP's attempt

Hole-finding picture mode: present dense 'busy' photos/illustrations (National Geographic-style); learner records an exhaustive oral description and taps any object/action they couldn't name, creating visual 'hole' markers that become the agenda for the next mentor meeting — image-based, zero translation

Video clarifying mode: for films/TV dramas, scene-by-scene playback with a describe-the-scene recording step before the mentor's insider interpretation, plus an on-screen reminder of the 'what you see is an illusion' caution

Hours dashboard and pacing planner: tracks the 500-hour budget with the built-in ratios (3 hours work per 1 hour of recording; 20 minutes of recording per meeting hour; 100-125 recording-hours target; social-visiting cap meter at 100-200 hours) and lets users model themselves as a Li Fang / Amelia / Sam schedule to see projected completion dates

Recording-acquisition pipeline: checklist workflows for Option A (hire a past interviewee to record a stranger's life story, GP absent, 20-60+ min) and Option B (arrange a hot-topic discussion), plus a community pool where GPs in the same languaculture share clarified native-to-native recordings — Thomson explicitly wishes later GPs could inherit earlier GPs' collections

Mentor read-aloud reader: paste or photograph a printed text; the app records the mentor reading it naturally, then enters clarifying mode with the TEXT HIDDEN by default (enforcing 'don't follow with your eyes'), revealing print only after listening comprehension is achieved

Strangers-to-intimates difficulty ladder: recordings tagged by speaker familiarity (strangers = explicit detail = easier; close friends = implicit = harder) so the app can sequence material from easier to harder discourse as Thomson prescribes

phase6.phaseName: Phase 6: Ever Participating/Growing (also called "Self-Sustaining Growth"; official guide title: "Balancing Your Competing Lives: A Guide to Phase 6 and Phase un-6, for People in 'Life after Full-Time Language Learning'", Greg Thomson, v1.0, Oct 2012) — ongoing, no fixed hours
phase6.summary:
Phase 6 is not a "next stage" with a curriculum like Phases 1-5; it is a road the grower hopes to be on after completing the recommended 1,500 hours of special-growth participation activities. Thomson gives a simple two-part definition of Phase 6: (1) you have the ability to understand most of what you hear host people say (and see them do) around you, AND (2) you do, in fact, keep hearing host people saying a lot around you. When both conditions hold, growth becomes self-sustaining: every hour of hearing speech advances your ability to understand speech, new words "blaze through your understanding machine" because context makes them clear, and your parsing (grouping sounds into words, words into phrases, sentences into discourses) keeps accelerating. The guide's counterpart concept is "Phase un-6": you are NOT in Phase 6 (one of the two conditions fails) and you are doing little or no concentrated special-growth activity — much of host speech is still "noise" to you, and you will plateau as a "Terminal 1+" or "Terminal 2+" (US government scale) no matter how many years you stay. A host person watching two videos of a Phase 6 person taken five years apart would see striking change; for a Phase un-6 person they could not guess which video was which.

The guide's central thesis, repeated as a mantra, is "It's not a language to be learned, but a life to be lived." The dominant practical content is therefore lifestyle: the Principle of Competition Between Lives says that whether you live two, three, or four lives (home life, Anglophone expat host life, national-language host life, minority-language host life), you only live one life at a time, and your ~100 waking hours per week are zero-sum. Most expats give under 10% of waking hours to their host life because their "home-away-from-home" world (expat archipelago, Little Americas, international schools, English-language teams) strangles it. The guide proposes concrete restructurings: make your workplace a host community of practice (host language as office language, hire a host person who doesn't know English), give your residence host-life time (host people living with you, getting children onto the road of growing participation, befriending domestic workers), social visiting, taking host-taught courses, and host-language team meetings.

For those who want to accelerate (Phase 6) or escape the plateau (Phase un-6), the guide prescribes special-growth participation activities drawn from Betty Lou Leaver's research: at least 100 hours of teacher-mediated special-growth activity produces a detectable change ("a new you") at low proficiency levels, and at least 300 hours at higher levels (Terminal 1+/2+). Phase un-6 people should go back and pick up the Six-Phase Programme where they quit (Phase 2 Story Building and Phase 3 activities are fruitful even for advanced growers). Phase 6 people can target specific weak "host discourses" (toasting, getting a car fixed, using a beauty parlor) through a needs analysis and a characteristic A/B activity pattern (grower-in-the-lead first, then nurturer-in-the-lead), supported by recording, "massaging" recordings, and a growing Listening Library. Once the social foundation is laid, formerly useless private activities — TV, radio, video, extensive reading — become genuinely special-growth and can be done solo.
phase6.hours: Ongoing/open-ended (Phase 6 follows the 1,500 recommended hours of Phases 1-5). Optional acceleration: ~5 hours/week of special-growth activities. For a detectable "new you": at least 100 hours of special-growth activity at low proficiency, at least 300 hours at higher levels (Leaver). Targeted discourse work: 10-30 hours per communication situation (e.g., 10-20 hours on Toast-Making-A before switching to B). Reference points: average 17 years of serious language use to reach US Govt Level 4 "Near-Native" (shortenable to ~6 years with intensive intervention); lifestyle goal of at least 10% (better 20%) of 100 waking hours/week in host life.
goals: Stay on the Phase 6 road of self-sustaining growth: keep understanding most of what host people say and keep hearing a lot of it, so growth continues automatically to the end of the sojourn

Protect host life from the competing lives (home life, home-away-from-home expat life, Anglophone life, national-language life) that threaten to strangle it; give host life at least 10-20% of the ~100 waking hours per week

For Phase un-6 growers: break off the plateau (Terminal 1+/2+) by accumulating at least 100-300 hours of genuine special-growth participation activities, producing a 'new you' that host people can detect
Become host-like in specific high-value 'host discourses' (e.g., toasting, car repair, beauty parlor talk) identified through needs analysis
Find and fill 'holes' in languacultural knowledge (things you cannot yet say or understand) even at advanced levels
Transition growth from purely social activities to include private special-growth: mass media (TV, radio, video) and extensive reading, now that the social foundation makes them comprehensible
Move beyond one-on-one foreigner-directed talk into host communities of practice and group life where host people relate to one another, largely ignoring your foreignness
Extend growing participation beyond the individual: growing-participating couples, families, teams, businesses, NGOs, and international schools
keyPrinciples: It's not a language to be learned, but a life to be lived — no life, no growth; lifestyle is the primary variable in Phase 6
Principle of Competition Between Lives: you only live one life at a time; every waking hour given to home life or expat life is taken from host life (100 waking hours/week are zero-sum)

Growing is participating and participating is growing: all growth is participation in host life at some level; being physically present is not participating — actions must be on host terms, in host language, following host practices

Special-growth participation must meet 5 characteristics: (1) you hear speech you understand but that challenges you; (2) you interact a lot, clarifying and negotiating meanings; (3) listening vocabulary grows by the hour (5-10 words/hour); (4) your understanding of host life keeps aligning with how host people experience it; (5) you talk a lot and get help expressing thoughts more host-likely

The 100/300-hour rule (Leaver): a detectable change — a 'new you' in host people's experience — requires at least 100 hours (low levels) or 300 hours (higher levels) of teacher-mediated special-growth; more of the same everyday conversation with a paid nurturer is NOT a growth strategy

A-B pattern keeps interaction in the growth zone: first the grower leads (produces, gets feedback), then after 10-20 hours the nurturer leads (models, grower retells); the nurturer's improvement of YOUR version feeds growth better than her spontaneous native version
Recordings let you relive participation: record efforts, 'massage' them (pause, rewind, look up, clarify), and build a Listening Library you replay repeatedly
Comprehension processes only improve by being carried out — 'you learn by doing'; in Phase 6 mere listening advances parsing, but speaking ability requires actual interactive speaking
Reject 'they stories': experience host life from inside the host story, not as an outsider's narrative about 'them'
Avoid individualism: growing participation should become the norm for couples, families, teams, workplaces, and schools, not lone learners
You don't choose a language; you choose a people group — national/lingua-franca learning is either folded into minority-world participation or given its own deliberate 'season'
Private media and reading become special-growth ONLY after the social foundation is laid in Phases 1-5; children don't learn language from radio, and neither do newcomers
terminology: Grower / Growing Participator (GP) — the person being nurtured into the host languacultural world; growth = increasingly host-like participation
Nurturer — host person (usually paid) who creates optimized participation contexts; in Phase 6 acts more like a content professor or discourse coach than a play partner
Languaculture / languacultural world — language and culture as one inseparable stream of shared practices; learning the word 'dog' and learning host dog-practices are one process

Home world vs host world — technical GPA terms independent of geography: home world = living on my terms in my language (even abroad, even with locals speaking English); host world = relating on their terms, in their language, following their practices
Home identity vs host identity — who I am in the experience of home-world members vs host people; the 'new you' is a change in host identity
Phase un-6 — not in Phase 6 (can't understand most of what's heard, or not hearing much) and doing little special-growth; the plateau condition

Special-growth participation sessions/activities — concentrated, optimized participation times with a nurturer; they 'distill life participation into a concentrate'; they ARE community, not a substitute for it
Seed community — you-plus-your-nurturer as the starting community that grows into a tree of relationships
Terminal 1+ / Terminal 2+ — US government proficiency levels at which un-6 people permanently plateau
They stories — outsider narratives expats tell about host people, disconnected from the story host people are living
Home-away-from-home life — the massive expat home-life subculture abroad; the 'expat archipelago' of islands (expat households) in a sea of nondescript locals
Little America (Little Korea, etc.) — a workplace turned into an outpost of the home world where locals become the growing participators in YOUR world
Host discourse — an ongoing area of host communication (what people say about a topic, what they take for granted, plus associated objects, actions, roles, statuses)
Community of practice — a group meeting periodically for a purpose, knowing who belongs; belonging means conforming to shared ways of talking and acting
Massaging (a recording/video) — going through a recording intensively: pausing, rewinding, looking up unfamiliar words, clarifying with nurturer
Listening Library — the grower's accumulated collection of recordings replayed many times
Record Yourself for Feedback — core technique carried from earlier phases: record your attempt, review with nurturer, note all suggested improvements
Hole finding — deliberately discovering things you can't say (e.g., narrating a silent movie live)
Parsing — the mental process of turning a sound stream into understood words, phrases, sentences, discourse; the 'parser' improves only with use
Growth zone — the zone where input/feedback is anchored to what the grower can almost do (the nurturer improving the grower's own version stays in it)
Wall of noise — the initial impenetrability of a new languacultural world that nurturing helps the grower cross
New you — a change in host identity big enough for host people (or a certified Oral Proficiency Interviewer) to detect; costs 100-300 special-growth hours

activities.name: Needs Analysis for choosing target discourses
activities.description: A scored brainstorm to decide which communication situations deserve special-growth time. Step 1: brainstorm with your nurturer, fellow expats, and host people a long list of communication situations you take part in (getting a taxi, making toasts, getting the car repaired, using the beauty parlor, playing football...). Step 2: for each item score (a) frequency 0-5 (0=never, 5=often), (b) importance-when-it-comes-up 0-5, then (c) SUBTRACT 0-10 for how well you can already do it (0=can't do at all, -10=highly skilled). Step 3: add the three numbers; high totals are your special-growth targets. Worked example from the guide: Getting a taxi 5+5-10=0 (skip — already skilled); Making toasts 1+5-2=4 (target — rare but high-stakes and weak); Getting car repaired 2+3-1=4 (target); Using beauty parlor 3+5-1=7 (top target); Playing football 2+2-5=-1 (skip). Rationale: things you (1) cannot do well, (2) do infrequently (so everyday life never trains them), but (3) are of utmost urgency when they occur (often performed before an audience) are gold-mine targets.
activities.materials: A table/spreadsheet with columns: Communication situation | How often (0-5) | How important when it comes up (0-5) | How well can you do it already (0 to -10) | Total. Input from nurturer, expats, host friends.
activities.timing: One-time planning exercise at the start of a Phase 6 / Phase un-6 special-growth push; revisited as targets are completed

activities.name: Toast-Making-A (GP in the lead) — template for any rare-but-urgent discourse
activities.description: Before the activity: brainstorm all possible toasting occasions (wedding, anniversary, birthday, housewarming) and possible toastees (a politician, an employer, an employee, a neighbour, a young person, mothers-in-law, janitors, New Zealanders...). Better still, recall real situations you were in and compose 'a toast you might have given'. Make each toast as elaborate as possible and perform the WHOLE act including the nonverbal parts (you may toast with milk!). During the activity — Step 1: GP leads; pretend you are in a particular setting making a toast for a particular person/group; hemming and hawing is fine; RECORD your effort as you do it. Step 2: go through the recording with your nurturer in the spirit of Record-Yourself-for-Feedback; keep track of every suggestion for improving the toast; often you are 'negotiating meanings' — getting the nurturer to understand what you were trying to convey. Step 3: record the nurturer performing the REVISED toast and add that recording to your Listening Library; listen to it before the next meeting and many times after, especially when an actual toast is coming up.
activities.materials: Audio recorder; brainstormed list of occasions and toastees; Listening Library (collection of recordings); a nurturer chosen for eloquence in the target discourse (in Russia/Kazakhstan some people can only toast in clichés — find an eloquent one)
activities.timing: 10-20 hours of the A version before moving to the B version

activities.name: Toast-Making-B (Nurturer in the lead)
activities.description: After 10-20 hours of Toast-Making-A, flip the lead to keep the interaction in the growth zone (this A-then-B pattern parallels Phases 2A/2B). Step 1: from your list of occasions/toastees, choose an example and have the NURTURER make up the toast; record her doing it. Step 2: massage the toast (work through the recording, clarifying and looking things up); add the recording to your Listening Library. Step 3: listen to the toast before the next meeting. Step 4: at the next meeting, make a SIMILAR toast yourself, drawing on the nurturer's version but NOT repeating it verbatim — as in all 'retelling tasks', do it in your own words, reflecting what you are personally able to do at the time.
activities.materials: Audio recorder, Listening Library, occasion/toastee list
activities.timing: Follows 10-20 hours of version A; the A-B cycle continues per discourse

activities.name: Getting-Car-Fixed — Prelude (back to Phase 1 techniques)
activities.description: Shows how Phase 6 growers loop back to early-phase techniques for new vocabulary domains. You and your nurturer go out to your actual car (or use a labelled diagram of all internal and external car parts). Fill holes in your vocabulary using the Phase 1 'Dirty Dozen' technique — covering both objects ('Where is the lug wrench?') and actions ('Loosen the lug nut.'). Also do a variety of listen-and-point activities (record them): the nurturer makes comments about different cars or parts and the grower responds physically ('Which one is four-wheel drive? Which is a four-door?').
activities.materials: A real car or a full diagram of internal/external car parts; audio recorder; Phase 1 Dirty Dozen and listen-and-point procedures
activities.timing: Prelude session(s) before the A/B cycle for this discourse

activities.name: Getting-Car-Fixed-A (GP in the lead)
activities.description: Step 1: go back over all the objects learned in the prelude (fuel injector, water pump, etc.) and record-for-feedback yourself telling your nurturer all the things that might go wrong with each part and need repair. Step 2: go over the recordings of what you said in the spirit of Record-for-Feedback, noting everything the nurturer feels a need to correct. Step 3: record the nurturer telling the FINAL corrected version of this text — naming car parts and all that might go wrong with them — and add it to your Listening Library.
activities.materials: Audio recorder; car-parts vocabulary from prelude; Listening Library
activities.timing: Several sessions; precedes the B version

activities.name: Getting-Car-Fixed-B (nurturer in the lead)
activities.description: Step 1: the nurturer chooses a list of car parts NOT yet dealt with and performs the same task the grower did in version A (describing what can go wrong with each); this is recorded. Step 2: massage the recording; add to Listening Library. Step 3: listen to it before the next meeting. Step 4: at the next meeting, retell in your own words, drawing from the nurturer's version but not reciting it verbatim from rote memory.
activities.materials: Audio recorder; Listening Library; remaining car-parts list
activities.timing: Follows version A

activities.name: Using-Beauty-Parlor-A (GP in the lead, picture-prompted)
activities.description: Before the activity: get magazines whose photos show a wide variety of hairstyles. Step 1: take the first picture and tell your nurturer what you think the pictured person might have SAID to the beautician to get that hairstyle; record yourself saying it ('It may be agony for you' — that is fine). Step 2: go over the recording with the nurturer; by negotiating meanings interactively you help her see what you were TRYING to say, and you note everything she would have expressed differently. Step 3: record the nurturer's version — explicitly NOT what she herself would have said, but her improved version of what YOU said. Repeat Steps 1-3 with many pictures. Step 4: listen to the recording before the next meeting. Key design insight stated in the guide: because the nurturer's version is founded on YOUR version, it stays in your growth zone; her fully spontaneous version would not feed your growth as much at this point.
activities.materials: Hairstyle magazines / large set of varied hairstyle photos; audio recorder; Listening Library
activities.timing: Repeat the 3-step cycle many times across sessions before moving to B

activities.name: Using-Beauty-Parlor-B (nurturer in the lead)
activities.description: Step 1: using a picture not yet used, the NURTURER says what SHE would have said to get that hairstyle; you record this. Step 2: massage the recording. Repeat steps 1-2 many times. Step 3: listen to the recordings before the next meeting. Step 4: retell in your own words, drawing on the nurturer's version.
activities.materials: Fresh hairstyle pictures; audio recorder; Listening Library
activities.timing: Follows version A

activities.name: Using-Beauty-Parlor — Scripts of Life (Phase 3 technique reapplied)
activities.description: Have your nurturer describe, in small sequential steps, the whole experience of visiting the beauty parlor (the 'script': arriving, greeting, describing what you want, the wash, the cut, paying, tipping...). Expand it if needed; massage it if needed; record it. In the NEXT session, the grower tells the script in his/her own words.
activities.materials: Audio recorder; Listening Library
activities.timing: One or more sessions within the beauty-parlor discourse sequence

activities.name: Using-Beauty-Parlor — Role-play
activities.description: Role reversal drama: the nurturer pretends she is YOU (the customer), and YOU play the beautician. She acts out the entire visit to the beauty parlor while you respond in role, using your knowledge from the script-of-life about what the beautician does and says. Then you SWITCH roles (you play yourself as customer, she plays beautician).
activities.materials: Optionally props; script-of-life knowledge from previous activity; recorder
activities.timing: After the scripts-of-life work

activities.name: Using-Beauty-Parlor — Shared experience + Reminiscing (Phase 3 technique, real-world capstone)
activities.description: Capstone: actually go make your visit to the beauty parlor WITH your nurturer accompanying you. Try to make small talk with the beautician about hairstyles — what you like and don't like. Then return home with the nurturer and do the Reminiscing Activity from Phase 3 (talking back through the shared experience together). The guide notes: 'You have now gone a long way toward becoming a host-like participant in the host discourse of beauty parlors.' This five-part sequence (A, B, Scripts-of-Life, Role-play, Shared-experience+Reminiscing) is the full template for mastering any chosen discourse.
activities.materials: A real-world venue visit; nurturer accompaniment; Phase 3 Reminiscing procedure
activities.timing: Final stage of a discourse sequence

activities.name: Hole Finding (silent-movie narration)
activities.description: Deliberately discover things you cannot say. The common version: watch a silent/wordless movie and try to narrate the plot LIVE as you watch — talking about the setting, activities, goals, motives, etc. Every place you stall is a 'hole' to fill with the nurturer. The guide notes this is 'fun and rewarding for those who thought they were more advanced than they actually were.' Bonus layer: discussing the wordless movie reveals how every action is meaningful within the host languaculture, and how many actions, objects, and situations host people understand differently than home people do. Recommended films: Charlie Chaplin, Mr. Bean, and especially 'Kelin' (Kazakh Film, ~80 min, no dialogue, very full plot) for Central Asia work — chosen because you are interested in the meanings HOST people see versus the meanings you see.
activities.materials: Wordless/silent films (Chaplin, Mr. Bean, 'Kelin'); recorder; nurturer to fill the holes and discuss host interpretations
activities.timing: Recurring activity; applicable to anyone below US Govt Level 4-5, i.e., almost everyone

activities.name: Phase 4-style Expert Interviewing (the low-creativity fallback)
activities.description: If you don't want to invent custom discourse activities, simply do Phase 4 (Deep Life Sharing) interviewing of a specialist in the walk of life you are targeting: interview a famous toastmaster, an auto mechanic, a beautician — whoever embodies the discourse. The guide says this alone 'has a strong impact on your ability to communicate and otherwise act in a more host-like way.' Caveat noted elsewhere: Phase 4 interviews often bring in little NEW vocabulary, so mix in earlier-phase activities (e.g., Phase 2 'busy picture' description) to keep the average up to ~10 new words per hour.
activities.materials: Access to host specialists; recorder; Phase 4 interviewing procedures
activities.timing: Alternative/parallel to custom discourse sequences

activities.name: Remedial pickup of earlier-phase activities (the Phase un-6 prescription)
activities.description: If you quit the Programme at some phase, go back and pick up THERE. For a Terminal 2+ in Phase un-6: all activities of Phases 2-5 (or at least 2-4) will be fruitful. Specifically recommended: Phase 2 Story Building with picture stories ('always useful, even in Phase 6' — every grower performs it at their current ability level and gets a burst of listening-vocabulary growth and possibly fluency); Phase 3 Scripts-of-Life (vocabulary infusion); Phase 3 World Stories (exposure to abstract vocabulary and discourse devices you may have been filtering out — one admired 'advanced' expat met dozens of new words in a 5-10 minute Cinderella telling); Phase 3 Reminiscing (learning how host people experience their world); then concentrate on Phase 4 Deep Life Sharing interviews. Target TEN new words per hour for these 300 remedial hours (vs the normal 7-8), i.e., ~3,000 new listening vocabulary in 300 hours. Critically: these hours must be genuinely special-growth — paying a nurturer to have the same unstructured chat you already have with your house helper and taxi driver is 'not a strategy for heavy change and growth.'
activities.materials: Phase 2-5 guides and their materials (picture stories, busy pictures, world-story scripts, interview question sets)
activities.timing: 300 hours (or 100 at low levels) — the 'new you' threshold

activities.name: Massaging recordings / videos and the Listening Library
activities.description: Core private technique. Record challenging real material (or nurturer sessions), then work through it intensively: listening, pausing, rewinding, looking up unfamiliar words, and continuing. Thomson's own case: after two years in Russia he spent 2+ hours/day in Canada massaging a large collection of Russian videos, and returned able to cope easily with the most challenging multi-person conversations. Guidance for choosing material: 'jump at anything you hear on TV or elsewhere that is challenging for you and try to record it'; he kept a sitcom he could simply watch with benefit (rich in revelations of Russian life) and a talk show with colloquial, spontaneous, high-energy multi-person argument that he needed to massage — the challenging one was 'especially valuable in Phase 6'. The Listening Library accumulates: revised toasts, nurturer texts, massaged broadcasts — all replayed many times, especially before relevant real-life events. For displaced/minority host groups, hundreds of hours of recordings on an mp3 player 'redeem the time on buses and sleepless nights' and let you RELIVE participation experiences when no host people are around.
activities.materials: Audio/video recorder, mp3 player or equivalent, TV/radio/video sources at optimal difficulty, online dictionary; nurturer for clarification when needed
activities.timing: Ongoing; valuable both in-country and during home-country stints; solitary massaging works ONLY on top of a face-to-face foundation

activities.name: Mass-media listening at optimal difficulty (private special-growth)
activities.description: Once in/near Phase 6, radio, television, video, documentaries, and news become genuine growth contributors (they were useless in Phases 1-2 because comprehension processes you can't perform don't improve). Strategy: prefer broadcasts at your optimal difficulty level — you understand most everyday talk, so seek the challenging material and record it. News broadcasts work from late Phase 3 onward (world news gives you background); documentaries similarly. Caveat the guide stresses: listening alone improves listening; without lots of actual interactive speaking your speaking lags — 'interacting conversationally changes people.' Media is a supplement that feeds face-to-face time, not a substitute (easier to buy a DVD than to reform your workplace — beware!).
activities.materials: TV, radio, DVDs, recorded broadcasts; recorder for capturing challenging material
activities.timing: Ongoing; hundreds-to-thousands of hours of parsing practice

activities.name: Extensive reading + discuss-with-nurturer (where literacy is a host practice)
activities.description: Leaver found most people reaching US Level 4 read extensively — 'promiscuously' — in the host language. Mechanics: read ON YOUR OWN (reading aloud to a paid nurturer is 'a pretty clear waste of money'); have the nurturer read the same materials on her own; then DISCUSS them together; discuss the new words you encountered, and RECORD those discussions to refresh and strengthen the words in your mental listening-vocabulary store. Reading moves you from everyday into academic language; start as soon as readable-for-you materials exist (struggling with material way over your head is not a good use of time). Look up unknown words in a MONOLINGUAL host dictionary, not a bilingual one (case study of a grower who grew far on face-to-face village time + solo reading + host-dictionary lookups). Diglossia case (e.g., Arabic): written language differs so much from spoken that learning to read requires extensive nurturer discussion — conducted in SPOKEN Arabic about the written text (like teacher-student talk about Latin) — which also builds ability with formal/news/public-address language.
activities.materials: Fiction, children's school textbooks, university textbooks, magazines, newspapers, product instructions; monolingual host dictionary; recorder for word-discussion sessions
activities.timing: Ongoing private hours once reading level permits; a key accelerator toward Level 4

activities.name: Content course with a host professor (Leaver-style '300 hours')
activities.description: The premier higher-level special-growth format: ~300 hours in, say, a history course taught by a host professor who does NOT know your language and has never taught his language. He treats you essentially like a local student, with one major difference: helping you grow in communication ability is also central to his understanding of his role. Thomson generalizes Leaver's picture into 5 characteristics any 300-hour block must have: (1) speech you understand but that challenges you; (2) heavy interaction, clarifying and negotiating meanings; (3) listening vocabulary growing by the hour (aim ~3,000 new words in the 300 hours); (4) constant learning about the host world as host people know it; (5) much talking with help to express thoughts more host-likely. Related lighter options: audit university courses (Thomson audited 2-3 as the only non-Russian student); take a host-taught course for host people (dancing, first aid, hygiene, job-related) where you may be the only foreigner — classroom plus coffee-shop plus post-course friendships all become host life and homework develops literacy.
activities.materials: Host educational institutions; subject-matter professor/nurturer committed to your growth; course texts
activities.timing: 300 hours for a full 'new you'; or 20-30 hours for growth in one specific communication area if 300 is impossible

activities.name: Lifestyle restructuring portfolio (the bulk of the guide)
activities.description: A set of concrete moves to raise host-life share of the 100 waking hours: (1) Workplace as host community of practice — make the host language THE office language; if all workers share a native language, HIRE at least one host person who does not know it (plus another host person) so fully normal host-to-host interaction exists; then only one language is understood by everyone in the room and using any other is plainly rude; conduct office life in the host way (do Phase 4-style interviews about host office life; make the ambience host: pictures, furniture arrangements, utensils). (2) Residence — get children (age 7+) onto the road with family Phase 1 (children need engaging activities — a quality control for adults' activities too; 5 h/week viable, 1-2 h/week won't accomplish much; kids then reach de-facto Phase 6 with neighbour children); host people living with you or you with them, with the politeness rule: whenever family members and one or more host people share a room, the family speaks the host language to one another; befriend domestic employees rather than staying aloof (Thomson's counter-example to the 'don't mix business and friendship' advice). (3) Get a television — let host life spray-hose into the home (instead of stacking shelves with home-world DVDs). (4) Social visiting — host guests to you, you to them; if work matters more than visitors, 'they may soon get the message.' (5) Refuse the 'expat magnet' — when fellow expats approach you in a host crowd, talk to them warmly but ONLY in the host language. (6) Team life — multinational teams should adopt the host language as the team language (even with no host person in the room, the team becomes a host community of practice); same-background teams should add host people to some activities and use the host language then; newcomers needing whispered sequential interpretation will see vividly that growing into host life 'is not an option but a necessity.' (7) International schools — could make growing participation an educational goal for staff, children, and parents instead of maximizing home life. (8) Displaced/limited-access host groups — spend intensive hours with whichever host people appear (e.g., hospital patients and caregiving relatives visiting the city), make many audio recordings, and listen devotedly between encounters; or grow via an immigrant/diaspora community before ever reaching the homeland (six of Leaver's Level-5 subjects grew mainly in US immigrant communities), then make brief homeland visits with personal referrals once conversational (Phase 3) ability exists. (9) National-language season — either fold the national language into minority-world participation or run a deliberate separate 'season for specially loving' the national group; meanwhile seek out minority-run shops and cafes.
activities.materials: Workplace staffing and policy changes; family activity kits (Phase 1-2 materials for children); host TV; visiting relationships; recordings
activities.timing: Permanent lifestyle, evaluated weekly against the 10-20%-of-100-waking-hours benchmark

phase6.sessionStructure: Phase 6 has no prescribed session curriculum — the guide explicitly reverts from the step-by-step format of Phases 1-5 to 'principles and a couple of examples', because possible target discourses are practically limitless and vary by languaculture. The operative structures are: (1) Weekly lifestyle budget: ~100 waking hours (16x7=112), with a goal of well over 10% (ideally 20%+) lived in the host world; Phase 6 people may optionally add ~5 hours/week of special-growth activities to accelerate; Phase un-6 people need many special-growth hours per week (2-3 h/week 'won't work' — the guide says to tell people that plainly rather than 'anything is better than nothing'). (2) Discourse-mastery sequence per chosen communication situation: Prelude (Phase 1-style vocabulary fill: Dirty Dozen, listen-and-point) → Version A, GP in the lead (grower performs/records → review with nurturer via Record-for-Feedback, negotiate meanings → record nurturer's improved version of the GROWER's text → Listening Library + relisten) for 10-20 hours → Version B, nurturer in the lead (nurturer performs/records → grower massages → relistens between meetings → retells in own words, never verbatim) → optionally Scripts-of-Life → Role-play with role switching → real shared experience in the venue with the nurturer → Phase 3 Reminiscing afterwards. (3) Block targets: 100 hours (low level) or 300 hours (Terminal 1+/2+) of activities meeting the 5 special-growth characteristics to produce a detectable 'new you'; if 300 is impossible, 20-30 hours buys growth in one specific communication area. (4) Between-session homework: listen to Listening Library items, massage recordings, read extensively, watch/record challenging broadcasts.
materials: Audio recorder (the single most-used tool: every activity records grower attempts, nurturer revisions, discussions, real encounters)
Listening Library — organized, growing collection of recordings replayed many times (revised toasts, nurturer texts, massaged broadcasts, word-discussion sessions, encounter recordings)
mp3 player loaded with hundreds of hours of recordings (for buses, sleepless nights, displaced-host-group situations)
Magazines with varied photos (e.g., hairstyle magazines for the beauty-parlor sequence)
Real-world objects and venues: your actual car, the beauty parlor, shops, cafes
Labelled diagrams (e.g., all internal/external car parts)
Wordless/silent films: Charlie Chaplin, Mr. Bean, 'Kelin' (Kazakh Film, 80-min dialogue-free drama) for hole-finding narration
Host TV/radio/video: sitcoms (watchable), talk shows with colloquial multi-person argument (massage-worthy), news broadcasts, documentaries
Print media for extensive reading: fiction, children's school textbooks, university textbooks, magazines, newspapers, product instructions
Monolingual host-language dictionary (explicitly preferred over bilingual); online dictionary in a second window for media massaging
Needs-analysis scoring table (frequency 0-5, importance 0-5, current ability 0 to -10)
Earlier-phase activity kits for remedial work: Phase 2 picture stories and busy pictures, Phase 3 scripts-of-life/world-stories/reminiscing procedures, Phase 4 interview frameworks
Host courses/institutions (dance, first aid, university courses to audit or enroll in)
milestones: Meets the Phase 6 definition: understands most of what host people say (and see them do) around them, and keeps hearing a lot of it — resulting in constant, automatic growth
Can follow a conversation BETWEEN two host people who are not deliberately including the grower (the litmus test separating Phase 6 from Phase un-6)
Can sit in multi-person, colloquial, high-energy host conversation and have the 'mental language processor racing right along'

Growth is visible to host people: a video from this year vs five years ago would look strikingly different (the anti-'Terminal' test); after 100-300 special-growth hours, host people (or a certified Oral Proficiency Interviewer) experience a detectable 'new you'

Has become a host-like participant in specifically targeted host discourses (e.g., can deliver an elaborate, non-cliché toast before an audience; can describe car faults to a mechanic; can banter with a beautician)
Listening vocabulary grows ~10 new words/hour during remedial special-growth (~3,000 in 300 hours); total listening vocabulary beyond the 10,000+ word range developed in Phases 1-5
Private media and reading are now genuinely growth-producing: can massage challenging broadcasts, read extensively with a monolingual dictionary, and feel words 'jump out' as the parser improves

Belongs to host communities of practice / small host social networks where host people relate to one another largely ignoring the grower's foreignness (group life, not just one-on-one foreigner-directed talk)
Sustains a lifestyle giving at least 10-20% of ~100 waking hours/week to host life; resists the expat magnet, 'they stories', and Little-America workplace patterns
Long-horizon trajectory: on the road toward US Govt Level 4 'Near-Native' (avg 17 years of heavy use; ~6 with intervention) — knowing the journey has no real summit ('not done', ever)
phase6.nurturerRole: In Phase 6 the nurturer's profile shifts decisively from playmate/storyteller (Phases 1-2) toward explainer, discourse coach, and subject-matter professor: 'the nurturer plays with us less and less, and explains life to us more and more.' Ideal higher-level nurturer (Leaver's model): a content instructor who does NOT know the grower's language, has never taught their own language, treats the grower like a local student, but sees helping the grower's communication growth as central to the role. Concrete duties in Phase 6 activities: brainstorm discourse lists and needs analysis with the grower; review the grower's recorded attempts (Record-for-Feedback), tracking every needed improvement while negotiating meanings to understand what the grower intended; record the IMPROVED version of the grower's own text — pointedly NOT the nurturer's own spontaneous version, because a version founded on the grower's version stays in the growth zone while a fully spontaneous native version 'may not feed your growth as much'; in B-stages, model the discourse from scratch for the grower to massage and later retell; narrate scripts-of-life in small steps; play both roles in role-plays; accompany the grower into real venues and lead Phase 3-style reminiscing afterward; read the same materials as the grower and discuss them (and the new words) on recording. Selection matters: 'all nurturers are not created equal' for special discourses — pick one who is eloquent in the target discourse, not one who can only produce clichés. What the nurturer must NOT do: translate or use the grower's language; carry on unstructured everyday chat (paying for 'the same sort of unstructured conversation' the grower already has with the house helper and taxi driver is wasted money); listen to the grower read aloud (waste of money); hand over spontaneous native versions detached from the grower's attempts; or let sessions drift out of the 5 special-growth characteristics.
phase6.vocabTargets: Standard GPA target is 7-8 new listening-vocabulary words per hour; for the remedial 100/300-hour push the guide raises it to TEN new words per hour (~3,000 new listening words in 300 hours) — and recommends splicing in earlier-phase activities (e.g., describing a Phase 2 'busy picture') whenever Phase 4-style interviewing alone fails to bring in enough new vocabulary to hold that hourly average. Background scale: Phases 1-5 build a listening vocabulary of over ten thousand words; even 'advanced' growers below US Level 4-5 still have 'a ton of holes' (e.g., dozens of unknown words in a 5-10 minute Cinderella telling; the Level-4 lexical bar includes near-universal native phrases like 'tent pegs'). Tracking is implicit per-hour bookkeeping of new words encountered, with recordings of word discussions used to 'refresh and strengthen those words in your mental listening vocabulary store.'
appIdeas: Needs Analysis wizard: digitize the scoring table — user brainstorms communication situations (with a seeded, culture-tagged suggestion bank), scores frequency (0-5), importance (0-5), and current ability (0 to -10); app auto-ranks targets and spins each high scorer into a ready-made discourse-mastery track

Discourse Track engine: for any chosen situation, generate the canonical 7-stage pipeline (Vocabulary Prelude → A-stage GP-led record/feedback cycles → nurturer-revised recording → B-stage nurturer-led model + own-words retell → Script-of-Life → Role-play → real-world visit + Reminiscing), with stage gating after logged hours (e.g., unlock B after 10-20 hours of A)

Record-for-Feedback workflow: in-app recorder where the grower performs (a toast, a car-fault description, a 'what she said to the beautician' guess); recording goes to the nurturer, who attaches timestamped improvement notes and then records the IMPROVED version of the grower's own text — the app enforces 'improve their version, don't replace it' as the feedback mode

Listening Library with smart replay: every nurturer revision, massaged clip, and word-discussion auto-files into a personal library; spaced-replay scheduling plus event-triggered prompts ('Wedding on Saturday? Re-listen to your toast recordings')

Retell-not-recite mode: after listening to the nurturer's B-stage recording, the app prompts a fresh own-words retelling (recording it for comparison), explicitly blocking verbatim playback during the attempt — operationalizing the 'all retelling tasks in your own words' rule

Massage Player: media player built for 'massaging' — one-tap pause/rewind loops, inline monolingual dictionary lookup, per-clip new-word capture that feeds the vocabulary counter, and a 'flag for nurturer' button for unparseable stretches

Hole-Finding studio: play a wordless film (Chaplin/Mr. Bean/Kelin-style) while the grower narrates live into the mic; pauses and stalls are marked as 'holes'; holes convert into nurturer agenda items and later re-narration attempts measure hole closure

100 Waking Hours dashboard: weekly time tracker splitting hours among the user's configured competing lives (home life, host life #1, host life #2...); visualizes the zero-sum tradeoff and scores progress against the 10%/20% host-life benchmarks with gentle 'expat magnet' nudges

300-Hours-to-a-New-You challenge: a long-horizon progress meter (100 h at low levels, 300 h at higher) counting ONLY sessions meeting the 5 special-growth characteristics (challenge-level input, heavy interaction, ~10 new words/hour, host-world learning, assisted production) via a quick post-session checklist; projects the 'new you' date

Per-hour vocabulary counter: log new listening-vocabulary words per session against the 10-words/hour remedial target; auto-suggest splicing in a Phase 2 busy-picture or Phase 3 world-story activity when the rolling average sags

Phase un-6 re-entry diagnostic: short self-assessment ('Can you follow two host people talking to each other?' etc.) that routes plateaued users back to the right earlier-phase activity sets (Phase 2 Story Building, Phase 3 Scripts-of-Life / World Stories / Reminiscing, Phase 4 interviews) inside the app

Shared-reading club: grower and nurturer mark the same text as read; app schedules a recorded discussion session and harvests the new words discussed into the Listening Library and vocab counter (supports the diglossia mode: spoken-language discussion of written text)

Lifestyle audit + playbook: interactive checklist of the guide's restructurings (host-language office policy, hire-a-host-person, family Phase 1 for kids at 5 h/week, host-language-when-host-present house rule, host TV, social visiting, host-language team meetings, take a host-taught course) with commitments and weekly review

Family/team mode: multi-user spaces so couples, families, and teams progress as growing-participating GROUPS — shared discourse tracks, kids' Phase 1-2 activity sets (engaging-for-a-seven-year-old as the quality bar), and team host-language meeting streaks

Encounter capture for displaced/diaspora contexts: quick-record real encounters (with consent), tag and shelve them for devoted relistening between rare host-people contact windows — 'relive those experiences over and over'

graphics.phaseName: Phase 1: Connecting (The First Hundred Hours) — Picture Set resource ("Phase 1 BW Graphics", drawings by Angela Thomson, Sept 2016 / Feb 2023 edition)
graphics.summary:
This 101-page PDF is the official companion picture set for GPA Phase 1 (Connecting) and Phase 1B meeting plans. It is not a book to read but a kit to manufacture: the introduction ("Phase 1 Resources: Picture Set and Shopping List") instructs the grower to print pages on light cardstock, hand-COLOR key drawings (especially to distinguish the man/woman/boy/girl stick figures that recur across scenes), laminate them, CUT each grid page apart into individual picture cards, and store the pieces in envelopes labeled by meeting plan and game number. Every card is coded on the back (e.g. "1.3.5" = Phase 1, Meeting plan 3, Activity 5) so a mixed-up kit can be re-sorted. Some pages must be photocopied twice (two identical sets for matching/info-gap games, the second set printed on a contrasting cardstock color), and a few full-page scenes (a house facade, a landscape, a two-copy "town" scene reflecting post-Soviet Central Asian city life) are assembled from parts with glue or tape. The intro explicitly says real manipulable objects are preferred whenever possible; the pictures fill gaps and, crucially, serve as the visual track when the grower re-listens to session audio recordings alone at home.

The body of the PDF falls into two broad types. Type 1 is "Lexicarry-like" communication strips (pages 3-6 and similar): comic-strip frames (6 per page, labeled 1A, 1B, 1C, 2A...) showing two or three people in social situations — peers greeting, a young man greeting an elder with a cane, question/answer exchanges, a confused listener with a foreign-script speech bubble and "???" thought bubble, offering tea, giving a gift — all with EMPTY speech bubbles (a "?" marks who is asking). These teach ~60 language functions/survival expressions: the nurturer says what each character might be saying, then asks "Who is saying 'May I help you?'... who is saying 'I'm sorry'?" and the grower responds by POINTING, not speaking. Type 2 is vocabulary/concept grids: pages of 6, 9, 12, 25, or 48 cells, one referent per cell, each page footer-labeled with its exact slot in the curriculum (e.g. "Phase 1, Meeting plan 3, Game 1, parts of the house"). Sampled domains: parts of the house with arrows pointing at wall/floor/ceiling/corner (p20); kitchen containers — wok, pot, kettle, cutting board, pitcher (p21); creatures — camel, sheep, bee, tiger, goat, rabbit, duck, goose, snake, lizard, chicken, pig (p22); hand-action verbs — grasping pencils, tipping a cup (p23); a large house facade plus bed/sofa furniture for a place-the-furniture game (p24); 25 emotion faces with an answer key (happy, sad, angry, frightened, surprised, embarrassed, worried, kind, cruel, sly, stubborn, stern, jolly, grieving, sleepy, exhausted, thirsty, hungry, cold, hot, sick, injured, messy, dirty, bored) (p50); stick figures showing those states for a "Which one is...?" pointing game (p51); kinship+emotion combination cards — e.g. surprised mother with crying son (p52-53); "Power Phrases" captioned strips teaching the grower's own survival questions: "What's he doing? / What am I doing? / What are you doing? / What are they doing? / What's this? It's a flower / I don't know / What's that? It's an elephant / Who's he?" (p53-54); a 48-cell emotions-and-nationalities set marked "Set #2" for duplicate-deck matching games (p85); a cut-and-assemble landscape with mountain, trees, climbing figures, motion arrows, and geometric shapes for spatial/motion language (p86, Phase 1B); abstract quantifier diagrams — piles of circles, dashed groupings, > and < signs, crossed-out sets — keyed to "a few, many, most of, some, all, more than, less than, a little of, any, each one, every, someone, everyone, no one, nothing, the last, the most, more, the next" (p87-88); and eight room-interior scenes (bedroom, balcony with clothesline, study, stairwell, bathroom, hallway, kitchen, living room) for "rooms in the house" (p89).

The pedagogical logic visible throughout: pictures exist so that meaning is established by SHOWING, never by translation; the grower's job in Phase 1 is to point, choose, arrange, and act — comprehension massively precedes production. The set also encodes the curriculum's progression: early meeting plans (3-4) cover concrete nouns and household objects; mid plans (11) add emotions, kinship, and the grower's first productive "power" questions; later plans (23, 27, 28) layer abstractions like nationalities, quantifiers, and composite scenes. The author notes drawings should be adapted to the local culture and that learners should freely add, delete, and modify cards as their own meeting plans diverge from the samples.
graphics.hours: 0–100 hours (Phase 1 "Connecting"); a few pages extend into Phase 1B (a supplementary continuation of the first hundred hours, e.g. p86 "Phase 1B Meeting plan 11 Game 5")
goals: Build a large comprehension vocabulary of concrete, here-and-now words (objects, animals, food, house parts, rooms, clothing, body, actions, emotions, kinship, numbers, quantities) recognized by sight and sound

Learn ~60 common language functions / survival expressions (greetings by age and status, apologizing, offering, thanking, asking what/who/where) via Lexicarry-style picture strips — recognition first, production soon after
Equip the grower with 'Power Phrases' — the survival questions (What's this? What's that? What are you doing? Who's he? I don't know) that let the grower elicit language from any host person
Train comprehension through physical response: pointing at cards, picking up cards, arranging cards and objects per the nurturer's instructions, with zero pressure to speak
Create reusable review media: the same picture sheets viewed while replaying the session's audio recording at home
Cover the semantic domains of daily life so the grower can begin connecting with host people in real situations (homes, market amounts, family, feelings, nationalities)
keyPrinciples: Comprehension before production — the grower responds by pointing/acting, not speaking; speech emerges later without pressure
No translation ever — meaning is grounded in pictures, real objects, and acted situations (real manipulable objects preferred over pictures whenever possible)
Here-and-now communication — all vocabulary is concrete and present in the room as a card, toy, or object
Massive listening with recycling — every session is audio-recorded; cards are re-used across many meeting plans for review, so items are met repeatedly in new combinations

Language functions vary by social context — the Lexicarry intro stresses there is no single sentence per function; choice depends on relative social standing, familiarity, audience, and circumstances (later explored via doll/puppet role-play, e.g. young-to-elder greetings)
