Learner as 'grower' who owns the kit — add, delete, modify, and culturally adapt the drawings; the town scene is Central Asian and should be redrawn for other regions
Combinatorial growth — later games cross domains (kinship x emotion, emotion x nationality, objects x quantifiers) so known words multiply into sentences
Logical ordering over rigid ordering — e.g. don't do 'asking prices' or 'asking time' functions until numbers are understood (Meeting plan 12+)

activities.name: Lexicarry-like function strips (survival expressions)
activities.description: Comic-strip frames with empty speech bubbles show social situations: two peers greeting and parting (frames 1A-1C), a young man greeting an elderly man with a cane (2A-2D), man/woman/child/grandmother question-answer pairs (3A-3D), a listener hearing incomprehensible speech (foreign-script bubble + '???' thought bubble, frame 4), asking about a flower / an unknown object / a distant elephant (5A-5D), a grandmother offering tea (6), giving a wrapped gift (7). Mechanic: the nurturer first tells the grower what each character might be saying in each frame; then quizzes — 'Who is saying "May I help you?" Who is saying "I'm sorry"?' — and the grower POINTS to the right bubble/person. Within minutes the grower recognizes ~10 new survival expressions per sitting; production follows naturally soon after. In later passes, multiple alternative utterances per bubble are discussed and role-played with dolls/puppets to explore register (younger-to-elder vs peer-to-peer).
activities.materials: Pages 4-6 ff.: 6 frames per page, ~60 functions total; optionally the commercial Lexicarry book or hand-drawn local equivalents; dolls/puppets for role-play variants
activities.timing: Spread across the first month and beyond; flexible order except numbered sequences done together; price/time functions deferred until after numbers (Meeting plan 12+)

activities.name: Vocabulary grid games / cut-apart picture cards ('Dirty Dozen'-style comprehension sets)
activities.description: Each grid page (6-12 cells, one drawing per cell) is cut into individual cards for one game of one meeting plan, e.g. 'Meeting plan 3, Game 1, parts of the house': door, window, wall, floor, ceiling, corner (arrows in the drawing disambiguate which feature is meant), whiteboard, ceiling lamp, framed picture, radiator, clock, coat hooks. Mechanic: nurturer lays out a small set of new cards, names each while pointing; then issues comprehension commands — 'Show me the window... point to the corner... where is the clock?' — grower points/picks up. New cards are mixed with previously learned cards and with real objects/toys; commands grow more complex (combine with location words, adjectives, two-step instructions). Other sampled sets: kitchen containers (wok, pot, cutting board+knife, stove, kettle, frying pan, lid, pitcher, dish set — Meeting plan 3 Game 3) and twelve creatures (camel, sheep, bee, tiger, goat, rabbit, duck, goose, snake, lizard, chicken, pig — Meeting plan 3 Game 3).
activities.materials: Dozens of grid pages keyed to meeting plans; cardstock, lamination, scissors; envelopes labeled by Meeting Plan + Game #; back-of-card codes like 1.3.5; sorting baskets by category (furniture/home, people, food, dishes, adjectives, animals, nature, tools, personal care)
activities.timing: Core mechanic of nearly every Phase 1 session from Meeting plan 1 onward; each game ~5-15 minutes inside a session, then recycled for review in later plans

activities.name: Action/verb picture commands
activities.description: Cards showing hands performing actions (a fist grasping a bundle of pencils; a finger tipping over a cup — Meeting plan 3, Game 6) anchor verbs. The nurturer demonstrates the action with real objects while saying the verb, then commands the grower to perform actions ('grab the pencils', 'knock over the cup') or to point to the card matching a spoken action. Combines with object cards so verbs and nouns recombine.
activities.materials: Verb-action cards plus the real props from the shopping list (pencils, cups, toy tools, etc.)
activities.timing: From early meeting plans onward; verbs accumulate alongside nouns

activities.name: House assembly and furniture placement
activities.description: A full-page two-storey house facade (Meeting plan 4, Game 1) plus separate furniture cards (bed, sofa, etc.). The grower follows spoken instructions to place furniture pictures onto/into the house ('put the bed upstairs', 'the sofa is next to the door'), exercising rooms, furniture nouns, and spatial prepositions. A toy dollhouse with furniture and a doll family is the preferred real-object version (per the shopping list). The companion page 89 (Meeting plan 28, Game 4, 'rooms in the house') provides eight detailed room interiors — bedroom, balcony with clothesline, study with computer and bookshelf, stairwell with numbered apartment doors, bathroom, entry hall with coat rack and mirror, kitchen, living room — for naming rooms and the objects within each scene ('point to the toilet... which room has the computer?').
activities.materials: House facade page (assembled with glue/tape), furniture cards, room-scene cards, or a real toy dollhouse with furniture and doll family
activities.timing: Meeting plan 4 (house intro) through Meeting plan 28 (rooms revisited in depth) — domains spiral back at higher complexity

activities.name: Emotions: faces grid + 'Which one is...?' stick figures
activities.description: A 5x5 grid of 25 cartoon faces (Meeting plan 11, Game 2) covers happy, sad, angry, frightened, surprised, embarrassed/ashamed, worried, kind, cruel/evil, sly/cunning, mean/stubborn, stern/strict, jolly/laughing, upset/grieving, sleepy, exhausted, thirsty, hungry, cold, hot, sick, hurt/injured, messy, dirty, bored (a printed answer key gives the suggested meanings reading order). Nurturer points and names with dramatic voice/face acting, then quizzes: grower points to the named emotion. Game 3 ('Which One Is...?') re-presents the same states on full-body stick figures whose torso patterns encode person type — black triangle = man, black dress = woman, striped shirt = boy, polka-dot dress = girl (the intro says to colorize these for even easier discrimination) — so the nurturer can ask compound questions: 'Which one is the thirsty woman? Show me the angry man.'
activities.materials: Page 50 faces grid (also reprinted in the 48-cell Set #2 on p85), page 51 stick-figure grid; suggested-meaning keys printed under the grids for the nurturer/grower's reference
activities.timing: Meeting plan 11; emotion cards then recycle constantly in later kinship and nationality games

activities.name: Kinship + Emotion combination cards
activities.description: Two pages (Meeting plan 11, Games 4&5) show two- and three-person stick-figure groupings where each person displays a distinct emotion/state: hungry mother with screaming daughter, sad father with hot sweating son, surprised husband with weeping wife, smiling mother with sleepy son, a whole family where the daughter is angry and the parents argue. Mechanic: nurturer describes a card in a full sentence ('The mother is hungry and the daughter is angry — which picture?') and the grower points; this forces parsing of two noun phrases plus two predicates — the first real sentence-level comprehension. Reversed later for early production: nurturer points, grower attempts the description.
activities.materials: Pages 52-53: 18 combination cards; relies on the gender/age torso-pattern code established in Game 3
activities.timing: Meeting plan 11, Games 4 and 5, immediately after emotions and kinship terms are separately known

activities.name: Power Phrases (the grower's survival questions)
activities.description: Captioned picture strips (Meeting plan 11, Game 6) teach the eight question-answer frames the grower will use as 'power tools' to keep learning outside sessions: 1) What's he doing? He is ____ (two boys watch a third do a headstand); 2) What am I doing? You are ____ (the headstander asks); 3) What are you doing? I'm ____; 4) What are they doing? They are ____ (two headstanders); 5) What's this? It's a flower; 6) What's this? I don't know (man shrugging at an unidentifiable object); 7) What's that? It's an elephant (distant referent — teaching this/that distance contrast); 8) Who's he? He's ____. Mechanic: nurturer plays both bubble roles, grower first points to who-says-what, then begins producing the questions themselves — these are deliberately among the grower's first spoken sentences because they unlock everything else.
activities.materials: Pages 53-54: 8 numbered frames with printed caption key; props (flower, toy elephant) echo the Lexicarry 5A-5D frames
activities.timing: Meeting plan 11, Game 6 — roughly a third of the way through Phase 1, once enough vocabulary exists for answers to be meaningful

activities.name: Info-gap / matching games with duplicate sets (emotions & nationalities)
activities.description: Page 85 (Meeting plan 23, Games 4&5, marked 'Set #2') is a 48-cell grid: 24 emotion faces plus 24 faces of people in distinctive national/ethnic dress (suit-and-tie businessman, Arab man in keffiyeh, cowboy, conical-hat farmer, Canadian in toque, Mexican in sombrero, woman in niqab, Russian woman in headscarf, Indian woman in dupatta, African man and woman, Central Asian hats, etc.). The intro explains the mechanic: print the second set on contrasting cardstock; one player describes a card the other can't see ('the surprised one', 'the woman from India'), the partner finds its twin — a true information-gap task where language alone carries the information. Also playable as memory/pairs and as comprehension pointing.
activities.materials: Two identical copies of the page on different-colored cardstock, cut into 96 cards total
activities.timing: Meeting plan 23 — later Phase 1, when the grower can produce short descriptive phrases

activities.name: Amounts and quantifiers (abstract concept cards)
activities.description: Pages 87-88 (Meeting plan 27, Game 5) teach quantifier vocabulary with purely diagrammatic cards: a few small circles ('a few/not much'), a big heap ('many/a lot'), dashed loop around most of a group ('most of'), '>' and '<' between piles ('more than/less than'), a sack with a small spilled pile ('a little of'), a jar and spoon, single circled item in a row ('one of them'), crossed-out person ('no one'), crossed-out set ('nothing'), diminishing trail of circles ending in a tiny one ('the last/final'), arrow to a next circle ('the next'), every-item-arrowed rows ('each one/every'), stick-figure crowds with one circled ('someone') or all bracketed ('everyone'). A printed key lists all ~21 meanings. Mechanic: nurturer pairs the diagrams with real demonstrations using seeds, candies, or pebbles from the shopping list (pour out a lot, a few, take some of them), then quizzes by pointing; diagrams later combine with any noun cards ('show me many sheep... a few cups').
activities.materials: 21 abstract diagram cards; bulk physical manipulables — seeds, small candies, pebbles, small plastic bags (explicitly on the shopping list)
activities.timing: Meeting plan 27 — near the end of Phase 1, bridging from concrete to relational/abstract meaning

activities.name: Composite scene assembly and narration (landscape, town, rooms)
activities.description: Full-page scenes are assembled from cut parts (glue/tape per the intro): page 86 (Phase 1B, Meeting plan 11, Game 5) is a landscape kit — large and small pine trees, a man and a girl, a mountain with figures climbing up and sliding down its slopes, dashed and solid path lines, double-headed arrows (back and forth, zigzag), and basic shapes (filled circle, circle, triangle, square) — used for motion verbs, directions, paths, sizes, and shapes: the nurturer moves a figure along the mountain while narrating ('he climbs up... she runs down... between the trees'), then directs the grower to move pieces. The colored 'town' scene (two identical copies required) similarly supports describe-and-find and barrier games about city life; the A3 folder stores these large scenes.
activities.materials: Landscape parts page, town scene (x2, identically colored), regional map, world map; A3 pocket folder for storage
activities.timing: Phase 1B and review periods; scenes also accompany audio-recording re-listening at home

activities.name: Audio-recording review with picture sheets
activities.description: The intro states some pictures are intended specifically for use 'when reviewing the meeting plan on your own, with an audio-recording, at which time the actual objects may not be available.' Mechanic: every session segment is recorded on the spot; at home the grower replays the recording while looking at the corresponding (uncut) picture page, re-experiencing the comprehension activity — pointing along — without the nurturer. This is the grower's 'personal re-living time' (the intro's basket workflow even sequences objects back through a basket for re-living before re-sorting).
activities.materials: Audio recorder/phone; master (uncut) copies of every picture page kept as the review track; envelope/code system so recordings and pages stay aligned per meeting plan
activities.timing: Daily, between sessions, throughout all 100 hours — roughly matching or exceeding live session time

graphics.sessionStructure: Inferred from the resource's organization (the cards themselves are indexed 'Phase 1, Meeting plan N, Game M'): Phase 1 consists of ~30 numbered 'meeting plans' (sampled pages reference plans 3, 4, 11, 12, 23, 27, 28), each one driving a session of roughly 2 hours with the nurturer, plus solo recording-review afterward. A session is built from several short 'Games' (Game 1, Game 2... Game 6 within a single plan), each a 5-15 minute comprehension activity with its own envelope of picture cards and/or real objects: typically (1) warm-up review of prior cards via rapid pointing commands, (2) introduction of 1-3 new card sets — nurturer names and points, grower points in response, sets mixed and shuffled as accuracy grows, (3) combination games crossing new and old domains (kinship+emotion, quantity+object), (4) a Lexicarry-strip or Power-Phrase segment for social expressions, and (5) recording of key segments for home review. The nurturer speaks only the target language during activities (the host language carries 100% of the activity); logistics may fall outside that frame. Preparation workflow is explicit: the night before, the nurturer/grower pulls the needed envelopes and objects into a staging basket so each game starts instantly. After the session the grower re-lives the activities with the audio recording and master picture sheets, then re-sorts materials into category baskets.
materials: The 101-page picture set itself: grid pages of 6/9/12/25/48 line drawings, cut into individual laminated cards, coded on the back (phase.plan.activity, e.g. 1.3.5), stored in labeled envelopes and sorted baskets
Lexicarry book or the included Lexicarry-like strips (~60 language functions, empty speech bubbles)
Full-page composite scenes: house facade, landscape kit, 'town' scene (two identically-colored copies) reflecting local city life, room interiors

Shopping list of real props: toy farm/wild animals and insects, doll family of varied ages/sexes, dollhouse with furniture, toy money, toy cars, toy fruits/vegetables/food, legos/duplos, real or toy tools (hammer, saw, pliers, scissors, wrench, nails, screws, wire, string), matches, seeds, small colored candies, small plastic bags, plain and colored paper, paper clips, thumbtacks, glue, pencils/pens/markers/crayons, world and regional maps, calendar, clock, comb/brush/toothbrush/toothpaste/soap, bowls/bottles/boxes/baskets, clothing items (hat, trousers, shirt, dress, skirt, sunglasses, shoes), plates/pots/pans/tray, kitchen utensils, rocks, pebbles, dirt, sand, flowers, grass, leaves, sticks, imitation flowers
Cardstock (light-colored, plus a contrasting shade for second info-gap sets), laminator, scissors, envelopes, stackable labeled sorting baskets, A3 pocket folder for large scenes
Audio recorder for session recording and home review
Coloring supplies — color is functionally important (distinguishes man/woman/boy/girl figures; both town-scene copies must be colored identically)
milestones: Recognizes by ear and can point to hundreds of pictured referents across the kit's domains: house parts, rooms, furniture, kitchen items, animals, food, clothing, tools, body, people types, nature items
Recognizes ~60 pictured social-situation expressions (greetings by status, apologies, offers, thanks) and uses many of them in real encounters

Comprehends and responds physically to multi-element instructions combining nouns, verbs, adjectives, spatial prepositions, kinship terms, emotions, and quantifiers ('put the angry boy next to the small house')
Distinguishes socially-conditioned variants (greeting an elder vs a peer) at recognition level via the strip sequences
Produces the eight Power-Phrase survival questions (What's this/that? What is he/are you/are they doing? Who's he? I don't know) to elicit language independently
Understands the ~21 quantifier/amount expressions (all, some, many, a few, more/less than, each, every, no one, nothing, the last, the next...) demonstrated with diagrams and loose objects
Can play describe-and-find info-gap games where language alone identifies one card among 48 (late Phase 1, Meeting plan 23+)
Has completed ~30 meeting plans and built a personal, culturally-adapted, coded card kit plus an audio archive used for daily re-living/review
graphics.nurturerRole: The nurturer (host-language speaker, not a 'teacher') drives every activity in the target language only: laying out card sets, naming each picture while pointing with expressive voice and gesture, acting out emotions with face and body, telling what each Lexicarry character 'is saying', issuing ever-richer pointing/manipulation commands, shuffling known and new cards to calibrate difficulty, role-playing register differences with dolls/puppets, demonstrating quantifiers with piles of seeds and candy, and recording segments for the grower's home review. The nurturer must NOT translate into the grower's language, must NOT require or pressure the grower to speak (pointing is the expected response mode for new material), must NOT turn sessions into grammar explanation, and should not insist on a single 'correct' sentence per function — the materials explicitly warn that fulfilling a social function has many context-dependent variants. The grower, meanwhile, owns and maintains the kit (printing, coloring, cutting, coding, adapting drawings to local culture) and directs which domains matter most for their survival needs.
graphics.vocabTargets: The picture set itself implies the inventory: ~30 meeting plans x several games x 6-12 items per game plus real-object vocabulary, consistent with the standard GPA Phase 1 target of roughly 750-1,000 comprehension words plus ~60 functional expressions by hour 100. Tracking is built into the physical system: every card is coded to its meeting plan/activity (1.N.M), envelopes are labeled per plan and game, and the intro tells learners to 'add, delete, and modify the drawings' as their personal vocabulary list diverges — i.e., the card collection IS the living vocabulary record, and the audio recordings indexed to the same codes provide the review log.
terminology: Grower / Growing Participator (GP) — the learner, framed as someone growing into a host community rather than studying a subject
Nurturer — the host-language speaker who feeds comprehensible experience to the grower (not a 'teacher')
Meeting plan — one session's lesson plan; Phase 1 has a numbered sequence (~30), and every picture page is indexed to one (e.g. 'Phase 1, Meeting plan 11')
Game — a discrete activity within a meeting plan (e.g. 'Game 4&5, Kinship+Emotion'); the unit each envelope of cards serves
Lexicarry / Lexicarry-like pictures — comic strips with empty speech bubbles depicting ~60 language functions; nurturer voices them, grower points
Power Phrases — the grower's survival questions (What's this?, What are you doing?, Who's he?...) — their 'power tools' for self-directed learning
Info-gap — paired activities where one party describes a card the other must find; requires duplicate card sets on contrasting cardstock
Phase 1B — a supplementary continuation block after the core hundred hours, with its own meeting plans using the same picture kit
Re-living time — the grower's solo review: replaying session audio while viewing the same pictures/objects
Host world — the target-language community the grower is connecting into; materials must be culturally adapted to it (the town scene is post-Soviet Central Asian and meant to be redrawn elsewhere)
appIdeas: Digital picture-card grid engine: reproduce each meeting-plan game as an on-screen grid of 6-48 images (the PDF's own layouts map 1:1 to CSS grids). The app plays the nurturer's audio (pre-recorded native speaker or live partner) naming an item; the grower taps the matching image — instant feedback, items shuffled each round, exactly replicating the point-at-the-card comprehension mechanic with zero translation and zero text

Curriculum indexing identical to the card codes: organize all content as Phase > Meeting Plan > Game (1.3.5), so the app mirrors the envelope/basket system; a 'review basket' queue automatically resurfaces cards from earlier plans mixed into current sessions (spaced repetition disguised as the kit's natural recycling)

Progressive difficulty mixing: start a new set with 3-4 images, then auto-mix mastered cards from other domains into larger grids, and graduate to compound spoken prompts ('the thirsty woman', 'the angry mother and the crying son') requiring multi-feature parsing — directly digitizing the Kinship+Emotion and 'Which One Is...?' games

Lexicarry strip player: show the comic frames with empty bubbles; audio plays an utterance and the grower taps the character/bubble who would say it ('Who is saying I'm sorry?'). Later modes attach multiple register variants per bubble (elder vs peer) and let the grower record themselves into the bubble

Power Phrases trainer with recording: the eight captioned frames become a speak-back module — app shows frame, plays the question, grower records their own production of 'What's this?' etc.; these unlock a 'wild card' camera feature for asking 'What's this?' about real-world photos with their nurturer asynchronously

Drag-and-drop scene assembly: digitize the house facade + furniture and the landscape kit as draggable sprites; audio instructs 'put the bed upstairs', 'move the boy up the mountain', and the app checks placement — replicating the glue-and-tape composite scenes and TPR object manipulation

Info-gap multiplayer mode: two devices each show the 48-card emotions & nationalities deck; one player hears/describes a target card, the other taps to find it — a true digital barrier game; solo fallback uses recorded descriptions

Quantifier diagram module: animate the amounts diagrams (piles growing/shrinking, dashed loops drawing themselves, items crossing out) synced to audio of 'many / a few / none / each one' — animation can demonstrate quantity semantics even better than static cards, then quiz with 'show me MANY sheep' applied to any noun's image multiplied on screen

Session recorder + re-living mode: record live nurturer sessions inside the app, time-stamped against the card grids in play; replay mode shows the same grids highlighting along with the audio — digitizing the audio-plus-master-sheets home review that the PDF explicitly designs for

Custom card authoring: since the intro mandates adapting/adding/deleting drawings per culture and per learner's actual sessions, let growers photograph real local objects or upload images to create their own coded cards that flow into the same game engines; color-tagging replaces the colored-pencil step (e.g. consistent colors for man/woman/boy/girl figures)

Emotion face mode using the printed answer keys: the PDF's suggested-meaning keys (25 emotions; 21 quantifiers) provide ready ground-truth labels for seeding the app's content database in any target language — store the key as nurturer-facing metadata, never shown as translation to the grower

Nurturer dashboard: a guided script per game telling an untrained native speaker exactly what to do ('name each picture while pointing... now ask: where is the camel?'), since GPA nurturers are ordinary speakers, not teachers — the app becomes the meeting-plan book they never have to read

website.overview: The Growing Participator Approach (GPA) is an alternative paradigm for second-language acquisition created by Greg Thomson. Its central reframe: the goal is not to "learn a language" but to grow as a participant in the life of a host community — "It's a life to be lived, not a language to be learned." Learners are called "growing participators" (GPs), not students; the native speakers who help them are "nurturers" (early phases) and "mentors" (later phases), most often not career teachers. Theoretically GPA draws on Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory (as interpreted by James Wertsch): mental life is socially mediated, and the Zone of Proximal Development is relabeled the "Growth Zone" — activities must be hard enough to stretch but not so hard they frustrate (the site compares it to keeping an engine at the right RPMs on a tachometer). Core metaphors: incomprehensible foreign speech is a "wall of noise" that gradually becomes a window into hearts and minds; language and culture are one inseparable "languaculture," so GPs grow into a "languacultural world" hosted by "host people"; the GP becomes "a new me" in the experience of host people, accepting a real loss of status ("radically less competent" than in the home world) whose weakness empowers hosts to give. Growth happens through two interlocking tracks: "special-growth participation" (designed activities with a hired nurturer, ~20-25 hrs/week) and "lifestyle participation" (ordinary immersion in host life), with the balance shifting from nearly all special-growth in Phase 1 to nearly all lifestyle by Phase 6. The practical engine is the Six-Phase Programme (SPP): an idealized ~1,500-hour roadmap of special-growth activities (plus ~400 lifestyle hours by end of Phase 5). Phase boundaries are defined relationally — by how host people experience the GP ("special connection to us," "probably somebody," a knowable person, a co-member) — not by internal linguistic milestones. The overarching cognitive principle is comprehension before production: massive structured listening builds the foundation, and the GP begins producing in each phase what they could only comprehend in the previous one.
philosophy: Language is life, not knowledge: 'It's a life to be lived, not a language to be learned.' Words don't amount to much apart from the life they are woven together with and understood through; language and culture form one inseparable 'languaculture.'

Participation over learning/acquisition: the goal is ever-deepening participation in a host community, so the person is a 'growing participator,' the helper a 'nurturer' (later 'mentor'), and progress is measured by how host people experience the GP, not by grammar mastered.

Comprehension before production: listening comprehension is the fundamental cognitive process; it develops through experience and provides the foundation for speech. GPs respond non-verbally first (pointing, acting, manipulating objects) and only later produce what they previously understood.

The Growth Zone (Vygotsky's ZPD relabeled): every activity should sit at the optimal challenge level — stretching but not frustrating — like keeping an engine at the right RPMs; growth is socially mediated through a more capable host person.

Relationships are the medium of growth: initial growth flows through one or a few nurturer relationships, expanding to wide networks; Phase 4's 'Deep-Life Conversations' are described as the 'sacred endeavor' of heart-to-heart connection.

Two participation tracks that trade places over time: 'special-growth participation' (designed, nurturer-led, ~20-25 hrs/week) dominates early phases; 'lifestyle participation' (ordinary immersion — streets, shops, homes, communities of practice) steadily takes over until Phase 6 growth is almost entirely lifestyle-based.

Identity transformation and embraced weakness: the GP becomes 'a new me' in the host world, accepting a loss of status that is never fully overcome; being 'radically less competent' is reframed as empowering host people to nurture.

Time-on-task realism: roughly 1,500 hours of special-growth activities plus ~400 lifestyle hours through Phase 5; activities must change radically month to month — 'what we do with a nurturer in month one will be radically different from what we do in month three or month seven.'
Plateaus are normal: extended periods where growth is imperceptible to observers are an expected part of the journey, addressed by changing activities rather than quitting.

Anti-classroom stance: nurturers are ordinary host friends, not career teachers; no textbooks required — locally bought objects, pictures, a notebook, and a recording device carry the whole programme.

sixPhases.name: Phase 1: Connecting (Here-and-Now Phase)
sixPhases.hours: ~100 hours (80-120 hrs over ~5 weeks at 20-25 hrs/week)
sixPhases.description: Goal: form an embryonic relationship in which host people feel the GP has a 'special connection to us,' while building a comprehension vocabulary of ~800-900+ words — without being required to speak. Mechanics: structured 'Here-and-Now Play.' The nurturer arranges real objects, toys, dolls, foods, plastic dishes, tools, colored paper, and printed picture sheets (a 'Phase 1 Graphics Packet' of action/location illustrations) on the table. For roughly the first 30 hours the nurturer gives instructions and asks questions in the host language ('Pick up the red cup,' 'Where is the dog?' 'Put the spoon under the plate') and the GP responds entirely non-verbally — pointing, grabbing, moving, acting out (TPR-style). Touching, holding, and moving objects gives stronger encounters with new words than pictures alone. New words are introduced in small comprehensible sets, recycled and recombined; sound-discrimination games train the GP to hear meaningful contrasts in word forms. The remaining ~70 hours layer in first verbal interaction activities ('Dirty Dozen'-style: a dozen survival phrases practiced until automatic) while comprehension games continue. The nurturer makes audio recordings of each session's vocabulary in instruction form; one recording style omits the correct response so the GP can replay it later and respond physically as self-review. Tools: Lexicarry picture book, dolls, toys, local objects, recordings device. Two orientations (1A before starting, 1B as speech begins) prepare GP and nurturer for their roles. Lifestyle track: mostly observational exposure (shopping, transport) while the nurturer scouts future relationships.

sixPhases.name: Phase 2: Emerging (Story-Building Phase)
sixPhases.description: Goal: the GP 'emerges' as a person — host people 'catch glimpses of your personality' and sense the GP is 'probably somebody'; ~1,200+ new words gained; speech moves from single utterances to connected sequences forming a story. Mechanics: first ~50 hours focus on 'loosening the tongue' — the GP begins speaking using the large comprehension base from Phase 1, supported by wordless picture stories. Core activity is Story-Building with Pictures: the nurturer takes a wordless picture book, a 'busy picture' (a detailed scene with many people doing things), or a picture series showing a familiar process (making tea, going to the doctor) and tells a simple story panel by panel while pointing; the GP follows, answers questions, then helps guide the story and asks for clarification, gradually retelling parts. Next 50-80 hours: nurturer-created stories from wordless books with growing GP co-narration. Final ~20 hours: collaborative autobiographical picture stories — the GP and nurturer build the GP's own life story with photos/drawings, giving the GP personally meaningful narrative language. Rhythm/pronunciation practice continues; sessions are recorded for replay. Lifestyle track: lots of public activities — streets, technology, possibly homes — and spotting people for deeper Phase 3 relationships. Materials: wordless picture stories, busy pictures, process picture series, out-of-print storybooks found online.

sixPhases.name: Phase 3: Becoming Knowable (Shared Story Phase)
sixPhases.description: Goal: become a 'knowable' person — host people can genuinely get to know the GP, who can now converse on diverse topics like a (simple) adult; ~2,000+ words gained. Mechanics: the engine is 'Stuff-We-Both-Know Conversations' — extended talk where shared context guarantees comprehensibility. Three concrete activity types: (1) detailed descriptions of familiar daily activities (the nurturer narrates, the GP follows and retells, building expository/explanatory discourse, not just narrative); (2) already-familiar stories — fairy tales, folk tales, religious/Old Testament narratives, biographies, 'bridge stories' known across cultures — where the GP knows the plot but not the host-language wording, so the nurturer's telling is comprehensible yet stretching; the GP then retells and the nurturer 'massages' the retelling (re-expressing it in better host-language form for the GP to absorb and re-record); (3) reminiscences of shared experiences — nurturer and GP do something together (an outing, cooking) and then talk about it repeatedly. Wordless video (Tom & Jerry, Mr. Bean, max7.org animations) serves the same shared-context function: watch together, nurturer narrates, GP retells. Recordings of nurturer tellings and massaged retellings become listening-review material. Lifestyle track: maximize public activities and cultivate individual host relationships; group settings are explicitly flagged as 'not fruitful' yet.

sixPhases.name: Phase 4: Deep Personal Relationships (Deep Life Sharing)
sixPhases.description: Goal: form genuinely deep relationships — host people come to know the GP well and treat them as a 'co-member'; ~3,000+ words gained; the GP handles everyday conversation but still struggles with complex stories and abstract talk. Mechanics: the centerpiece is 'Deep-Life Conversations' — systematic heart-to-heart sharing with nurturers and a widening circle. Concretely: ethnographic interviewing about everyday host life (the GP asks structured questions about how hosts live, celebrate, work, raise children); exploration of host people's life histories through guided discussion; and reciprocal sharing where the GP tells their own life story and background, deepening mutual knownness. 'Walk-of-Life Conversations' prepare the GP for specific occupational/social roles by talking through those domains with insiders. 'Record-Yourself-for-Feedback': the GP records their own extended speech; the mentor reviews it and helps identify where speech and behavior differ from host norms, then the GP re-records improved versions. For spiritually motivated GPs the site mentions comparative-belief discussion via chronological storytelling. Materials are minimal by design: 'a notebook and your recording device are all it takes.' The phase motto: learn the host world broadly and deeply by learning individual lives broadly and deeply. Lifestyle track: participate in nearly all kinds of public activities, deepen and multiply relationships, scout communities of practice to join — while accepting that in host group settings the GP still 'can't fully participate and misses a lot.'

sixPhases.name: Phase 5: Widening Understanding (Native-to-Native Discourse Phase)
sixPhases.description: Goal: cross the final comprehension barrier — understanding host people talking among themselves (not slowed-down foreigner talk); become a 'reasonable co-member' though still obviously foreign; recognition vocabulary grows toward ~10,000 items (speaking vocabulary remains much smaller). Mechanics: native-to-native discourse study. The GP (now with a 'mentor' rather than nurturer) collects authentic insider speech: TV programs, movies, radio talk shows, campfire stories, speeches, sermons, songs, novels, school textbooks — or, for unwritten/minority languages, extensive recordings the GP makes of host people conversing in varied natural settings, including work-role-specific discourse. The GP and mentor then work through these recordings together: listening repeatedly, pausing, with the mentor explaining unknown vocabulary, idioms, cultural references, and register; the GP studies the differences between formal and informal styles and the socially appropriate ways to perform functions (requesting, refusing, joking, condoling). Occupational apprenticeship-style participation connects this to real roles. By phase end the GP also joins at least one 'community of practice' (workplace group, club, recurring gathering). Lifestyle track expands to ~10+ hrs/week on top of special-growth sessions; cumulative totals reach ~1,500 special-growth + ~400 lifestyle hours.

sixPhases.name: Phase 6: Ever Participating, Ever Growing (Self-Sustaining Growth)
sixPhases.description: Goal: self-sustaining growth — the GP no longer needs designed sessions because ordinary life now does what special-growth activities once did. Mechanics: heavy lifestyle participation in host life with natural comprehension; deep membership in communities of practice — 'networks of relationships with native speakers within which I can grow in my language abilities.' Hosts increasingly treat the GP as 'more or less one of us.' Growth strategies become self-directed: noticing gaps, asking insiders, occasionally returning to recording/feedback techniques. Familiarity with the languaculture 'will continue to steadily grow for many years' — the phase has no end point, embodying the approach's name: ever participating, ever growing.

terminology: Growing Participator (GP) — the person growing into the host community (replaces 'language learner'); 'I can become a new me in the experience of host people'
Nurturer — 'the first host people who help us to start participating'; a hired/committed native speaker (usually not a career teacher) who runs special-growth activities in Phases 1-4
Mentor — the later-phase counterpart of the nurturer, guiding native-to-native discourse study and feedback (Phases 4-6)
Host people / host world — the community being joined; their activities are 'host practices,' their communication 'host speech'
Home-world — 'the people group you grew up among, and that you consider yourself one of,' whose practices you keep even abroad
Languaculture / languacultural world — language and cultural practices as one inseparable whole; the unified world insiders inhabit

Growth Zone — Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development relabeled: the optimal challenge band (stretching, not frustrating) where all activities should sit; compared to keeping an engine at the right RPMs
Wall of noise — incomprehensible foreign speech experienced as 'a wall of meaningless noise, utterly opaque, hiding some rich world of meaning' that gradually becomes a window
Special-growth participation — intentionally designed nurturer-led activities that accelerate growth (~20-25 hrs/week, ~1,500 hours over Phases 1-5)
Lifestyle participation — natural immersion in everyday host life (streets, shops, homes), which gradually replaces special-growth time
Here-and-Now Play — Phase 1 structured play: nurturer speech made comprehensible through objects, pictures, and physical response (comprehension before production / TPR-style)
Story-Building with Pictures — Phase 2 core activity using wordless picture books, busy pictures, and process picture series
Stuff-We-Both-Know Conversations — Phase 3 conversations grounded in shared context: familiar routines, pre-known plots, shared reminiscences
Massaging (a story) — the nurturer re-expresses the GP's retelling in better host-language form for re-absorption and re-recording
Deep-Life Conversations — Phase 4+ heart-to-heart life-history sharing; the 'sacred endeavor' of heart-to-heart connection
Walk-of-Life Conversations — talk that prepares the GP for a specific occupational or social role
Record-Yourself-for-Feedback — GP records extended speech; mentor flags divergences from host norms; GP re-records
Native-to-native discourse — authentic insider-to-insider speech (TV, stories, speeches, songs, textbooks) studied with a mentor in Phase 5
Community of practice — a pre-existing natural group united by shared purpose (workplace, club) that GPs join by Phase 5
Comprehension before production — the SPP is sequenced so the GP produces in each phase what they could only comprehend in the previous phase
Plateau — an extended period in which growth is imperceptible to observers; expected and normal
Practices — 'things I do many times in a similar way,' individually or collectively; shared practices form group identity
Lived story — each person's ongoing experiential narrative (past, present, anticipated future) interwoven with the community's story
Six-Phase Programme (SPP) — Thomson's idealized ~1,500-hour roadmap of special-growth activities guiding a GP into deep community involvement
